document.title: Utah Secondary Earth Science Core Standards

E041BDF0DFE701314B5068A86D17958E.description: Investigate and report how social, economic, and environmental issues affect decisions about human-engineered structures (e.g., dams, homes, bridges, roads).

E0417960DFE701314B4F68A86D17958E.description: Document how scientists use technology to continually improve estimates of when and where natural hazards occur.

E0413310DFE701314B4E68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate and give examples of human activities that can contribute to the frequency and intensity of some natural hazards (e.g., construction that may increase erosion, human causes of wildfires, climate change).

E040EBC0DFE701314B4D68A86D17958E.description: Identify and describe natural hazards that occur locally (e.g., wildfires, landslides, earthquakes, floods, drought) and globally (e.g., volcanoes, tsunamis, hurricanes).

E040A0C0DFE701314B4C68A86D17958E.description: Indicate how natural hazards pose risks to humans.

E0405200DFE701314B4B68A86D17958E.description: Justify the claim that Earth science literacy can help the public make informed choices related to the extraction and use of natural resources.

E03FFFF0DFE701314B4A68A86D17958E.description: Describe the role of scientists in providing data that informs the discussion of Earth resource use.

E03FBA70DFE701314B4968A86D17958E.description: Predict how resource development and use alters Earth systems (e.g., water reservoirs, alternative energy sources, wildlife preserves).

E03F7380DFE701314B4868A86D17958E.description: Research and report on how human populations depend on Earth resources for sustenance and how changing conditions over time have affected these resources (e.g., water pollution, air pollution, increases in population).

E03F2AA0DFE701314B4768A86D17958E.description: Investigate how Earth's resources (e.g., mineral resources, petroleum resources, alternative energy resources, water resources, soil and agricultural resources) are distributed across the state, the country, and the world.

E03EDB30DFE701314B4668A86D17958E.description: Describe how humans depend on Earth's resources.

E03E8420DFE701314B4568A86D17958E.description: Research and report on how scientists study feedback loops to inform the public about Earth's interacting systems.

E03E23C0DFE701314B4468A86D17958E.description: Design and conduct an experiment that investigates how Earth's biosphere, geosphere, atmosphere, or hydrosphere reacts to human-caused change.

E03DC2D0DFE701314B4368A86D17958E.description: Explain how technological advances lead to increased human knowledge (e.g., satellite imaging, deep sea ocean probes, seismic sensors, weather radar systems) and ability to predict how changes affect Earth's systems.

E03D7730DFE701314B4268A86D17958E.description: Explain how Earth's systems are dynamic and continually react to natural and human-caused changes.

E03D3040DFE701314B4168A86D17958E.description: Illustrate how energy flowing and matter cycling within Earth's biosphere, geosphere, atmosphere, and hydrosphere give rise to processes that shape Earth.

E03CE400DFE701314B4068A86D17958E.description: Characterize Earth as a changing and complex system of interacting spheres.

E03C9180DFE701314B3F68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand how Earth science interacts with society.

E03C4B00DFE701314B3E68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the impact of human activities (e.g., sediment, pollution, overfishing) on ocean systems.

E03BFF50DFE701314B3D68A86D17958E.description: Model energy flow in the physical dynamics of oceans (e.g., wave action, deep ocean tides circulation, surface currents, land and sea breezes, El Niño, upwellings).

E03B9830DFE701314B3C68A86D17958E.description: Design and conduct an experiment comparing chemical properties (e.g., chemical composition, percent salinity) and physical properties (e.g., density, freezing point depression) of freshwater samples to saltwater samples from different sources.

E03B5040DFE701314B3B68A86D17958E.description: Investigate how salinity, temperature, and pressure at different depths and locations in oceans and lakes affect saltwater ecosystems.

E03B03C0DFE701314B3A68A86D17958E.description: Research how the oceans formed from outgassing by volcanoes and ice from comets.

E03AB080DFE701314B3968A86D17958E.description: Analyze the physical, chemical, and biological dynamics of the oceans and the flow of energy through the oceans.

E03A6640DFE701314B3868A86D17958E.description: Research and report how communities manage water resources (e.g., distribution, shortages, quality, flood control) to address social, economic, and environmental concerns.

E03A1CC0DFE701314B3768A86D17958E.description: Using data collected from local water systems, evaluate water quality and conclude how pollution can make water unavailable or unsuitable for life.

E039CC30DFE701314B3668A86D17958E.description: Plan and conduct an experiment to investigate biotic and abiotic factors that affect freshwater ecosystems.

E0397920DFE701314B3568A86D17958E.description: Investigate the properties of water: exists in all three states, dissolves many substances, exhibits adhesion and cohesion, density of solid vs. liquid water.

E0391200DFE701314B3468A86D17958E.description: Analyze the characteristics and importance of freshwater found on Earth's surface and its effect on living systems.

E038B720DFE701314B3368A86D17958E.description: Model the natural purification of water as it moves through the water cycle and compare natural purification to processes used in local sewage treatment plants.

E03869E0DFE701314B3268A86D17958E.description: Describe how the processes of evaporation, condensation, precipitation, surface runoff, ground infiltration and transpiration contribute to the cycling of water through Earth's reservoirs.

E0381710DFE701314B3168A86D17958E.description: Identify oceans, lakes, running water, frozen water, ground water, and atmospheric moisture as the reservoirs of Earth's water cycle, and graph or chart the relative amounts of water in each.

E037CC50DFE701314B3068A86D17958E.description: Characterize the water cycle in terms of its reservoirs, water movement among reservoirs and how water has been recycled throughout time.

E0378760DFE701314B2F68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the dynamics of the hydrosphere.

E0373F90DFE701314B2E68A86D17958E.description: Investigate the current and potential consequences of climate change (e.g., ocean acidification, sea level rise, desertification, habitat loss) on ecosystems, including human communities.

E036EC80DFE701314B2D68A86D17958E.description: Explain the differences between air pollution and climate change and how these are related to society's use of fossil fuels.

E0369F10DFE701314B2C68A86D17958E.description: Describe how human activity influences the carbon cycle and may contribute to climate change.

E0365550DFE701314B2B68A86D17958E.description: Explain how Earth's climate has changed over time and describe the natural causes for these changes (e.g., Milankovitch cycles, solar fluctuations, plate tectonics).

E0360E70DFE701314B2A68A86D17958E.description: Explain differences between weather and climate and the methods used to investigate evidence for changes in climate (e.g., ice core sampling, tree rings, historical temperature measurements, changes in the extent of alpine glaciers, changes in the extent of Arctic sea ice).

E035C590DFE701314B2968A86D17958E.description: Examine the natural and human-caused processes that cause Earth's climate to change over intervals of time ranging from decades to millennia.

E0356FF0DFE701314B2868A86D17958E.description: Design and conduct a weather investigation, use an appropriate display of the data, and interpret the observations and data.

E0352150DFE701314B2768A86D17958E.description: Diagram and describe cold, warm, occluded, and stationary boundaries (weather fronts) between air masses.

E034D400DFE701314B2668A86D17958E.description: Explain a difference between a low pressure system and a high pressure system, including the weather associated with them.

E0347770DFE701314B2568A86D17958E.description: Describe conditions that give rise to severe weather phenomena (e.g., thunderstorms, tornados, hurricanes, El Niño/La Niña).

E0341CE0DFE701314B2468A86D17958E.description: Identify the elements of weather and the instruments used to measure them (e.g., temperature—thermometer; precipitation—rain gauge or Doppler radar; humidity— hygrometer; air pressure—barometer; wind—anemometer; cloud coverage—satellite imaging).

E033BDA0DFE701314B2368A86D17958E.description: Describe elements of weather and the factors that cause them to vary from day to day.

E0336910DFE701314B2268A86D17958E.description: Explain how the presence of ozone in the stratosphere is beneficial to life, while ozone in the troposphere is considered an air pollutant.

E0331E70DFE701314B2168A86D17958E.description: Explain how uneven heating of Earth's atmosphere at the equator and polar regions combined with the Coriolis effect create an atmospheric circulation system including, Hadley cells, trade winds, and prevailing westerlies, that moves heat energy around Earth.

E032CF90DFE701314B2068A86D17958E.description: Conduct an investigation on how the tilt of Earth's axis causes variations in the intensity and duration of sunlight striking Earth.

E0327A60DFE701314B1F68A86D17958E.description: Construct a model that demonstrates how the greenhouse effect contributes to atmospheric energy.

E0322C00DFE701314B1E68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the amount of energy coming from the Sun that is reflected, absorbed or scattered by the atmosphere, oceans, and land masses.

E031DDD0DFE701314B1D68A86D17958E.description: Relate how energy from the Sun drives atmospheric processes and how atmospheric currents transport matter and transfer energy.

E0318900DFE701314B1C68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the atmospheric processes that support life and cause weather and climate.

E03143A0DFE701314B1B68A86D17958E.description: Design, build, and test a model that investigates local geologic processes (e.g., mudslides, earthquakes, flooding, erosion) and the possible effects on human-engineered structures (e.g., dams, homes, bridges, roads).

E030FD80DFE701314B1A68A86D17958E.description: Model tectonic plate movement and compare the results of plate movement along convergent, divergent, and transform boundaries (e.g., mountain building, volcanoes, earthquakes, mid-ocean ridges, oceanic trenches).

E030B660DFE701314B1968A86D17958E.description: Model the factors that cause tectonic plates to move (e.g., gravity, density, convection).

E0306CE0DFE701314B1868A86D17958E.description: Describe how earthquakes and volcanoes transfer energy from Earth's interior to the surface (e.g., seismic waves transfer mechanical energy, flowing magma transfers heat and mechanical energy).

E0301B30DFE701314B1768A86D17958E.description: Describe a lithospheric plate and identify the major plates of the Earth.

E02FBFA0DFE701314B1668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate how the motion of tectonic plates affects Earth and living things.

E02F6A90DFE701314B1568A86D17958E.description: Organize and evaluate the evidence for the current theory of plate tectonics: sea floor spreading, age of sea floor, distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes.

E02F0A60DFE701314B1468A86D17958E.description: Explain how mantle plumes (hot spots) provide evidence for the rate and direction of tectonic plate motion.

E02EAED0DFE701314B1368A86D17958E.description: Establish the importance of the discovery of mid-ocean ridges, oceanic trenches, and magnetic striping of the sea floor to the development of the modern theory of plate tectonics.

E02E6660DFE701314B1268A86D17958E.description: Cite examples of how the geologic record preserves evidence of past change.

E02E12C0DFE701314B1168A86D17958E.description: Explain Alfred Wegener's continental drift hypothesis, his evidence (e.g., fossil record, ancient climates, geometric fit of continents), and why it was not accepted in his time.

E02DCBC0DFE701314B1068A86D17958E.description: Describe the development of the current theory of plate tectonics and the evidence that supports this theory.

E02D83B0DFE701314B0F68A86D17958E.description: Model how convection currents help distribute heat within the mantle.

E02D3A00DFE701314B0E68A86D17958E.description: Trace the lines of scientific evidence that led to the inference that Earth's lithosphere, asthenosphere, mesosphere, outer core, and inner core are separated based on physical properties.

E02CE050DFE701314B0D68A86D17958E.description: Trace the lines of scientific evidence (e.g., seismic studies, composition of meteorites, and samples of the crust and mantle) that led to the inference that Earth's core, mantle, and crust are separated based on composition.

E02C8EF0DFE701314B0C68A86D17958E.description: Identify that radioactive decay and heat of formation are the sources of Earth's internal heat.

E02C32E0DFE701314B0B68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the source of Earth's internal heat and the evidence of Earth's internal structure.

E02BE150DFE701314B0A68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand Earth's internal structure and the dynamic nature of the tectonic plates that form its surface.

E02B8E80DFE701314B0968A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the conditions that currently support life on Earth (biosphere) and compare them to the conditions that exist on other planets and moons in the solar system (e.g., atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere, amounts of incoming solar energy, habitable zone).

E02B4550DFE701314B0868A86D17958E.description: Compare the size and scale of objects within the solar system.

E02AFDB0DFE701314B0768A86D17958E.description: Compare the size of the solar system to the Milky Way galaxy.

E02AABF0DFE701314B0668A86D17958E.description: Relate the composition of objects in the solar system to their distance from the Sun.

E02A4F50DFE701314B0568A86D17958E.description: Analyze Earth as part of the solar system, which is part of the Milky Way galaxy.

E029F500DFE701314B0468A86D17958E.description: Provide an example of how technology has helped scientists investigate the universe.

E029A4D0DFE701314B0368A86D17958E.description: Investigate and report how science has changed the accepted ideas regarding the nature of the universe throughout history.

E0295DA0DFE701314B0268A86D17958E.description: Explain that heavy elements found on Earth are formed in stars.

E0291320DFE701314B0168A86D17958E.description: Describe the nebular theory of solar system formation and the evidence supporting it (e.g., solar system structure due to gravity, motion and temperature; composition and age of meteorites; observations of newly forming stars).

E028C0D0DFE701314B0068A86D17958E.description: Describe the big bang theory and the evidence that supports this theory (e.g., cosmic background radiation, abundance of elements, distance/redshift relation for galaxies).

E02879D0DFE701314AFF68A86D17958E.description: Identify the scientific evidence for the age of the solar system (4.6 billion years), including Earth (e.g., radioactive decay).

E0283340DFE701314AFE68A86D17958E.description: Describe both the big bang theory of universe formation and the nebular theory of solar system formation and evidence supporting them.

E027EB40DFE701314AFD68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the scientific evidence that supports theories that explain how the universe and the solar system developed. They will compare Earth to other objects in the solar system.

comments: Life and physical science content are integrated in a curriculum with two primary goals: (1) students will value and use science as a process of obtaining knowledge based on observable evidence, and (2) students' curiosity will be sustained as they develop the abilities associated with scientific inquiry. This course builds upon students' experience with integrated science in grades seven and eight and is the springboard course for success in biology, chemistry, geology, and physics.

E02743D0DFE701314AFB68A86D17958E.description: Understand that science and technology may raise ethical issues for which science, by itself, does not provide solutions.

E026CD80DFE701314AFA68A86D17958E.description: Understand that scientific inquiry is characterized by a common set of values that include logical thinking, precision, open-mindedness, objectivity, skepticism, replicability of results and honest and ethical reporting of findings. These values function as criteria in distinguishing between science and non-science.

E02682B0DFE701314AF968A86D17958E.description: Understand that various disciplines of science are interrelated and share common rules of evidence to explain phenomena in the natural world.

E0263ED0DFE701314AF868A86D17958E.description: Understand the use of the term "theory" in science, and that the scientific community validates each theory before it is accepted. If new evidence is discovered that the theory does not accommodate, the theory is generally modified in light of this new evidence.

E025FA20DFE701314AF768A86D17958E.description: Understand that scientific conclusions are based on the assumption that natural laws operate today as they did in the past and that they will continue to do so in the future.

E025B1C0DFE701314AF668A86D17958E.description: Understand that science conclusions are tentative and therefore never final. Understandings based upon these conclusions are subject to revision in light of new evidence.

E02560E0DFE701314AF568A86D17958E.description: Science findings are based upon evidence.

E0250B00DFE701314AF468A86D17958E.description: Understand that science investigations use a variety of methods and do not always use the same set of procedures; understand that there is not just one "scientific method."

E024C4F0DFE701314AF368A86D17958E.description: Science is a way of knowing that is used by many people, not just scientists.

E0247D80DFE701314AF268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate Understanding of the Nature of Science

E02437F0DFE701314AF168A86D17958E.description: Recognize contributions to science knowledge that have been made by both women and men.

E023EF40DFE701314AF068A86D17958E.description: Understand the cumulative nature of scientific knowledge.

E023A150DFE701314AEF68A86D17958E.description: Give instances of how technological advances have influenced the progress of science and how science has influenced advances in technology.

E0235060DFE701314AEE68A86D17958E.description: Cite examples of how science affects human life.

E0230720DFE701314AED68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate Awareness of Social and Historical Aspects of Science

E022B060DFE701314AEC68A86D17958E.description: Use mathematical language and reasoning to communicate information.

E0225CE0DFE701314AEB68A86D17958E.description: Use reference sources to obtain information and cite the sources.

E0220690DFE701314AEA68A86D17958E.description: Use proper English in oral and written reports.

E021AE00DFE701314AE968A86D17958E.description: Use precise scientific language in oral and written communication.

E02156C0DFE701314AE868A86D17958E.description: Provide relevant data to support their inferences and conclusions.

E020FDB0DFE701314AE768A86D17958E.description: Communicate Effectively Using Science Language and Reasoning

E020B780DFE701314AE668A86D17958E.description: Solve problems by applying science principles and procedures.

E0206EF0DFE701314AE568A86D17958E.description: Apply principles and concepts of science to explain various phenomena.

E0202110DFE701314AE468A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between examples and non-examples of concepts that have been taught.

E01FCDF0DFE701314AE368A86D17958E.description: Know and explain science information specified for the subject being studied.

E01F8670DFE701314AE268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate Understanding of Science Concepts, Principles and Systems

E01F40B0DFE701314AE168A86D17958E.description: Reject pseudoscience as a source of scientific knowledge.

E01EFAF0DFE701314AE068A86D17958E.description: Evaluate scientifically related claims against available evidence.

E01EB380DFE701314ADF68A86D17958E.description: Accept responsibility for actively helping to resolve social, ethical and ecological problems related to science and technology.

E01E6970DFE701314ADE68A86D17958E.description: Maintain an open and questioning mind toward ideas and alternative points of view.

E01E13B0DFE701314ADD68A86D17958E.description: Raise questions about objects, events and processes that can be answered through scientific investigation.

E01DBD90DFE701314ADC68A86D17958E.description: Voluntarily read and study books and other materials about science.

E01D0CA0DFE701314ADA68A86D17958E.description: Form alternative hypotheses to explain a problem.

E01CBEF0DFE701314AD968A86D17958E.description: Use mathematics as a precise method for showing relationships.

E01C73D0DFE701314AD868A86D17958E.description: Construct models, simulations and metaphors to describe and explain natural phenomena.

E01BD290DFE701314AD668A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between factual statements and inferences.

E01B33C0DFE701314AD468A86D17958E.description: Prepare written and oral reports of investigations.

0030B4AE056444BC80C07714CD9B69C6.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

945FDE21D1904A5C8A4A6C8E2CAF8443.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
EAABFD9421D74032991C20922EA0AC8E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

comments: Modeling is best interpreted not as a collection of isolated topics but in relation to other standards. Making mathematical models is a Standard for Mathematical Practice, and specific modeling standards appear throughout the high school standards indicated by a star symbol (★). The star symbol sometimes appears on the heading for a group of standards; in that case, it should be understood to apply to all standards in that group.

2CD8F44C37734ECBAB44991A882CB470.description: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational; that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational; and that the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is irrational.

5D81891A517D4463981E867337FCB839.description: Extend the properties of exponents to rational exponents.

779A135C207F490A80DB4B84B3E941D5.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

9B3A2969D06645E7A09331E7BD3F44BE.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

B133BD260397428D96FF321C109A3F04.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

D396C660DFE7013136ED68A86D17958E.description: Explore a variety of art media, techniques, and processes.

D39653B0DFE7013136EC68A86D17958E.description: Making: Students will assemble and create works of art by experiencing a variety of art media and by learning the art elements and principles.

document.title: Utah Social Studies Core Curriculum Secondary 7-12

E0C8AD90DFE701314C7F68A86D17958E.description: Participate in community activities respecting the environment and personal property.

E0C85630DFE701314C7E68A86D17958E.description: Investigate career opportunities available through the application of geography skills and concepts.

E0C81360DFE701314C7D68A86D17958E.description: Examine how the unequal distribution of resources affects economic development.

E0C7CEB0DFE701314C7C68A86D17958E.description: Apply geographic concepts to interpret the present and plan for the future.

E0C78B00DFE701314C7B68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that both human choices and natural events have consequences.

E0C74610DFE701314C7A68A86D17958E.description: Relate economic development to the distribution of resources.

E0C70350DFE701314C7968A86D17958E.description: Explain why and how individuals, groups, and institutions respond to continuity and change.

E0C69EC0DFE701314C7868A86D17958E.description: Apply an understanding of cultures as an integrated whole including traditions, behavior patterns, and technologies.

E0C63770DFE701314C7768A86D17958E.description: Apply geographic concepts to interpret the past.

E0C5E850DFE701314C7668A86D17958E.description: Students will use geographic knowledge to connect to today's world.

E0C5A9C0DFE701314C7568A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the role of energy resources as they are consumed, conserved, and recycled.

E0C56900DFE701314C7468A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the use of renewable and nonrenewable resources.

E0C52190DFE701314C7368A86D17958E.description: Identify worldwide distribution and use of human and natural resources.

E0C4DEF0DFE701314C7268A86D17958E.description: Describe the roles of natural and human resources in daily life.

E0C49E60DFE701314C7168A86D17958E.description: Assess the importance of natural and human resources.

E0C45C30DFE701314C7068A86D17958E.description: Predict the potential effect of human modification on the physical environment.

E0C41210DFE701314C6F68A86D17958E.description: Discuss regional issues; e.g., desertification, deforestation, pollution.

E0C3C4C0DFE701314C6E68A86D17958E.description: Explain how historical events affect physical and human systems.

E0C36D50DFE701314C6D68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the role of technology in modifying the physical environment.

E0C31A00DFE701314C6C68A86D17958E.description: Explore how humans change the environment and how the environment changes humans.

E0C2D770DFE701314C6B68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the interaction of physical and human systems.

E0C293E0DFE701314C6A68A86D17958E.description: Determine the role of government in contemporary and historical world issues.

E0C24EB0DFE701314C6968A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast political systems within world regions.

E0C20D40DFE701314C6868A86D17958E.description: Investigate various forms of governance and how they affect peoples and landscapes.

E0C1C4A0DFE701314C6768A86D17958E.description: Assess how nations and cultures are linked through transportation, communication, language, currency, goods, and services.

E0C17A30DFE701314C6668A86D17958E.description: Examine economic networks, from local to global.

E0C13740DFE701314C6568A86D17958E.description: Analyze economic interdependence among regions and countries.

E0C0EE40DFE701314C6468A86D17958E.description: Investigate how people adapt to their environment.

E0C08730DFE701314C6368A86D17958E.description: Explain why people who modify their physical environment in one place cause change in other places.

E0C02C00DFE701314C6268A86D17958E.description: Examine the importance of water to settlement patterns.

E0BFE080DFE701314C6168A86D17958E.description: Describe how physical environments provide geographic advantage or disadvantage.

E0BF9B30DFE701314C6068A86D17958E.description: Analyze the characteristics, distribution, and migration of human populations on the earth's surface.

E0BF5D00DFE701314C5F68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand how human activities shape the earth's surface.

E0BF1D20DFE701314C5E68A86D17958E.description: Compare regions of the earth with similar physical features, such as semiarid regions in Utah with other semiarid regions of the world.

E0BEDBB0DFE701314C5D68A86D17958E.description: Use geographic tools to identify the location and distribution of global ecosystems.

E0BE49F0DFE701314C5B68A86D17958E.description: Assess the characteristics and locations of ecosystems.

E0BE0B10DFE701314C5A68A86D17958E.description: Explain the factors that combine to shape climatic and vegetation patterns on earth.

E0BDCD30DFE701314C5968A86D17958E.description: Assess the external forces of weathering and erosion.

E0BD8F20DFE701314C5868A86D17958E.description: Examine the role of plate tectonics in shaping the earth's surface.

E0BD4E70DFE701314C5768A86D17958E.description: Examine the physical processes that shape the earth's surface.

E0BD0D20DFE701314C5668A86D17958E.description: Students will understand how physical processes shape the earth's surface.

E0BCC8A0DFE701314C5568A86D17958E.description: Explain the effects of cultural diffusion from country to country.

E0BC7A80DFE701314C5468A86D17958E.description: List and define components of culture; e.g., race, gender roles, education, religion.

E0BC2A10DFE701314C5368A86D17958E.description: Evaluate how culture and experience influence the way people live in places and regions.

E0BBE160DFE701314C5268A86D17958E.description: Characterize the similarities and differences within and between regions.

E0BB9000DFE701314C5168A86D17958E.description: Recognize how peoples create regions to understand a large, complex, and changing world.

E0BB4A00DFE701314C5068A86D17958E.description: Assess how people create regions to interpret the earth's surface.

E0BB0020DFE701314C4F68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that places change over time.

E0BAA870DFE701314C4E68A86D17958E.description: Investigate physical characteristics such as landforms, climates, water cycle, vegetation, and animal life.

E0BA6830DFE701314C4D68A86D17958E.description: Examine human characteristics, including language, religion, population, political and economic systems, and quality of life.

E0BA26C0DFE701314C4C68A86D17958E.description: Interpret place by its human and physical characteristics.

E0B9E540DFE701314C4B68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the human and physical characteristics of places and regions.

E0B9A300DFE701314C4A68A86D17958E.description: Define absolute and relative location, recognizing political and physical boundaries.

E0B95B50DFE701314C4968A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the locational importance of human and natural resources using maps, satellite images, and databases.

E0B90EC0DFE701314C4868A86D17958E.description: Apply the geographic mode of inquiry (What? Where? How? And So What?) to world regions.

E0B8C3E0DFE701314C4768A86D17958E.description: Describe the importance and role of location in geographic studies.

E0B88130DFE701314C4668A86D17958E.description: Analyze the spatial organization of people, places, and environments on the earth's surface.

E0B835B0DFE701314C4568A86D17958E.description: Appraise mental maps, from simple to complex.

E0B7A2D0DFE701314C4368A86D17958E.description: Explore the concept of mental maps to organize information about people, places, and environments.

E0B75B30DFE701314C4268A86D17958E.description: Collect and interpret geographic data using maps, charts, population pyramids, cartograms, remote sensing, and Geographic Information Systems (GIS).

E0B70D00DFE701314C4168A86D17958E.description: Explain selected map concepts, including rotation, revolution, axis, seasons, solstice, equinox, and the earth/sun relationship of weather patterns.

E0B6CE20DFE701314C4068A86D17958E.description: Examine characteristics of maps and globes such as latitude, longitude, great circle routes, cardinal directions, compass rose, legend, scale, relief, grid system, and time zones.

E0B68790DFE701314C3F68A86D17958E.description: Explain the differences between major types of map projections.

E0B641E0DFE701314C3E68A86D17958E.description: Use maps and other geographic tools to acquire information from a spatial perspective.

E0B5FAE0DFE701314C3D68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the world in spatial terms.

CF409AA0DFE70131310168A86D17958E.description: These particular masterworks are chosen for their appeal, their potential in demonstrating different music elements, and their suitability to this grade level. There are many other selections which could be substituted and/or added to the list. Consider equally powerful works from the various "non-Western" cultures of the world.

CF404F40DFE70131310068A86D17958E.description:
Suggested listening for sixth grade:
  • Examples of Styles: (Select additional examples as desired)
  • Folk: Simple Gifts, The Water is Wide, Annie Lee
  • Gospel: Rock-a My Soul
  • Popular: Lean On Me, Top of the World
  • Jazz: I Got Rhythm
  • Minor Key: Joshua Fought the Battle of Jericho

CF400B80DFE7013130FF68A86D17958E.description: Hypothesize the universal message, meaning, and/or purpose of the music.

CF3FB590DFE7013130FE68A86D17958E.description: Summarize personal preferences in music selections according to excellence of performance, meaning/purpose, and use of music elements.

CF3F6F50DFE7013130FD68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate familiarity with suggested listening selections.

CF3F2AA0DFE7013130FC68A86D17958E.description: Identify major and minor sounds in familiar songs and listening selections.

CF3EE730DFE7013130FB68A86D17958E.description: Explain the differences between these types of music: opera, symphony, ballet, oratorio, suite, concerto, musical.

CF3EA240DFE7013130FA68A86D17958E.description: Describe and identify the following styles in familiar songs and listening selections: jazz, popular, classical, folk, rock, gospel, hymns/anthems, spirituals, country, blues, rhythm and blues, bluegrass.

CF3E5C30DFE7013130F968A86D17958E.description: Analyze and demonstrate how timbre, rhythm, melody, form, texture, and performing style are used to create styles of music.

CF3E0AC0DFE7013130F868A86D17958E.description: Explain how the music can communicate a certain meaning or serve a specific purpose.

CF3DC0F0DFE7013130F768A86D17958E.description: Explain, demonstrate, and judge own ability to exhibit appropriate audience etiquette according to type of musical performance.

CF3D7B60DFE7013130F668A86D17958E.description: Perceive and respond to the messages in music and the use of music elements.

CF3CA380DFE7013130F368A86D17958E.description: Examine personal success and the achievement of others in stage presence; watching the conductor; keeping a steady beat; singing in a voice free from strain; using proper playing and handling techniques of instruments; performing correct volume, pitches, and rhythm; starting and stopping together.

CF3D34C0DFE7013130F568A86D17958E.description: Plan, practice, self-assess, refine, present, and reflect on a simple performance that demonstrates all of the skills learned in each of the standards.

CF3CF040DFE7013130F468A86D17958E.description: Formulate suggestions for improvement in music performances referring to the skills listed above.

CF3C4FC0DFE7013130F268A86D17958E.description: Recognize quality while creating a music performance.

CF3BE020DFE7013130F168A86D17958E.description: Listening: The student will listen to, analyze, and describe music.

CF394550DFE7013130E868A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast creating style in music with creating style in dance movements, paintings, stories, plays, statues, buildings, commercials, movies, etc.

CF390050DFE7013130E768A86D17958E.description: Build and demonstrate a simple instrument to provide sound effects for any of the above projects.

CF38B930DFE7013130E668A86D17958E.description: Create together a new song and/or a new chant ("rap").

CF387A00DFE7013130E568A86D17958E.description: Create, plan, practice, and perform a familiar song in various styles.

CF383A00DFE7013130E468A86D17958E.description: Improvise a soundtrack for a story and/or a poem.

CF37F640DFE7013130E368A86D17958E.description: Improvise simple rhythm and/or melody patterns to echo back and forth and manipulate in a variety of ways to create various styles, first with the voice and then with found sounds or instruments.

CF37A750DFE7013130E268A86D17958E.description: Create original music and add expression and style to existing music.

CF3B7820DFE7013130F068A86D17958E.description: Draw and explain the use of sharps, flats, and key signatures.

CF3B29D0DFE7013130EF68A86D17958E.description: Identify and explain the various intervals in pitch patterns notated on staff and the use of ledger lines.

CF3AE890DFE7013130EE68A86D17958E.description: Explain fermata, tempo markings, sixteenths, half notes, dotted half notes, 2/4, 3/4, and 4/4 meter, and the subsequent bar lines and measures in rhythm patterns.

CF3A9EA0DFE7013130ED68A86D17958E.description: Notate as a class shorty rhythm and pitch patterns created by the teacher, individuals, and the class.

CF3A5D20DFE7013130EC68A86D17958E.description: Use the staff system to document arrangements and compositions limited rhythmically to beamed sets of 4 sixteenth notes, whole note/rest, half note/rest, dotted half note, quarter note/rest, and eighth note pairs; and limited melodically to ti, fa, do, re, mi, so, la.

CF3A1C40DFE7013130EB68A86D17958E.description: Balance reason and emotion in creating, practicing, and performing.

CF39D4C0DFE7013130EA68A86D17958E.description: Exhibit through music an appreciation for the subtle beauties inherent in everyday life.

CF3985F0DFE7013130E968A86D17958E.description: Express ideas, thoughts, and emotions aesthetically through singing, playing, and/or creating.

CF375410DFE7013130E168A86D17958E.description: Creating: The student will create music through improvising, arranging, and composing.

CF36FF90DFE7013130E068A86D17958E.description: Determine success in playing according to the style of the music.

CF36B4D0DFE7013130DF68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate success in playing even, dotted, and syncopated rhythm/melody patterns in echo to teacher.

CF366F30DFE7013130DE68A86D17958E.description: Judge success in playing simple melodies on the recorder or keyboard by rote and/or note reading.

CF362520DFE7013130DD68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate success in playing with a beautiful tone, precision, and expression on a variety of classroom instruments.

CF35B600DFE7013130DC68A86D17958E.description: Perform independently or with others simple melodies and accompaniments on classroom instruments.

CF356980DFE7013130DB68A86D17958E.description: Add instrumental sounds to known songs of various cultures.

CF352C30DFE7013130DA68A86D17958E.description: Judge success in using proper playing and handling techniques on a variety of classroom instruments.

CF34EE50DFE7013130D968A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate various timbres and effects of simple instruments.

CF34AE70DFE7013130D868A86D17958E.description: Discover and demonstrate sounds on simple instruments of the classroom and various cultures.

CF346BD0DFE7013130D768A86D17958E.description: Playing: The student will play instruments as a means of musical expression.

CF342650DFE7013130D668A86D17958E.description: Play singing games, enjoy traditional folk dances and patriotic songs that have originated in the cultures of the world, and explain what they mean personally.

CF33DD00DFE7013130D568A86D17958E.description: Describe how music is used by cultures in world history.

CF339FB0DFE7013130D468A86D17958E.description: Share songs, instruments, and music enjoyed by various cultures in the history of the world.

CF336190DFE7013130D368A86D17958E.description: Discover how songs, singing games, and dances relate to various cultures in the history of the world.

CF325A70DFE7013130CF68A86D17958E.description: Rate success in sight reading short melodic patterns together.

CF320120DFE7013130CE68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate group success in singing expressively.

CF31BE90DFE7013130CD68A86D17958E.description: Decide success in singing an assigned part.

CF317AE0DFE7013130CC68A86D17958E.description: Use the speaking and singing voice in a creative way to characterize a chosen text.

CF313720DFE7013130CB68A86D17958E.description: Sing a variety of simple songs in tune, in a natural voice, free from strain. Include descants, melodic ostinato, counter melodies, rounds, call/response, and spoken/sung accompanying chants.

CF30F000DFE7013130CA68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate ability to sing in tune on an assigned part, with expression, accuracy, and free from strain.

CF3321E0DFE7013130D268A86D17958E.description: Show changes in melodic direction, dynamics, timbre, tempo, rhythm, form, mood, texture, and style through body movement.

CF32E0E0DFE7013130D168A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the difference between beat and rhythm.

CF329FF0DFE7013130D068A86D17958E.description: Use body movement to internalize sounds.

CF309990DFE7013130C968A86D17958E.description: Singing: The student will develop the voice and body as instruments of musical expression.

document.title: Utah Social Studies Core Curriculum Secondary 7-12

E21BF2F0DFE701314EF168A86D17958E.description: Describe the role of the United States in international organizations.

E21B9160DFE701314EF068A86D17958E.description: Explain how developments in other nations affect United States society and life.

E21B2D00DFE701314EEF68A86D17958E.description: Describe the impact of the United States' concepts of democracy and individual rights on the world.

E21AD030DFE701314EEE68A86D17958E.description: Explore how the United States influences other nations, and how other nations influence the United States.

E21A7620DFE701314EED68A86D17958E.description: Explain how United States domestic politics affect United States foreign policy.

E21A17A0DFE701314EEC68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the various ways in which United States foreign policy is carried out; e.g., diplomatic, economic, military, humanitarian.

E219ABF0DFE701314EEB68A86D17958E.description: Describe the process by which United States foreign policy is made; e.g., federal agencies, domestic interest groups, the public, the media.

E2194110DFE701314EEA68A86D17958E.description: Explain the powers that the Constitution gives to the president and Congress in foreign affairs, and how these powers have been used.

E218DC80DFE701314EE968A86D17958E.description: Evaluate how United States foreign policy affects the world.

E21880E0DFE701314EE868A86D17958E.description: Analyze and evaluate conditions, actions, and motivations that contribute to conflict and cooperation within and among nations.

E2182320DFE701314EE768A86D17958E.description: Compare different political systems with that of the United States; e.g., dictatorship, democracy, theocracy, monarchy, totalitarianism.

E217BFC0DFE701314EE668A86D17958E.description: Explain the purpose of government and analyze how government powers are acquired, used, and justified.

E2174C20DFE701314EE568A86D17958E.description: Examine major government structures and functions outside the United States.

E216D790DFE701314EE468A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the relationship between the United States and the international system.

E2167580DFE701314EE368A86D17958E.description: Analyze the role of specialization and exchange in the economic process.

E2160A40DFE701314EE268A86D17958E.description: Examine how the private and public sectors contribute to an economic system.

E215AF60DFE701314EE168A86D17958E.description: Determine how scarcity and choice influence governmental economic decision making.

E21552A0DFE701314EE068A86D17958E.description: Analyze the role that prices, incentives, and profits play in determining what is produced and distributed in a competitive market system.

E214F760DFE701314EDF68A86D17958E.description: Determine how supply and demand affect the availability of goods and services.

E21493E0DFE701314EDE68A86D17958E.description: Examine the problems of newly developing economies in today's world.

E2141EF0DFE701314EDD68A86D17958E.description: Develop an understanding of capitalism, communism, socialism, and mixed economic systems.

E213B5E0DFE701314EDC68A86D17958E.description: Explain how the scarcity and abundance of productive resources contribute to economic systems.

E212FE70DFE701314EDA68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand basic economic principles and how they influence everyday life.

E212A380DFE701314ED968A86D17958E.description: Develop an understanding of the role of civility in dealing with individual and group differences.

E21239B0DFE701314ED868A86D17958E.description: Analyze and evaluate conditions, actions, and motivations that contribute to conflict and cooperation.

E211D7F0DFE701314ED768A86D17958E.description: Assess methods for respectfully dealing with differences.

E2117610DFE701314ED668A86D17958E.description: Participate in activities that promote the public good; e.g., the voting process, jury duty, community service.

E2111850DFE701314ED568A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the need for civic dialogue in maintaining a democratic society; e.g., public meetings, mass meetings.

E210B2C0DFE701314ED468A86D17958E.description: Investigate ways in which responsible citizens take part in civic life.

E2105150DFE701314ED368A86D17958E.description: Investigate the major political parties and their ideas.

E20FF290DFE701314ED268A86D17958E.description: Recognize the need for selective service in maintaining a military.

E20F90E0DFE701314ED168A86D17958E.description: Examine the United States tax system.

E20F0780DFE701314ED068A86D17958E.description: Examine the election and voting process.

E20E8740DFE701314ECF68A86D17958E.description: Assess the need to obey laws.

E20E2C50DFE701314ECE68A86D17958E.description: Investigate the responsibilities and obligations of a citizen.

E20DCF80DFE701314ECD68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the responsibilities of citizens in the United States.

E20D73D0DFE701314ECC68A86D17958E.description: Examine how public education is a function of state and local government.

E20D1340DFE701314ECB68A86D17958E.description: Explore current issues affecting local governments; e.g., spending, state v. local control, land use.

E20CAEF0DFE701314ECA68A86D17958E.description: Assess how federal monies influence local policy and decision-making.

E20C4E30DFE701314EC968A86D17958E.description: Investigate the structure and function of local government.

E20BCE10DFE701314EC868A86D17958E.description: Describe the powers given to local governments.

E20B5730DFE701314EC768A86D17958E.description: Analyze the role of local government in the United States federal system.

E20AE890DFE701314EC668A86D17958E.description: Assess the unique relationship between the sovereign American Indian nations and the United States government.

E20A8E70DFE701314EC568A86D17958E.description: Examine the debate between federal supremacy and states' rights.

E20A2ED0DFE701314EC468A86D17958E.description: Identify and explain the concept of federalism.

E209CC80DFE701314EC368A86D17958E.description: Determine the relationship between the national government and the states.

E2096510DFE701314EC268A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the distribution of power among the national, state, and local governments in the United States federal system.

E208F520DFE701314EC168A86D17958E.description: Identify landmark cases and their impact on civil rights and individual liberties; e.g., Dred Scott, Plessey, Brown, Miranda, Gideon, Bakke.

E20899B0DFE701314EC068A86D17958E.description: Summarize the differing interpretations of the strict versus loose constructionists.

E2083C10DFE701314EBF68A86D17958E.description: Examine how the Bill of Rights promotes a just legal system.

E207DB70DFE701314EBE68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how civil rights and liberties have been changed through court decisions.

E2076D20DFE701314EBD68A86D17958E.description: Assess the significance of the First and Fourteenth Amendments.

E206FCD0DFE701314EBC68A86D17958E.description: Examine how the Bill of Rights promotes civil rights and protects diversity.

E2069B80DFE701314EBB68A86D17958E.description: Determine the rights and liberties outlined in the Bill of Rights.

E2061E60DFE701314EBA68A86D17958E.description: Assess the freedoms and rights guaranteed in the United States Constitution.

E2059C60DFE701314EB968A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the protections and privileges of individuals and groups in the United States.

E2053480DFE701314EB868A86D17958E.description: Investigate how laws are interpreted by courts through an adversarial process; i.e., plaintiff, defendant.

E204D9E0DFE701314EB768A86D17958E.description: Examine the ways in which the executive branch carries out laws.

E2047ED0DFE701314EB668A86D17958E.description: Describe how the United States Congress makes laws.

E2042230DFE701314EB568A86D17958E.description: Explain how legislative, executive, and judicial powers are distributed and shared among the three branches of national government.

E203C2C0DFE701314EB468A86D17958E.description: Investigate the organization and functions of the United States government.

E20360D0DFE701314EB368A86D17958E.description: Investigate the necessity for civic virtue.

E2030350DFE701314EB268A86D17958E.description: Examine how the rule of law affects everyday life.

E2029D00DFE701314EB168A86D17958E.description: Determine how judicial review makes the Constitution a living document.

20D4B9458B0A47FB9424F79BBD560907.description: Develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach, focusing on addressing what is most significant for a specific purpose and audience.

EB55CFE01B75404EA4DC1734B1956674.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

F372D61410B847F7A1EB92C5FC0C14AE.description: Provide a conclusion that follows from and reflects on what is experienced, observed, or resolved over the course of the narrative.

58FBC6183DD74E23B80D0CA75B9082F2.description: Use precise words and phrases, telling details, and sensory language to convey a vivid picture of the experiences, events, setting, and/or characters.

BA1C461725F74624A8A1D105D70412DF.description: Use narrative techniques, such as dialogue, pacing, description, reflection, and multiple plot lines, to develop experiences, events, and/or characters.

C869B8F6925B45C88A3E068063FA5A5C.description: Engage and orient the reader by setting out a problem, situation, or observation, establishing one or multiple point(s) of view, and introducing a narrator and/or characters; create a smooth progression of experiences or events.

A94FB7F2B06147C6865C1A1F89D32318.description: Provide a concluding statement or section that follows from and supports the information or explanation presented (e.g., articulating implications or the significance of the topic).

0D3DE14C655A4824B4979C06E07B105A.description: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to manage the complexity of the topic.

77E59962D75F4241AFCA101A66018C76.description: Use appropriate and varied transitions to link the major sections of the text, create cohesion, and clarify the relationships among complex ideas and concepts.

60A620827B584C719F7109D740E2B7A9.description: Develop the topic with well-chosen, relevant, and sufficient facts, extended definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples appropriate to the audience's knowledge of the topic.

9AF955AC5CF04BEFA81C7127B50E380E.description: Introduce a topic; organize complex ideas, concepts, and information to make important connections and distinctions; include formatting (e.g., headings), graphics (e.g., figures, tables), and multimedia when useful to aiding comprehension.

57202546017F4D4F814402FFE02E22DC.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas, concepts, and information clearly and accurately through the effective selection, organization, and analysis of content.

74C2EA4DC77848D29F319761696401F8.description: Provide a concluding statement or section that follows from and supports the argument presented.

FAEA675FB5EB4175BB9BB7095438634F.description: Establish and maintain a formal style and objective tone while attending to the norms and conventions of the discipline in which they are writing.

A25FBE9FDEF04C698245901106DC7FF6.description: Use words, phrases, and clauses to link the major sections of the text, create cohesion, and clarify the relationships between claim(s) and reasons, between reasons and evidence, and between claim(s) and counterclaims.

6E2768D7BE6A499FB9A83940ADDE9BA9.description: Develop claim(s) and counterclaims fairly, supplying evidence for each while pointing out the strengths and limitations of both in a manner that anticipates the audience's knowledge level and concerns.

2CDA9FA1DA274A52B50236630A495E96.description: Introduce precise claim(s), distinguish the claim(s) from alternate or opposing claims, and create an organization that establishes clear relationships among claim(s), counterclaims, reasons, and evidence.

724995C8B7CD4B858CF08B6B8439DD54.description: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.

01B5FF3746DF48928A1C062D07BBCD0B.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.

593EB367E0964A2CB697F729E7A23133.description: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

58F4471C2230439CB0419DC48D719EA2.description: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, assess the credibility and accuracy of each source, and integrate the information while avoiding plagiarism.

0A763F0335CF462D86456A5152C0354D.description: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects based on focused questions, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.

8FD91522BDF04B7FA5D1C8618A274C61.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas and information clearly and accurately through the effective selection, organization, and analysis of content.

EBA4CAE496054A65BDA7B9384956F5BC.description: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.
