82FCEA75B67E471D869142408B7AA3E0.description: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend science/technical texts in the grades 9—10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

BAD2175CDA054622B94AF201DA1DB01F.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

03681B03B0454F44AD735D9849EA6E59.description: Compare and contrast findings presented in a text to those from other sources (including their own experiments), noting when the findings support or contradict previous explanations or accounts.

FE6362A8C4184C21AB0DDB46EC306C23.description: Assess the extent to which the reasoning and evidence in a text support the author's claim or a recommendation for solving a scientific or technical problem.

C184D2B4A43F457E8843D27224135DE4.description: Translate quantitative or technical information expressed in words in a text into visual form (e.g., a table or chart) and translate information expressed visually or mathematically (e.g., in an equation) into words.

EED732141D004B5F9AA17735150BE5D5.description: Analyze the author's purpose in providing an explanation, describing a procedure, or discussing an experiment in a text, defining the question the author seeks to address.

AF34003971AB46BDB4CDB757737E2092.description: Analyze the structure of the relationships among concepts in a text, including relationships among key terms (e.g., force, friction, reaction force, energy).

20AFC47934374860BA340467469BCC32.description: Determine the meaning of symbols, key terms, and other domain-specific words and phrases as they are used in a specific scientific or technical context relevant to grades 9—10 texts and topics.

2B840B4EDD1D487DA4291FD707E3D511.description: Follow precisely a complex multistep procedure when carrying out experiments, taking measurements, or performing technical tasks, attending to special cases or exceptions defined in the text.

7B71C6A2972E490B94FCF3DF69FC7C66.description: Determine the central ideas or conclusions of a text; trace the text's explanation or depiction of a complex process, phenomenon, or concept; provide an accurate summary of the text.

B0820CD3141A488384264A9B1DE939B8.description: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of science and technical texts, attending to the precise details of explanations or descriptions.

2FC59D69BEE345DB83D2EFF8F01D06C2.description: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects 6—12

42DAFBE49D034DF48183FFE2C9A980BD.description: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend history/social studies texts in the grades 9—10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

19F76DD41F18429BB6362B17C18301D0.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

9FA7578B860341DCA310F6672325C273.description: Compare and contrast treatments of the same topic in several primary and secondary sources.

8695F60F191549ABB326EA5AA62616C8.description: Assess the extent to which the reasoning and evidence in a text support the author's claims.

1E626AF491CD452D980E321132C8F226.description: Integrate quantitative or technical analysis (e.g., charts, research data) with qualitative analysis in print or digital text.

B6B06254FB6A405886D16A554653482A.description: Compare the point of view of two or more authors for how they treat the same or similar topics, including which details they include and emphasize in their respective accounts.

B67381464D45487DA738E3286BBD2AA4.description: Analyze how a text uses structure to emphasize key points or advance an explanation or analysis

C230135B948949F8A865590DD702A0D7.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including vocabulary describing political, social, or economic aspects of history/social studies.

15C36F735F70445DBD6FFE53FB68E608.description: Analyze in detail a series of events described in a text; determine whether earlier events caused later ones or simply preceded them.

0631C7C425E8497289A95D9F37BDED85.description: Determine the central ideas or information of a primary or secondary source; provide an accurate summary of how key events or ideas develop over the course of the text.

90F411C3C23A4859B6DB0C4F50C52D88.description: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of primary and secondary sources, attending to such features as the date and origin of the information.

B9631C8854CA4AF9A30CD451D0852DA0.description: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies 6—12

202EF12432AF46168193764F2EB379B3.description:
By the end of grade 9, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 9—10 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9—10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

AD164121380445A3B4C46F9AF017704B.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

613E5C11874C49E38266346834300F5A.description: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance (e.g., Washington's Farewell Address, the Gettysburg Address, Roosevelt's Four Freedoms speech, King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail"), including how they address related themes and concepts.

8B52EAAD75A64319AB5C7A89894EE462.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.

65857CE3E79C48AFA7472BB4FDDA3E9E.description: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums (e.g., a person's life story in both print and multimedia), determining which details are emphasized in each account.

A0433E06B7AE4AD0AE44902D67199042.description: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.

0FAC5E7325C34743B9C20482851D8A4A.description: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text (e.g., a section or chapter).

DBB2829342264059B376077FC1200E26.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone (e.g., how the language of a court opinion differs from that of a newspaper).

A01CC9AE640845F0818827B4D70E80CB.description: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.

8E64D78F1505407787652E873E0E3834.description: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.

2F4F09E33A6B4B33B92BC04D9195A5BD.description: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

5EED0E7CCCC4460998A00A49C28D89F3.description:
By the end of grade 9, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, in the grades 9—10 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, at the high end of the grades 9—10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

DC737BA01DB245B78AEE18DBFA360AA6.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

E53171951D22496499008F096C0F256C.description: Analyze how an author draws on and transforms source material in a specific work (e.g., how Shakespeare treats a theme or topic from Ovid or the Bible or how a later author draws on a play by Shakespeare).

B6E82D012DCB467BAAD94C0149A9225D.description: Analyze the representation of a subject or a key scene in two different artistic mediums, including what is emphasized or absent in each treatment (e.g., Auden's "Musée des Beaux Arts" and Breughel's Landscape with the Fall of Icarus).

539E0FF728F54CB1BC0EF6C3EF2B3F32.description: Analyze a particular point of view or cultural experience reflected in a work of literature from outside the United States, drawing on a wide reading of world literature.

A54862763ED244CBBFD301127B370A79.description: Analyze how an author's choices concerning how to structure a text, order events within it (e.g., parallel plots), and manipulate time (e.g., pacing, flashbacks) create such effects as mystery, tension, or surprise.

CA2CD1738058411C8DA17C8B2F781677.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone (e.g., how the language evokes a sense of time and place; how it sets a formal or informal tone).

ECF02EE7FD5040928D7F8870837BE4BB.description: Analyze how complex characters (e.g., those with multiple or conflicting motivations) develop over the course of a text, interact with other characters, and advance the plot or develop the theme.

C17E7DCA6254455FB4E64B884E668BD5.description: Determine a theme or central idea of a text and analyze in detail its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.

F73173386F82481FB00868947D52EF10.description: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

0EEDDD0807E741C09A701744BE0B3387.description: Read and comprehend complex literary and informational texts independently and proficiently.

FA8F725913E54CDD9DFCE67154A19436.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

439A92FE74474C938A935FDBAC2FBF1F.description: Analyze how two or more texts address similar themes or topics in order to build knowledge or to compare the approaches the authors take.

DFE22CE828404EE882043E84FB21E0EA.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.

14B5C380726A4CBE9AA2A038E0E35BAF.description: Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse media and formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words.
comments: Please see "Research to Build and Present Knowledge" in Writing and "Comprehension and Collaboration" in Speaking and Listening for additional standards relevant to gathering, assessing, and applying information from print and digital sources.

A60A62DDEB8E42DF98A0ADCA55C85C3D.description: Assess how point of view or purpose shapes the content and style of a text.

8BC63F713AA24A5CA2FF098B4609DA0B.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

1CCFA641CA9840E795A948B4E6DA3A1F.description: Interpret words and phrases as they are used in a text, including determining technical, connotative, and figurative meanings, and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning or tone.

6ADD2ACBC9814A94B27B01353AA3450D.description: Analyze how and why individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over the course of a text.

108F5ADB77B147C48F299D3B5871912C.description: Determine central ideas or themes of a text and analyze their development; summarize the key supporting details and ideas.

96EA36C22202461C8BAEF7AFC2B49BB2.description: Read closely to determine what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences from it; cite specific textual evidence when writing or speaking to support conclusions drawn from the text.

26FB481B87AF49ABBA703EE9E209911A.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Reading

98B242CE761C48A4AA19C84635065578.description: Compare two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two decimals refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual model.

7C5C2C9112E34F3888CE15D10028B2EE.description: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100.
comments: For example, rewrite 0.62 as 62/100; describe a length as 0.62 meters; locate 0.62 on a number line diagram.

899FC2019036489BB144D458783CC052.description: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, and use this technique to add two fractions with respective denominators 10 and 100.
comments: Students who can generate equivalent fractions can develop strategies for adding fractions with unlike denominators in general. But addition and subtraction with unlike denominators in general is not a requirement at this grade.
For example, express 3/10 as 30/100, and add 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100.

56F9D968EF29433F923309E8CD3906D0.description: Understand decimal notation for fractions, and compare decimal fractions.

E19F571BB5FF4139B021E2B196400C9D.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
comments: For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be 5 people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
For example, use a visual fraction model to express 3 × (2/5) as 6 × (1/5), recognizing this product as 6/5. (In general, n × (a/b) = (n × a)/b.)
A12C7DAF0FA14DEDB26C38CF1D6DB09C.description: Understand a multiple of a/b as a multiple of 1/b, and use this understanding to multiply a fraction by a whole number.

E84B96EB712D4A7EAF958BDDB459F619.description: Understand a fraction a/b as a multiple of 1/b.
comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to represent 5/4 as the product 5 × (1/4), recording the conclusion by the equation 5/4 = 5 × (1/4).

876C206F5AD845E3BD465AA775960BF7.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction by a whole number.

A8A973C24B1E45D98673001452060831.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

0E2760B2B3A946ADAA2E9EFFB629BA92.description: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

787E57C6C35149CFA133800991133B90.description: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way, recording each decomposition by an equation. Justify decompositions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

A3E11D4DA6AB4F98AAFF9F78DA5A5B62.description: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole.

0CA4A047F3524F8E88722AC121E18053.description: Understand a fraction a/b with a > 1 as a sum of fractions 1/b.

DD785F35725B4609955A78AF36CBB74A.description: Build fractions from unit fractions by applying and extending previous understandings of operations on whole numbers.

D6D0CD6059E846E1837F7078F6F96754.description: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators, e.g., by creating common denominators or numerators, or by comparing to a benchmark fraction such as 1/2. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

881B79F4B1094940BAFB4D1A004AF390.description: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to a fraction (n × a)/(n × b) by using visual fraction models, with attention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.

BBDF5C66B13541DFA85FA86F45215864.description: Extend understanding of fraction equivalence and ordering.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

FF8003AA85D1454A840118CADC2E1664.description: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.

7648E42E486946FBBC5D23EF0E96BCE2.description: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size. Recognize right triangles as a category, and identify right triangles.

E1227613EB314D13B90370F8A5B10993.description: Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.

5AF42574EFEC40A883B4EBAB0E3162ED.description: Draw and identify lines and angles, and classify shapes by properties of their lines and angles.

19DE57B412C34F6DAE93D70DDB9AF948.description: Recognize angle measure as additive. When an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the angle measure of the whole is the sum of the angle measures of the parts. Solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram in real world and mathematical problems, e.g., by using an equation with a symbol for the unknown angle measure.

B90F1E91A43C44D58864991F55DED176.description: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor. Sketch angles of specified measure.

837E3F8F45CD426D85B6A506DAFD026C.description: An angle that turns through n one-degree angles is said to have an angle measure of n degrees.

744FC63B2CA143058AEC90B86FA7D237.description: An angle is measured with reference to a circle with its center at the common endpoint of the rays, by considering the fraction of the circular arc between the points where the two rays intersect the circle. An angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is called a "one-degree angle," and can be used to measure angles.

79598A3F8E304793AAC931AF75F4B1B7.description: Recognize angles as geometric shapes that are formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint, and understand concepts of angle measurement:

42EA4978D19B497384DE1653FFA93231.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of angle and measure angles.

A8BC192C41DB4CFCA9BB1C327F2D3097.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.
comments: For example, from a line plot find and interpret the difference in length between the longest and shortest specimens in an insect collection.
For example, find the width of a rectangular room given the area of the flooring and the length, by viewing the area formula as a multiplication equation with an unknown factor.
EE8ECE82C3724156B3011D5AB51E2718.description: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real world and mathematical problems.

4E09533D824C4894A29074AD24F78D03.description: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale.

860D23328B1E462395906BCAA7EA9964.description: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system of units including km, m, cm; kg, g; lb, oz.; l, ml; hr, min, sec. Within a single system of measurement, express measurements in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Record measurement equivalents in a two column table.
comments: For example, know that 1 ft is 12 times as long as 1 in. Express the length of a 4 ft snake as 48 in. Generate a conversion table for feet and inches listing the number pairs (1, 12), (2, 24), (3, 36), …

3833AEF2FC954C01B6FE63902F965A40.description: Solve problems involving measurement and conversion of measurements from a larger unit to a smaller unit.

84786DB7FC5C4788A6B46F9623DC481E.description: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

AB2387C01C0C4BA789F5E5F84C432DAF.description: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

1A413B4C77034D59BA25E903CD80A791.description: Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

A6898B5FF11741C9B8617FD75C2B9E03.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.

7B07DD0025A94364B8DBED3C10A14A6E.description: Use place value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.

6603803A08AA48C6B84C86446BD321D7.description: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form. Compare two multi-digit numbers based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

FE8D37B55CDD411982562673AAA8E6DC.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right.
comments: For example, recognize that 700 ÷ 70 = 10 by applying concepts of place value and division.

0A459EFE280A48DBA7B885B36FB38444.description: Generalize place value understanding for multi-digit whole numbers.

6FDD72A6839C4ADD8EBBEFFAE37C89C6.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

DAEB771DAF2A451DA120CE9B3D8ADAE3.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself.
comments: For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.

4CB39DF1375D4D8DBE11F3FA7AA4DCA0.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

BCE956AA76C24A9C817D575F102D72D9.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

F50C833318754C4782CEFBB1796589DF.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

B0AE4C205E8A4962A519D95A603ACD62.description: Compare the strong nuclear force to the amount of energy released in a nuclear reaction and contrast it to the amount of energy released in a chemical reaction.

FD7CF272EA7644D39D79E8666980EF2D.description: Compare the mass, energy, and penetrating power of alpha, beta, and gamma radiation.

8AC74545C23B46969F4D34E638DD73FC.description: Interpret graphical data relating half-life and age of a radioactive substance.

E34C105AE561408D915B1F28BA125CE6.description: Recognize that radioactive particles and wavelike radiations are products of the decay of an unstable nucleus.

37B941379ACC4F8299DB644D3C37D44C.description: Evaluate how changes in the nucleus of an atom result in emission of radioactivity.

1409F3223E38406FBF6E2ED53D92FAC7.description: After observing spectral emissions in the lab (e.g., flame test, spectrum tubes), identify unknown elements by comparison to known emission spectra.

A2A231DE49D44ABDA6852864247A083F.description: Correlate the energy in a photon to the color of light emitted.

249EB12019B842CAAC51B65B6AB476F9.description: Examine evidence from the lab indicating that energy is absorbed or released in discrete units when electrons move from one energy level to another.

9BFFF5774A7B463DBD985FF0580DD06B.description: Identify the relationship between wavelength and light energy.

64BFEEBF58F44832B1FD94CC28452AD8.description: Evaluate quantum energy changes in the atom in terms of the energy contained in light emissions.

02F508F0302C4240A6EA0F56A1FDA22F.description: Students will understand the relationship between energy changes in the atom specific to the movement of electrons between energy levels in an atom resulting in the emission or absorption of quantum energy. They will also understand that the emission of high-energy particles results from nuclear changes and that matter can be converted to energy during nuclear reactions.

6609D47CFD364E9C81A2827605A61DC8.description: Compare the properties of elements (e.g., metal, nonmetallic, metalloid) based on their position in the periodic table.

8608B362652E490EAD060215410B862A.description: Generalize trends in reactivity of elements within a group to trends in other groups.

A10349B49E9A407ABAB9ED3BD7F7E48B.description: Identify similarities in chemical behavior of elements within a group.

2893CC8069EF4C7F8355AB0875C51862.description: Compare the number of protons and neutrons in isotopes of the same element.

38ED0182200B4089B5B3A58EF35CE073.description: Use the periodic table to correlate the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in an atom.

B7076D6AF756468A85913AC250133EE6.description: Correlate atomic structure and the physical and chemical properties of an element to the position of the element on the periodic table.

B889D056DDF641E3A3981B140DF7E8AE.description: Relate the mass and number of atoms to the gram-sized quantities of matter in a mole.

7F23CF70F3ED4AB9A458E38809D34F05.description: Generalize the relationship of proton number to the element's identity.

32C22E762A124AD89AAB686FA5F74AF6.description: Discriminate between the relative size, charge, and position of protons, neutrons, and electrons in the atom.

670E4E9B01434BE09C9030220ADD1696.description: Evaluate the limitations of using models to describe atoms.

3DC80A08168542068DA16863C21B1A35.description: Summarize the major experimental evidence that led to the development of various atomic models, both historical and current.

470942CC1A524D0C95682201DE0B617A.description: Relate the structure, behavior, and scale of an atom to the particles that compose it.

25602A3366484744BAA72311732F73CD.description: Compare the occurrence of heavier elements on earth and the universe.

0AA48E7FFA454E45B6F75A772AAFE588.description: Identify the distribution of elements in the universe.

301FD8E447F04A5E8BBF6B0A994CFB8B.description: Recognize that all matter in the universe and on earth is composed of the same elements.

38ED1C40CEAD4B38B921A73C2D6BE188.description: Identify evidence supporting the assumption that matter in the universe has a common origin.

1F985F34AA474EBB8F4B6439B493E8D0.description: Recognize the origin and distribution of elements in the universe.

13BACCF16FFF47CA8B286D1EB8FA90BA.description: Students will understand that all matter in the universe has a common origin and is made of atoms, which have structure and can be systematically arranged on the periodic table.

BCF46987FA5543FD870D6914B1A45B68.description: Justify the ongoing changes to classification schemes used in biology.

08D50ACEE76E4EB4BEC86FF63B91133D.description: Explain how evolutionary relationships are related to classification systems.

328FB57CA4AC496296038AF4A83DCCA0.description: Generalize criteria used for classification of organisms (e.g., dichotomy, structure, broad to specific).

BEF94B4353C2458DAEE93273B4AB6F12.description: Classify organisms using a classification tool such as a key or field guide.

FEC737DCC93F40BB94CBE1869C443AA5.description: Classify organisms into a hierarchy of groups based on similarities that reflect their evolutionary relationships.

D81C793A8C474620BA4315D02AB70783.description: Review a scientific article and identify the research methods used to gather evidence that documents the evolution of a species.

55DB0F5E38A44164804E68F7B7DF6FA4.description: Distinguish between observations and inferences in making interpretations related to evolution (e.g., observed similarities and differences in the beaks of Galapagos finches leads to the inference that they evolved from a common ancestor; observed similarities and differences in the structures of birds and reptiles leads to the inference that birds evolved from reptiles).

CEC6EED472C242F6891817B616708D10.description: Relate the nature of science to the historical development of the theory of evolution.

D1EF1704805E4E629BA4ADFABC078D6C.description: Identify the role of mutation and recombination in evolution.

54B5F0E0EF6749A6BB926AEB123599F3.description: Cite evidence that supports biological evolution over time (e.g., geologic and fossil records, chemical mechanisms, DNA structural similarities, homologous and vestigial structures).

D71256469D734FD2AFBAC46F90C08C98.description: Cite evidence for changes in populations over time and use concepts of evolution to explain these changes.

65A8CCBEB5E840AFABB2FAF5443E30FC.description: Compare selective breeding to natural selection and relate the differences to agricultural practices.

3CAD861395D54954B5C074AF5B4C7BE1.description: Relate genetic variability to a species' potential for adaptation to a changing environment.

3055305077754AB4B71878542E0CA86A.description: Describe the effects of environmental factors on natural selection.

1781B960A5414FE5B245CA656462337B.description: Relate principles of evolution to biological diversity.

46C54FD95A0447749B125CBB9F7FE0A0.description: Students will understand that biological diversity is a result of evolutionary processes.

DAB1D455C4CF4CC9A0A8810C879EC3C5.description: Research, report, and debate genetic technologies that may improve the quality of life (e.g., genetic engineering, cloning, gene splicing).

98B4114CA5A4450CB2D8D2466703967B.description: Relate the historical events that lead to our present understanding of DNA to the cumulative nature of science knowledge and technology.

79D7E43A03704A5984CFB3ED87150103.description: Describe how mutations may affect genetic expression and cite examples of mutagens.

8EAA0F3DFC1749AE82E3EE6CE41CCCE2.description: Summarize how genetic information encoded in DNA provides instructions for assembling protein molecules.

DA38A6651BE74E8990A485FC38EE0397.description: Explain the importance of DNA replication in cell reproduction.

5010D6DFB27D493EA7BF872F52C13D23.description: Use a model to describe the structure of DNA.

EC4D4515BF9F434AA19EEAC9A5CC5D3F.description: Explain how the structure and replication of DNA are essential to heredity and protein synthesis.

B3284E9DAFC746B8A3C6017F5278A21D.description: Analyze bioethical issues and consider the role of science in determining public policy.

922BAB869B9442DF9CD370338E2F1AB4.description: Relate Mendelian principles to modern-day practice of plant and animal breeding.

9E024E1B4EB54830828FFB406D6EBAAC.description: Demonstrate possible results of recombination in sexually reproducing organisms using one or two pairs of contrasting traits in the following crosses: dominance/recessive, incomplete dominance, codominance, and sex-linked traits.

C8A177D0B4054C5599DA8AE3E82B5D76.description: Explain Mendel's laws of segregation and independent assortment and their role in genetic inheritance.

CC62A45176B540AF91D8144B8DABF9EE.description: Predict and interpret patterns of inheritance in sexually reproducing organisms.

35CCFF93C9CD42C5910DA11E30738D90.description: Formulate, defend, and support a perspective of a bioethical issue related to intentional or unintentional chromosomal mutations.

3DDB860112B24320BC8B7B7FD084DE73.description: Compare the advantages/disadvantages of sexual and asexual reproduction to survival of species.

320C9D803BFB4BF58AA3261AE80C6366.description: Explain the significance of meiosis and fertilization in genetic variation.

4496725392D24338B420113DD638CBA3.description: Students will understand that genetic information coded in DNA is passed from parents to offspring by sexual and asexual reproduction. The basic structure of DNA is the same in all living things. Changes in DNA may alter genetic expression.

1B918DBD06484200A805D9D03249A147.description: Compare the structure and function of organ systems in one organism to the structure and function in another organism (e.g., chicken to sheep digestive system; fern to peach reproductive system).

C4D5CE24AF4445738480ED3027302D76.description: Relate the tissues that make up organs to the structure and function of the organ.

FD90DC8AE55640AAA4724883C6EEB4A4.description: Examine the relationships of organ systems within an organism (e.g., respiration to circulation, leaves to roots) and describe the relationship of structure to function in the relationship.

4D8DF26B68F64776B81471BD69471005.description: Describe the structure and function of various organ systems (i.e., digestion, respiration, circulation, protection and support, nervous) and how these systems contribute to homeostasis of the organism.

75F893393EDE470583AF51E8E21378D3.description: Relate the function of an organ to the function of an organ system.

33CE4092BC7F4990A33C877DC627197B.description: Describe the relationship between structure and function of organ systems in plants and animals.

EC164EBC69814E2BAB0DFB7F10743717.description: Research and report on technological developments related to organs.

1851A7FCEA384CD9A55EDC484C06B7EF.description: Compare the structure and function of organs in one organism to the structure and function of organs in another organism.

10E2EF1A9CAF49DBB508E8EBD79CDD71.description: Relate the structure of organs to the function of organs.

BE3A1700B8D6491E8DE7916A5C142F8F.description: Describe the function of various organs (e.g. heart, lungs, skin, leaf, stem, root, ovary).

904217047F4A41128620A303DEDF0004.description: Diagram and label the structure of the primary components of representative organs in plants and animals (e.g., heart - muscle tissue, valves and chambers; lung - trachea, bronchial, alveoli; leaf - veins, stomata; stem - xylem, phloem, cambium; root - tip, elongation, hairs; skin - layers, sweat glands, oil glands, hair follicles; ovaries - ova, follicles, corpus luteum).

350406BB8CF449CF81910073588B8FA3.description: Describe the structure and function of organs.

F38192C5D596429FB1496E874B5EF1FE.description: Students will understand the relationship between structure and function of organs and organ systems.

59BAF3CF4CF54AD2ACD53C9AFD49770D.description: Experiment with microorganisms and/or plants to investigate growth and reproduction.

DC75CC00B2CB4BCD94D005CA22F651BE.description: Describe the relationship between the organelles in a cell and the functions of that cell.

040DDD7D308D44E691B0A3B797519C00.description: Describe how the transport of materials in and out of cells enables cells to maintain homeostasis (i.e., osmosis, diffusion, active transport).

DC68F68D3ACE4305930D7339FC7B6E49.description: Describe cell theory and relate the nature of science to the development of cell theory (e.g., built upon previous knowledge, use of increasingly more sophisticated technology).

6251EF6E6B12409F81459C11485518BF.description: Explain how cells divide from existing cells.

BED033B992184D97B580E6DA5C473E52.description: Investigate the structure and function of cells and cell parts.

9B6EF63252A24D0685B5C3561E95A764.description: Measure the production of one or more of the products of either photosynthesis or respiration.

908C334DE6654D3E97607C0B3FCE404F.description: Illustrate the cycling of matter and the flow of energy through photosynthesis (e.g., by using light energy to combine CO2 and H2O to produce oxygen and sugars) and respiration (e.g., by releasing energy from sugar and O2 to produce CO2 and H2O).

6FCE67C932954A528CBCCE034DA982C6.description: Distinguish between autotrophic and heterotrophic cells.

FC11342EEC6E4076938A27496D0E075A.description: Describe the flow of energy and matter in cellular function.

1FAD4DDB5D4546F3A13D629B41147C16.description: Explain the role of enzymes in cell chemistry.

82C2FD93AC9D4C8C989C82C8D44EF3CF.description: Explain how the properties of water (e.g., cohesion, adhesion, heat capacity, solvent properties) contribute to maintenance of cells and living organisms.

F95DD7AD18784CBA8D251F7AC1B1F797.description: Identify the function of the four major macromolecules (i.e., carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids).

F8FC859FBC8E43C28E4DCAA004170293.description: List the major chemical elements in cells (i.e., carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorous, sulfur, trace elements).

A6037F005D0048CE80EE4FFCE61D92CA.description: Describe the fundamental chemistry of living cells.

FF1F423AA8894453A4E565DB56274C6D.description: Students will understand that all organisms are composed of one or more cells that are made of molecules, come from preexisting cells, and perform life functions.

23C7C32D5DBC49AFB3C9A488A07035B4.description: Research and evaluate local and global practices that affect ecosystems.

F37B1579806F41EBAAA74BC2F65CB461.description: Investigate an ecosystem using methods of science to gather quantitative and qualitative data that describe the ecosystem in detail.

7175E2920CAD462E93D45366639BEC52.description: Use data to interpret interactions among biotic and abiotic factors (e.g., pH, temperature, precipitation, populations, diversity) within an ecosystem.

EAB30063E2324D378FE05F755C5CA879.description: Formulate and test a hypothesis specific to the effect of changing one variable upon another in a small ecosystem.

CC81219D9D174A7F8E6F447E9A47E21D.description: Categorize relationships among living things according to predator-prey, competition, and symbiosis.

A4D8D501544848AC9A203F13884E98E5.description: Describe how interactions among organisms and their environment help shape ecosystems.

39BA7278954644918D6395147F66C274.description: Evaluate the impact of personal choices in relation to the cycling of matter within an ecosystem (e.g., impact of automobiles on the carbon cycle, impact on landfills of processed and packaged foods).

A234E16417DA4CD8ABA3E74046A94A2C.description: Distinguish between inference and evidence in a newspaper, magazine, journal, or Internet article that addresses an issue related to human impact on cycles of matter in an ecosystem and determine the bias in the article.

21D94A05EEE2489697BE80A9D3D22564.description: Explain how water is a limiting factor in various ecosystems.

9AEB1C90B31B44778CAD9C6F997A72E3.description: Use diagrams to trace the movement of matter through a cycle (i.e., carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, water) in a variety of biological communities and ecosystems.

F931A0EB14034876AA1313B47F7734F5.description: Explain relationships between matter cycles and organisms.

1A8B67F4B7D64860B44CBF510401C08B.description: Research food production in various parts of the world (e.g., industrialized societies' greater use of fossil fuel in food production, human health related to food product).

1BD2A31D9C4146E097CAAFFC660D4CA0.description: Compare the relative energy output expended by an organism in obtaining food to the energy gained from the food (e.g., hummingbird - energy expended hovering at a flower compared to the amount of energy gained from the nectar, coyote - chasing mice to the energy gained from catching one, energy expended in migration of birds to a location with seasonal abundance compared to energy gained by staying in a cold climate with limited food).

0B42D7EAA6454C18BEC76E138E54A3DD.description: Describe strategies used by organisms to balance the energy expended to obtain food to the energy gained from the food (e.g., migration to areas of seasonal abundance, switching type of prey based upon availability, hibernation or dormancy).

230ACF184BAB49879E291592642EE1F1.description: Compare the quantity of energy in the steps of an energy pyramid.

709497FCE47842F5A40D2179E4098495.description: Arrange components of a food chain according to energy flow.

3FBCF954783C4FA8900B3B7D50DB81AB.description: Summarize how energy flows through an ecosystem.

079D703E1F2843BBB1495BA06E6005BF.description: Students will understand that living organisms interact with one another and their environment.

document.title: Utah Core Standards for English Language Arts

01951BDEB4DF4570A39AE7733AE43831.description: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, reading and being read to, and responding to texts, including using frequently occurring conjunctions to signal simple relationships (e.g., because).

1F8AD2C0DFE94B7F927619F0B0E05AF9.description: Distinguish shades of meaning among verbs differing in manner (e.g., look, peek, glance, stare, glare, scowl) and adjectives differing in intensity (e.g., large, gigantic) by defining or choosing them or by acting out the meanings.

B8F4DF584700467FB76FF86B5CDEF81E.description: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (e.g., note places at home that are cozy).

01B1F5B261734179AA943E31873C1424.description: Define words by category and by one or more key attributes (e.g., a duck is a bird that swims; a tiger is a large cat with stripes).

40D9F8B84C8F4BF386EA4E289B8BFEB9.description: Sort words into categories (e.g., colors, clothing) to gain a sense of the concepts the categories represent.

72A22DCA80DD47A391A08C42F6DDCA57.description: With guidance and support from adults, demonstrate understanding of word relationships and nuances in word meanings.

42C4E691224342A69ED30A6D7F2BAB2A.description: Identify frequently occurring root words (e.g., look) and their inflectional forms (e.g., looks, looked, looking).

E7656301E663449D935C54F4E4D997DC.description: Use frequently occurring affixes as a clue to the meaning of a word.

70BD3F41BAEC40B59F1F4C200B54CE4A.description: Use sentence-level context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

6D600256378145208E0E4C00E47AFC23.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 1 reading and content, choosing flexibly from an array of strategies.

9B5D6435B54A4DEAA4BA0E05F3ADB81F.description: Spell untaught words phonetically, drawing on phonemic awareness and spelling conventions.

39B5E4933D4E4620AA658BBC538932FB.description: Use conventional spelling for words with common spelling patterns and for frequently occurring irregular words.

BA01F225421E44EB95D30180BB28A9D9.description: Use commas in dates and to separate single words in a series.

5EFC2C0F54524A6D80217C8FB590D2B7.description: Capitalize dates and names of people.

781A8C363A324393B061BDD75EF5AF63.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

03F397930ACE472E8FC5676A9D8F5929.description: Produce and expand complete simple and compound declarative, interrogative, imperative, and exclamatory sentences in response to prompts.

F6E48F95A1224F59915A6DAA32711C20.description: Use frequently occurring prepositions (e.g., during, beyond, toward).

6F54989821B64F2A82D616155AC7BCEA.description: Use frequently occurring conjunctions (e.g., and, but, or, so, because).

8B6F2F5CEDC94670AF7E68E0BE3BECA7.description: Use verbs to convey a sense of past, present, and future (e.g., Yesterday I walked home; Today I walk home; Tomorrow I will walk home).

B968795A83464C7497FA3C17A3A4E187.description: Use personal, possessive, and indefinite pronouns (e.g., I, me, my; they, them, their; anyone, everything).

497CD48EB15F49ED823822A9B044D871.description: Use singular and plural nouns with matching verbs in basic sentences (e.g., He hops; We hop).

8D9315E003E147D884C5663689789518.description: Use common, proper, and possessive nouns.

F04C4681D1C54A27A866894B6DDBD2DE.description: Print all upper- and lowercase letters.

424B3E96972F41859FDDB2565AB1A53E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

20BAB9DC6283407A9310F31EE407FC99.description: Acquire and use accurately a range of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when encountering an unknown term important to comprehension or expression.

D2A17A40D4A14512ABC73FF3F3CBA990.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

EDE0A5561E4D40AA85406740A34858D8.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases by using context clues, analyzing meaningful word parts, and consulting general and specialized reference materials, as appropriate.

B36C4DC9DCB045F1830A3A687EE63AEC.description: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when reading or listening.

017A6FAC6FD64BBE861C9533F2DDD77A.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

2F2AED9C78D044CE9C1EB0AFC88345BD.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

30B61A674ABA4B238499F2213D8FE487.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Language

7A897CBF5D464F5E8200681A2B20A9A3.description: Produce complete sentences when appropriate to task and situation.

0E2C3BFB81DA4C9D940D8531B6157AEB.description: Add drawings or other visual displays to descriptions when appropriate to clarify ideas, thoughts, and feelings.

E4B7FFF378F34E308E2BBD74FC2F5DC1.description: Describe people, places, things, and events with relevant details, expressing ideas and feelings clearly.

C0207C76FCB746BA9963080BD78120D7.description: Ask and answer questions about what a speaker says in order to gather additional information or clarify something that is not understood.

C032E97E244144CFA958481B1299E839.description: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media.

59CB85B7107E4FC898BD4BA1CCD8C347.description: Ask questions to clear up any confusion about the topics and texts under discussion.

FCDC20609F8A46A9A8B61D92E856A6A1.description: Build on others' talk in conversations by responding to the comments of others through multiple exchanges.

08CF1790D1EB45409D98B9214C702F9F.description: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions (e.g., listening to others with care, speaking one at a time about the topics and texts under discussion).

AD8817DBD41E4C43A29D069D69546536.description: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about grade 1 topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups

295A60EC994445CFA1B5A350B3BDEF9F.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and communicative tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

9F6DD682DD444F648179B3AC8462339F.description: Make strategic use of digital media and visual displays of data to express information and enhance understanding of presentations.

AC8430FDA20241089E41132477D0B795.description: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning and the organization, development, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

F7AA6AF2B6904ECD89B364F91733577A.description: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.

EC224DA1E3E64461A4B2B445AFC0B29F.description: Integrate and evaluate information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.

CAC9FC8A28CF47EE87D1174360F75008.description: Prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations with diverse partners, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.

A5194448F16D4130973F793D5257D96D.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Speaking and Listening

20B7D74EF360439FB53F7688C8139724.description: With guidance and support from adults, recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.

17BC83AE17704E2B8C2C1D483CB0CC45.description: Participate in shared research and writing projects (e.g., explore a number of "how-to" books on a given topic and use them to write a sequence of instructions).

D42ED6F4ADDB461C949FCEBA890BF479.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

1447DAE1DD604F8A9ABC05FD224D9B0A.description: With guidance and support from adults, use a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers.

5FE6FD3C56EB4C9F825DB04D9CCF5943.description: With guidance and support from adults, focus on a topic, respond to questions and suggestions from peers, and add details to strengthen writing as needed.

D04A26D605674C299D83C43C9FC251EB.description: Write narratives in which they recount two or more appropriately sequenced events, include some details regarding what happened, use temporal words to signal event order, and provide some sense of closure.

5ABB83903ABD4C17822779B6150FA86B.description: Write informative/explanatory texts in which they name a topic, supply some facts about the topic, and provide some sense of closure.

9C01B43E35BC42D28F97EBD10599C034.description: Write opinion pieces in which they introduce the topic or name the book they are writing about, state an opinion, supply a reason for the opinion, and provide some sense of closure.

4D4FC994DC724706841327E97FF4D211.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.

172AA9B315F34380A1B4013FCB1796B2.description: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

5E9D874236CC4B58BBADC864FCDED8E2.description: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, assess the credibility and accuracy of each source, and integrate the information while avoiding plagiarism.

73BF68B66672463D95E90E24F73E3A6B.description: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects based on focused questions, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.

76297DA380D141B491B984224BADDF1E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

CF37BF5C692B47D1AAAB9AC410111824.description: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing and to interact and collaborate with others.

E1C657211DFB42F7957A52952001F9B3.description: Develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.

D25472E0DFE7013134FF68A86D17958E.description: Analyze and critique the constructed meanings in a play.

D2543080DFE7013134FE68A86D17958E.description: Suggest ideas for improving artistic quality in classroom dramatizations and student productions.

D253F000DFE7013134FD68A86D17958E.description: Suggest ideas for improving student effectiveness in planning and playing dramatic presentations.

D253AAC0DFE7013134FC68A86D17958E.description: Describe and critique the perceived effectiveness of students' contributions to the collaborative process of developing dramatic presentations for informal and formal theatre.

D2534B20DFE7013134FB68A86D17958E.description: Identify and describe real life omissions left out of the play's world.

D252D0F0DFE7013134FA68A86D17958E.description: Identify and explain the similarities and differences between the play's world and one's own world.

D2529510DFE7013134F968A86D17958E.description: Analyze and explain how the world of the play, with its own identity, conflicts, and problems, is similar to and different from one's own world in real life.

D2525780DFE7013134F868A86D17958E.description: Analyzing and Constructing Meanings: The student will explain personal preferences and construct meanings by responding to improvised and scripted scenes and to theatre, film, television, and electronic media productions.

D25218A0DFE7013134F768A86D17958E.description: Plan and subordinate dance, music, and theatre equally in the service of one another in an original performance piece.

D251D930DFE7013134F668A86D17958E.description: Plan and integrate dance, music, and theatre equally in an original performance piece.

D25195F0DFE7013134F568A86D17958E.description: Select and integrate dance, music, and theatre equally in an original dramatic presentation.

D25152F0DFE7013134F468A86D17958E.description: Identify visual, aural, oral, and kinetic elements and explain how they are used to express ideas and emotions in television.

D25105B0DFE7013134F368A86D17958E.description: Identify visual, aural, oral, and kinetic elements and explain how they are used to express ideas and emotions in a performing arts event.

D2500350DFE7013134EF68A86D17958E.description: Understand the unique relationship between the audience and the performing arts.

D24FBF50DFE7013134EE68A86D17958E.description: Understanding Art Forms: The student will compare, connect, and incorporate art forms by describing and analyzing methods of presentation and audience response for theatre and dramatic media, including film, television, electronic media, and other art forms.
