comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
AED2D4A35E67494C9B841C33685540B7.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
594BAB12468F45D09B2AE7566131313D.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
B1AE7F1D837D43B09B17073F3700EE6F.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

989D9FF2BC1341C290934658C737FCDF.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

A39261E1581B4BDDA5FA99C83EFD45B2.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Utah Secondary Physical Education Core Curriculum

E5E05BAFE6CF462C893DE89445F33749.description: Participate in activities that offer social interaction with people of varying ability levels and different social and cultural backgrounds.

79ABD299459D49439C4F66B187A2E5D0.description: Resolve interpersonal conflicts with sensitivity to the rights and feelings of others.

0CF22EDD7C074F31950FF5E00998B646.description: Identify positive and negative peer influences.

F0BBD6ED83AC468A992D88459F6E2178.description: Analyze factors contributing to performance outcomes without blaming others.

BB9723E3411B474486425870333CF6A9.description: Work with a partner in fitness activities.

5156E8D9176E4BF38BF7E0A822C4A1D7.description: Demonstrate leadership in a number of activities.

C37BA65457304BBBA8A71ED46D484C51.description: Demonstrate the ability to work with others in activity settings.

5EC955BA73A14E9C8BFDC2CFD7A6FA95.description: Work to improve physical fitness and motor skills.

DBBC86A963D44A93A5F8EAA9EA4E945F.description: Strive to act independently of peer pressure.

3E9141BA77574B9EAA0B3C17FABA7D11.description: Accept the consequences of personal behavior choices.

C9F726889BE54BD3B338E01B71D855BE.description: Make responsible choices based on the safety of self and others when participating in physical activities.

E268FD7DCF9341199A79F80BCF5591BF.description: Identify and follow rules while playing sports and games, while keeping winning and losing in perspective.

3C0E2E7CCD084412B6195BCE3FCA2B95.description: Demonstrate the ability to make responsible choices in activity settings.

DBD49A9F339F4A1E965AC42ABA4FC061.description: Students will exhibit responsible personal and social behaviors that show respect for themselves and others in physical activity settings.

08BBDC7788F74725BBF6121C49E35126.description: Assess and adjust personal fitness plan utilizing computer software for feedback.

2033B4A31FA0405DAD0C45E9432B32EA.description: Adjust and monitor fitness and exercise programs using a variety of technological resources.

B26345667D874AAC9D38DC03D3BC9BCC.description: Discuss the importance of balance in developing strength in opposing muscle groups.

22DA73FAE86C4921ADE1896EF30B3519.description: Identify exercises that contribute to trunk stabilization.

7F5D1607B0884E8B870647E5C0CBD7F0.description: Demonstrate correct posture when lifting heavy objects.

E2478D989E8F4F2394975E514BF105D7.description: Demonstrate the biomechanical principles of posture during activity.

7C16EA5C78BC4E3F92E3E8E24FC7279C.description: Identify poor food choices and healthy alternatives.

332D88323BCA46B99187C9266E17FD89.description: Create a meal plan based on the food pyramid.

A859A9DEB3654B4EBCAFD924FC4840C7.description: Using a diet and activity log, analyze the balance between food intake and energy expenditure.

60CC13FDD19F44048FD309A99D1AB88F.description: Review the concept of energy balance.

74623EBC92AB46AFB6D197A21D50C76A.description: Describe the relationship between physical activity and proper nutritional choice.

D424690C851046F88332B8B4BB3152C9.description: Participate in a daily stretching program to promote flexibility.

325C6FC8CACD45DA8B3F59B4BC88E74E.description: Apply the FITT (frequency, intensity, time, type) guidelines to a number of activities.

895813A31C1246BDB26841CCDCC37E3F.description: Maintain a daily activity journal as a record of physical fitness activities.

6AE509A054F641AD8C168EE00AA7CDC0.description: Learn to relate pulse rate and physical energy expenditure.

C16212158C954AF98F469D41223D98C4.description: Define the elements of physical fitness.

8E448A80F3A34B92A278B32CA28E03AE.description: Demonstrate knowledge of the elements of physical fitness.

E8E6E87D90B54965AA8F14483AB4501A.description: Students will achieve and maintain health-enhancing levels of physical fitness.

AD2BC0EC3CF14229AD34D2DA3672E1E9.description: Explore a variety of nontraditional physical activities such as orienteering, field hockey, and rock climbing during and after school hours.

48EC7D8882AF41ABBD8F80FE118F463D.description: Participate on small teams to promote maximum participation and fitness outcomes.

809E3D53E3FF42D5BBC44EF2C69B17F9.description: Utilize the overload principle to improve all elements of physical fitness.

D7109DC23E864D1F9437A7088A76452B.description: Participate in activities that develop flexibility, muscular strength and endurance, and cardiovascular fitness.

3431C4940D92421AB95F0C3353CCB2AF.description: Participate in activities that promote physical fitness.

B5E7F5256D5D4B64B0F90BABF20799E7.description: Evaluate progress and adjust fitness plan to meet individual needs.

BC2DCB7E31114208839F436D54BA56B6.description: Monitor progress through periodic fitness tests, activity journals, and computer software programs.

AF47983D9AA54418B9D146ADAAEAE9C9.description: Design and implement a personal fitness program based on the fitness assessment results.

556A84731A704D86B7022BF21944A275.description: Determine personal fitness levels using a variety of assessment instruments.

970899DD0EB447B5B4D566EF3A02919D.description: Assess personal fitness level and maintain a basic exercise plan that incorporates all elements of physical fitness. Caution: Assessment of body composition is inappropriate at this level.

99EB2E84786F4A0CA7CDC96DA98A67C2.description: Students will participate regularly in physical activity.

B9DD84A636E44829B50DB168740A71A6.description: Understand the use of rubrics to assess performance levels.

01AD02D7E7124041B19B422026DCF0DB.description: Use visual and mental cues to learn and self-assess performance.

DB7C25D012DA4E5FB675D0BAFB9EB609.description: Recognize that time and effort are prerequisites for skill improvement.

358BAC18871C4C7890325D78E39CF20D.description: Set goals and monitor changes in the development of movement skills to improve performance.

54F9E6DB0DE9466B9F10A0A8613F48E4.description: Describe the key elements, such as balance and follow-through, in the execution of sport-specific skills.

881598BEB6B94B9E84453E07CC5EA181.description: Identify and analyze offensive and defensive strategies in a number of different activities.

37DA8CBF4145446BBA34AA08E50AE4B5.description: Apply the principle of transfer of learning by identifying similarities and differences of movement concepts to facilitate the learning of a new skill.

C6E978FD600C46B6946EE9F562B67CB5.description: Demonstrate ways to link and transfer basic manipulative skills and concepts to specialized sports activities.

6BC71125C4FE433A9F888380D119E713.description: Students will demonstrate an understanding of movement concepts, principles, strategies, and tactics as they apply to the learning and performance of physical activities.

B9C34256965847A1B40774CB5706099B.description: Perform rhythmic activities representing various cultures such as Native American, African, and Latin American dances.

AA942B6F12C84502B710CDEC7718AD54.description: Participate in a variety of dances such as square, folk, aerobic, modern, ballroom, and line.

AA835E72265647FD837A3E65B73CDCBB.description: Demonstrate correct technique in a variety of improvised rhythmic activities.

696484A5232F474E9663F55701BD64AF.description: Review and demonstrate correct weight transfer, follow-through, and body-target alignment in a variety of activities.

8CF9A8DA1C054101A41658FD3A515FAB.description: Combine skills with basic offensive and defensive strategies to participate in modified versions of individual and team sports.

1F3F8EB643AD4C429A552CDF75D830C7.description: Demonstrate the correct technique for a variety of movement skills.

56CF942B6D9A4AACA8AE079A9A346DA6.description: Students will demonstrate competency in motor skills and movement patterns needed to perform a variety of physical activities.

document.title: Utah Social Studies Core Curriculum Elementary Grades 3-6

E2F928F0DFE70131510B68A86D17958E.description: Identify a current issue facing the world and propose a role the United States could play in being part of a solution (e.g. genocide, child labor, civil rights, education, public health, environmental protections, suffrage, economic disparities).

E2F8E790DFE70131510A68A86D17958E.description: Assess differing points of view on the role of the US as a world power (e.g. influencing the spread of democracy, supporting the rule of law, advocating human rights, promoting environmental stewardship).

E2F8A670DFE70131510968A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the role of the United States as a world power.

E2F86360DFE70131510868A86D17958E.description: Identify leaders of social and political movements

E2F81B80DFE70131510768A86D17958E.description: Identify major social movements of the 20th century (e.g. the women's movement, the civil rights movement, child labor reforms).

E2F7CFF0DFE70131510668A86D17958E.description: Assess the impact of social and political movements in recent United States history.

E2F78CA0DFE70131510568A86D17958E.description: Analyze how the United States' involvement in World War II led to its emergence as a superpower.

E2F73D30DFE70131510468A86D17958E.description: Summarize the consequences of the Great Depression on the United States (e.g. mass migration, the New Deal).

E2F6EF70DFE70131510368A86D17958E.description: Review the impact of World War I on the United States.

E2F68BD0DFE70131510268A86D17958E.description: Describe the role of the United States during World War I, The Great Depression, and World War II.

E2F643E0DFE70131510168A86D17958E.description: The United States now has a range of influence that spans the globe. This emergence of power gained fullest expression in the 20th century. The touchstone events of war and worldwide economic depression, coupled with social movements based on the democratic ideals central to the United States Constitution, positioned the United States as a world superpower. With this power comes questions about the role and responsibilities the United States can and should play in the world.

E2F5EFF0DFE70131510068A86D17958E.description: Students will address the causes, consequences and implications of the emergence of the United States as a world power.

E2F5AD40DFE7013150FF68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the roles new immigrants played in the economy of this time.

E2F56330DFE7013150FE68A86D17958E.description: Describe the wide-ranging impact of the Industrial Revolution (e.g. inventions, industries, innovations).

E2F4FD50DFE7013150FD68A86D17958E.description: Assess how the free-market system in the United States serves as an engine of change and innovation.

E2F4A620DFE7013150FC68A86D17958E.description: Understand the impact of major economic forces at work in the post-Civil War.

E2F46120DFE7013150FB68A86D17958E.description: Examine the difficulties of reconciliation within the nation.

E2F40AE0DFE7013150FA68A86D17958E.description: Explain how the Civil War helped forge ideas of national identity.

E2F3C720DFE7013150F968A86D17958E.description: Contrast the impact of the war on individuals in various regions (e.g. North, South, West).

E2F382E0DFE7013150F868A86D17958E.description: Identify the key ideas, events, and leaders of the Civil War using primary sources (e.g. Gettysburg Address, Emancipation Proclamation, news accounts, photographic records, diaries).

E2F33E20DFE7013150F768A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the course of events of the Civil War and its impact both immediate and long-term.

E2F2F790DFE7013150F668A86D17958E.description: Identify the range of individual responses to the growing political conflicts between the North and South (e.g. states rights advocates, abolitionists, slaveholders, enslaved people).

E2F2B300DFE7013150F568A86D17958E.description: Compare how cultural and economic differences of the North and South led to tensions.

E2F26890DFE7013150F468A86D17958E.description: Describe the impact of physical geography on the cultures of the northern and southern regions (e.g. industrial resources, agriculture, climate).

E2F20900DFE7013150F368A86D17958E.description: Assess the geographic, cultural, political, and economic divisions between regions that contributed to the Civil War.

E2F1BB70DFE7013150F268A86D17958E.description: Assess the impact of expansion on native inhabitants of the west.

E2F16C00DFE7013150F168A86D17958E.description: Compare the trails that were important during westward expansion (e.g. Oregon, Mormon, Spanish, California).

E2F129D0DFE7013150F068A86D17958E.description: Examine causes and consequences of important events in the United States expansion (e.g. Louisiana Purchase, Lewis and Clark expedition, treaties with American Indians, Homestead Act, Trail of Tears, California Gold Rush).

E2F0E760DFE7013150EF68A86D17958E.description: Identify key reasons why people move and the traits necessary for survival.

E2F09D60DFE7013150EE68A86D17958E.description: Investigate the significant events during America's expansion and the roles people played.

E2F058A0DFE7013150ED68A86D17958E.description: As the United States expanded westward, major issues, some of them from the first years of the nation, began to challenge the stability of the nation. As the nation expanded, issues of states rights, the institution of slavery, and economic development culminated in a Civil War. This war formally ended slavery and strengthened the power of the Federal government. The era after the Civil War was a time of major economic development and technological innovation.

E2F01390DFE7013150EC68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand that the 19th century was a time of incredible change for the United States, including geographic expansion, constitutional crisis, and economic growth.

E2EFBFC0DFE7013150EB68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the impact of the Constitution on their lives today (e.g. freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly, petition).

E2EF5D80DFE7013150EA68A86D17958E.description: Identify how the rights of selected groups have changed and how the Constitution reflects those changes (e.g. women, enslaved people).

E2EF0B60DFE7013150E968A86D17958E.description: Explain the significance of the Bill of Rights.

E2EEBCD0DFE7013150E868A86D17958E.description: Assess how the US Constitution has been amended and interpreted over time, and the impact these amendments have had on the rights and responsibilities of citizens of the United States.

E2EE7CC0DFE7013150E768A86D17958E.description: Discover the basis for the patriotic and citizenship traditions we have today (i.e. Pledge of Allegiance, flag etiquette, voting).

E2EE3B80DFE7013150E668A86D17958E.description: Describe the concept of checks and balances.

E2EDF980DFE7013150E568A86D17958E.description: Explain the process of passing a law.

E2EDB550DFE7013150E468A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between the role of the Legislative, Executive, and Judicial branches of the government.

E2ED6D00DFE7013150E368A86D17958E.description: Analyze goals outlined in the Preamble.

E2ED1A70DFE7013150E268A86D17958E.description: Recognize ideas from documents used to develop the Constitution (e.g. Magna Carta, Iroquois Confederacy, Articles of Confederation, Virginia Plan).

E2ECB410DFE7013150E168A86D17958E.description: Assess the underlying principles of the US Constitution.

E2EC61B0DFE7013150E068A86D17958E.description: The new United States needed a set of rules. A group of leading thinkers of the Revolutionary era met to create a new document to lay out the form of the new government. Drawing upon ideas both old and new, and finding ways to compromise to meet the needs and demands of multiple interests, they created this new government charter called the Constitution. The Constitution created a strong national government with separate branches within the government to insure there were checks on power and balances of responsibilities. The Constitution has been changed, or amended, numerous times since then, first with the addition of the Bill of Rights.

E2EC2290DFE7013150DF68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the rights and responsibilities guaranteed in the United States Constitution and Bill of Rights.

E2EBE380DFE7013150DE68A86D17958E.description: Explain how the winning of the war set in motion a need for a new government that would serve the needs of the new states.

E2EBA250DFE7013150DD68A86D17958E.description: Assess how the Revolutionary War changed the way people thought about their own rights.

E2EB5D70DFE7013150DC68A86D17958E.description: Profile citizens who rose to greatness as leaders.

E2EB11E0DFE7013150DB68A86D17958E.description: Plot a time line of the key events of the Revolutionary War.

E2EAD2C0DFE7013150DA68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the Revolutionary War's impact on self-rule.

E2EA91C0DFE7013150D968A86D17958E.description: Explain the content and purpose for the Declaration of Independence.

E2EA4DC0DFE7013150D868A86D17958E.description: Analyze arguments both for and against declaring independence using primary sources from Loyalist and patriot perspectives.

E2EA0070DFE7013150D768A86D17958E.description: Explain the role of events that led to declaring independence (e.g., French and Indian War, Stamp Act, Boston Tea Party).

E2E9B0A0DFE7013150D668A86D17958E.description: Describe how the movement toward revolution culminated in a Declaration of Independence.

E2E95680DFE7013150D568A86D17958E.description: The English colonies in North America began to organize and discuss creating an independent form of government separate from England's rule. After making their case in their Declaration of Independence, the colonies engaged in a Revolutionary war that culminated in their independence and the creation of a new nation, the United States of America.

E2E91780DFE7013150D468A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the chronology and significance of key events leading to self-government.

E2E8D6E0DFE7013150D368A86D17958E.description: Describe the basic principles and purposes of the Iroquois Confederacy.

E2E89650DFE7013150D268A86D17958E.description: Explain how early leaders established the first colonial governments (e.g. Mayflower compact, charters).

E2E85640DFE7013150D168A86D17958E.description: Compare the varying degrees of freedom held by different groups (e.g. American Indians, landowners, women, indentured servants, enslaved people).

E2E812F0DFE7013150D068A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between the rights and responsibilities held by different groups of people during the colonial period.

E2E7C9E0DFE7013150CF68A86D17958E.description: Analyze and explain the population decline in American Indian populations (i.e. disease, warfare, displacement).

E2E77880DFE7013150CE68A86D17958E.description: Describe the cultural and economic impacts that occurred as a result of trade between North America and other markets (e.g., arts, language, ideas, the beginning and expansion of the slave trade, new agricultural markets).

E2E73300DFE7013150CD68A86D17958E.description: Assess the global impact of cultural and economic diffusion as a result of colonization.

E2E6EFF0DFE7013150CC68A86D17958E.description: Analyze contributions of American Indian people to the colonial settlements.

E2E6AB50DFE7013150CB68A86D17958E.description: Compare the geographic and cultural differences between the New England, Middle, and Southern colonies (e.g., religious, economic, political).

E2E66640DFE7013150CA68A86D17958E.description: Determine reasons for the exploration of North America (e.g., religious, economic, political).

E2E61DE0DFE7013150C968A86D17958E.description: Identify explorers who came to the Americas and the nations they represented.

E2E5C920DFE7013150C868A86D17958E.description: Explain how advances in technology lead to an increase in exploration (e.g. ship technology)

E2E58530DFE7013150C768A86D17958E.description: Using maps -- including pre-1492 maps -- and other geographic tools, locate and analyze the routes used by the explorers.

E2E53820DFE7013150C668A86D17958E.description: Describe and explain the growth and development of the early American colonies.

E2E4E7A0DFE7013150C568A86D17958E.description: The era of the exploration and colonization of the Americas by Europeans marked the beginning of the recorded history of what is now the United States. This period also marked the beginning of global trade and cultural exchanges that would alter the lives of people around the world. This era would significantly affect the range of personal freedom among individuals and groups in the Americas. The growing conflicts between American Indian populations and European colonists, and the expansion of the African slave trade provide contrasts to the emerging development of self-rule.

E2E4A450DFE7013150C468A86D17958E.description: Students will understand how the exploration and colonization of North America transformed human history.

D5810D50DFE7013139C368A86D17958E.description: Create a dance project from the sciences.

D580B2E0DFE7013139C268A86D17958E.description: Create a dance project that reveals understanding of a concept or idea from literature or poetry.

D5806CE0DFE7013139C168A86D17958E.description: Explore moving using these contrasts and mood of the painting. Set phrases, create dance. After showing, discuss choices.

D58029F0DFE7013139C068A86D17958E.description: Create a dance project that reveals similarities and differences between the arts.

D57FD1F0DFE7013139BF68A86D17958E.description: Make connections between dance and other disciplines.

D57F6950DFE7013139BE68A86D17958E.description: Compare traditional folk or ethnic dances around the world. Classify the form and compare the style and role various dances play in each culture.

D57F2470DFE7013139BD68A86D17958E.description: Identify the unique role of classical dances in world history; e.g., ballet, kabuki, and modern dance.

D57ED460DFE7013139BC68A86D17958E.description: Identify the unique role which theatrical dance has played in world history; e.g., the royal courts such as Japanese Bugaku, Indonesian Bedoyo, and stately ceremonies of African Kings.

D57E94F0DFE7013139BB68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and use the language of dance in world culture.

D57E55C0DFE7013139BA68A86D17958E.description: Create and perform an original dance which reflects a particular historical period, nation, region, or culture.

D57E1700DFE7013139B968A86D17958E.description: Learn and perform social dances; e.g., waltz, fox-trot, cha-cha, triple swing, or a current popular dance. Discuss proper social dance etiquette.

D57DD740DFE7013139B868A86D17958E.description: Learn and perform folk dances from around the world; e.g., D'Hammerschmidt Geseln from Germany, Mayim, Mayim from Israel, and Tiniklink from the Philippines.

D57D9760DFE7013139B768A86D17958E.description: Perform and understand dances and singing games from different time periods and cultures.

D57D4D20DFE7013139B668A86D17958E.description: Contextualizing: The student will understand and demonstrate dance in relation to its historical and cultural origins.

D57D0D00DFE7013139B568A86D17958E.description: After observing a dance, create a story, poem, prose, sculpture, painting, picture, one-act play, or music.

D57CCEC0DFE7013139B468A86D17958E.description: After seeing a dance, discuss the elements of form.

D57C8E80DFE7013139B368A86D17958E.description: Identify the skills a dancer must have.

D57C41B0DFE7013139B268A86D17958E.description: After observing a concert, discuss production aspects; e.g., lighting, music, costumes, scenery, props.

D57BF5C0DFE7013139B168A86D17958E.description: Explain how to progress from improvisation to making choices to the composition to choreographed dances to responding.

D57BA3C0DFE7013139B068A86D17958E.description: Observe and discuss movement solutions of other classmates/dancers; e.g., describe the unique or creative movement in the dance.

D57B4E20DFE7013139AF68A86D17958E.description: Create movement phrases demonstrating individual, partner, and group capabilities.

D57B0CF0DFE7013139AE68A86D17958E.description: Create and set sequences by recalling phrases from the above improvisations.

D57AC9D0DFE7013139AD68A86D17958E.description: Create and discuss movement solutions derived from movement exploration.

D57A86B0DFE7013139AC68A86D17958E.description: Explore in small groups choosing a theme and developing it, using the formative parts of choreography; e.g., repetition, transition, unity, variety, contrast, and climax.

D57A39F0DFE7013139AB68A86D17958E.description: Explore abstractions of shared feelings between people; e.g., using time, space, and energy, abstract feelings such as greetings and partings.

D579C170DFE7013139AA68A86D17958E.description: Explore with the class abstracting a visual or verbal image to movement; e.g., sculpture, painting, poem, feeling, texture, etc.

D5784C60DFE7013139A968A86D17958E.description: Explore the process of making a dance.

D5780420DFE7013139A868A86D17958E.description: Creating: The student will improvise, create, perform, and respond to movement solutions in the art form of dance.

D577B6B0DFE7013139A768A86D17958E.description: After seeing a dance, discuss energy; e.g., recall a movement phrase that used three or more kinds of energy qualities.

D5775CE0DFE7013139A668A86D17958E.description: Create a dance phrase in small groups that uses at least three contrasting kinds of energy. Create a beginning and an end. Show the class.

D576F410DFE7013139A568A86D17958E.description: Improvise moving to a variety of accompaniments using different kinds of energy; e.g., sustained, percussive, swing, collapse, vibratory, suspend, and explode.

D5767A70DFE7013139A468A86D17958E.description: Expand dance vocabulary with movement experiences using the basic qualities of energy and motion.

D5761750DFE7013139A368A86D17958E.description: Create a sequence using three different body parts as focal points while changing levels, directions, and timing. Perform for the class.

D575B710DFE7013139A268A86D17958E.description: Explore using isolated body parts as a focal point.

D5756530DFE7013139A168A86D17958E.description: Draw and create a diagram for movement on the floor.

D57513B0DFE7013139A068A86D17958E.description: Expand dance vocabulary with movement experiences in space.

D574B7B0DFE70131399F68A86D17958E.description: After seeing a dance, discuss time elements; e.g., identify a place where the dancers moved in syncopation.

D5743F00DFE70131399E68A86D17958E.description: Create, notate, and perform an 8-count rhythm pattern; e.g., 1-2-3-4 stretch, 5-6 turn, 7 jump, 8 run, run.

D573CD70DFE70131399D68A86D17958E.description: Clap and then move in syncopation (accenting in an unexpected place).

D5738F10DFE70131399C68A86D17958E.description: Review how to accent the first beat of 2/4, 3/4, 4/4, and 6/8 meters with body parts or by changing the shape of the whole body.

D5735050DFE70131399B68A86D17958E.description: Clap and then move to the beats of slow, medium, and fast tempi.

D5731100DFE70131399A68A86D17958E.description: Expand dance vocabulary with movement experiences in time.

D572D060DFE70131399968A86D17958E.description: Investigating: The student will identify and demonstrate movement elements in performing dance.

D5728870DFE70131399868A86D17958E.description: Design and execute student-created complex locomotor patterns. Variation: Create unusual combinations and variations; e.g., skipping with arms circling to the sides, galloping with legs extended to the side, sliding backward.

D57246A0DFE70131399768A86D17958E.description: Execute teacher directed combinations of locomotor steps; e.g., slide, slide, slide, straight-legged skip to the back, repeat across floor. Repeat other side.

D57207B0DFE70131399668A86D17958E.description: Review and demonstrate simple locomotor steps (walk, run, leap, hop, and jump) and the complex locomotor steps (skip, slide, and gallop).

D571C900DFE70131399568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate axial movements of stretching, bending, twisting, reaching, turning, and balancing.

D5718460DFE70131399468A86D17958E.description: Identify and execute axial and locomotor steps.

D57135A0DFE70131399368A86D17958E.description: Identify three personal goals that challenge the mind and the body and list specific steps to achieve those goals; e.g., focus the mind and body toward specific dance tasks, allow the movement to reflect inner feelings, explore activities that require immediate response to commands.

D570F220DFE70131399268A86D17958E.description: Create own warm-up and discuss how that warm-up prepares the body and mind for expressive purposes.

D5709BA0DFE70131399168A86D17958E.description: Increase balance, strength, and flexibility; e.g., stand on one leg and stretch the body with the other leg parallel to the floor.

D57057F0DFE70131399068A86D17958E.description: Warm up the body properly for activity.

D5700F50DFE70131398F68A86D17958E.description: Discuss and understand personal and group space.

D56FCBE0DFE70131398E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and implement safe dance practices; e.g., warm up the body before stretching, land toe-ball-heel, never bounce on a stretched muscle or force a stretch, always stretch after strengthening a muscle group to keep it healthy and in balance, knees over toes.

D56F8950DFE70131398D68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and avoid possible room or outdoor hazards; e.g., cement or tile floor, fixed obstacles, temperature extremes. Practice taking safety measures to prevent injuries such as wear tennis shoes, drink water, stay away from obstacles.

D56F4540DFE70131398C68A86D17958E.description: Participate safely and regularly in warm-up activities followed by strengthening, endurance, and flexibility exercises.

D56EF420DFE70131398B68A86D17958E.description: Moving: The student will identify and safely demonstrate knowledge of the body and movement skills in performing dance.

D51E5D90DFE70131394D68A86D17958E.description: Create a dance project from the sciences.

D51E1F60DFE70131394C68A86D17958E.description: Create a dance project from literature or poetry.

D51DDF80DFE70131394B68A86D17958E.description: Create a dance project from another art form.

D51D9C00DFE70131394A68A86D17958E.description: Make connections between dance and other disciplines.

D51D55D0DFE70131394968A86D17958E.description: Define and discuss classical dance forms; e.g., ballet, modern dance, jazz, or tap dance.

D51D0C60DFE70131394868A86D17958E.description: Attend a performance or watch a video of dancers from various ethnic communities and discuss the characteristics of the traditional dances.

D51CBE70DFE70131394768A86D17958E.description: Gather information and discuss the culture and the contributions made by various ethnic groups who make up the state's diverse community; e.g., Hispanic, Pacific Islanders, Native American, Asian, and African American.

D51C7A20DFE70131394668A86D17958E.description: Recognize and use the language of dance in world culture.

D51C3740DFE70131394568A86D17958E.description: Create an event that explores dance, music, food, and art of chosen cultures.

D51BF740DFE70131394468A86D17958E.description: Create a group folk dance to celebrate a historic event or holiday.

D51BB6F0DFE70131394368A86D17958E.description: Learn and perform folk dances associated with the history of the state.

D51B70B0DFE70131394268A86D17958E.description: Perform and understand dances and singing games from different time periods and cultures.

D51B20A0DFE70131394168A86D17958E.description: Contextualizing: The student will understand and demonstrate dance in relation to its historical and cultural origins.

D51ABE50DFE70131394068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate by moving, drawing, or writing an awareness of how dance can communicate an idea, feeling, or purpose.

D51A6EB0DFE70131393F68A86D17958E.description: After seeing a concert, evaluate the performance.

D51A2970DFE70131393E68A86D17958E.description: After seeing a dance concert, discuss dance production.

D519D9B0DFE70131393D68A86D17958E.description: Explain how to progress from exploration, to making choices, to creating choreography.

D51992F0DFE70131393C68A86D17958E.description: Observe and discuss movement solutions of other classmates/dancers.

D51931F0DFE70131393B68A86D17958E.description: Create and set sequences of spatial relationships by recalling phrases from the above improvisations.

D518E3E0DFE70131393A68A86D17958E.description: Create and discuss movement solutions derived from movement exploration.

D5189F10DFE70131393968A86D17958E.description: Explore with a partner the spatial relationship of meeting, parting, and passing.

D5185B40DFE70131393868A86D17958E.description: Pantomime sports activities, then abstract them into dance.

D5181910DFE70131393768A86D17958E.description: Explore contrasting qualities, such as heavy and light movement, with various body parts and discuss the differences.

D517D4D0DFE70131393668A86D17958E.description: Explore the process of making a dance.

D5178D00DFE70131393568A86D17958E.description: Creating: The student will improvise, create, perform, and respond to movement solutions in the art form of dance.

D5173D10DFE70131393468A86D17958E.description: After seeing a dance, recall a movement phrase that used a particular kind of energy. Identify the energy quality.

D516FBD0DFE70131393368A86D17958E.description: Create a sequence demonstrating varying qualities of motion; e.g., hover, slither, slash, press, and perch.

D516B9B0DFE70131393268A86D17958E.description: Improvise movement to demonstrate various qualities of motion; e.g., hover, slither, slash, press, and perch.

D5167490DFE70131393168A86D17958E.description: Expand dance vocabulary with movement experiences using the basic qualities of energy and motion.

D5162550DFE70131393068A86D17958E.description: After seeing a dance, identify spacial qualities such as use of focus, range of motion, positive and negative space.

D515BAD0DFE70131392F68A86D17958E.description: Explore spatial concepts by drawing patterns.

D5156B20DFE70131392E68A86D17958E.description: Explore shapes with a partner, connecting body parts; e.g., knee, elbow, foot, head, leg, back.

D5152B40DFE70131392D68A86D17958E.description: Create shapes that are off-balance or off-center, shapes that have a narrow base (e.g., balancing on one foot or one knee), and shapes that have a wide base (e.g., supporting the body's weight on two hands and two feet).

D514EB40DFE70131392C68A86D17958E.description: Identify and demonstrate positive and negative space by making shapes individually and with each other.

D514A9B0DFE70131392B68A86D17958E.description: Expand dance vocabulary with movement experiences in space.

D5146610DFE70131392A68A86D17958E.description: After seeing a dance, identify the musical forms used in the dance; e.g., ABA, round.

D5140BB0DFE70131392968A86D17958E.description: Recognize simple forms; e.g., ABA (chorus, verse, chorus) and simple rounds. Create movement phrases using the above forms.

D513A2B0DFE70131392868A86D17958E.description: Listen to various forms of music and (1) brainstorm about movement possibilities in relationship to the music, (2) improvise movement possibilities, and (3) discuss new or unusual solutions discovered for making dances.

D5136080DFE70131392768A86D17958E.description: Move the length of a 16-count metric phrase.

D5131DE0DFE70131392668A86D17958E.description: Clap and move the primary and secondary accents of 4/4 and 6/8 measures.

D512D930DFE70131392568A86D17958E.description: Expand dance vocabulary with movement experiences in time.

D5128F40DFE70131392468A86D17958E.description: Investigating: The student will identify and demonstrate movement elements in performing dance.

D5124500DFE70131392368A86D17958E.description: Create one's own locomotor pattern that moves across the floor and that can be repeated; utilize no more than four different locomotor steps.

D511FE10DFE70131392268A86D17958E.description: Understand and demonstrate teacher-created combinations of the basic locomotor steps of walk, run, leap, hop, jump, skip, gallop, and slide.

D511B4E0DFE70131392168A86D17958E.description: Review and execute the locomotor steps of walk, run, leap, hop, and jump, skip, slide, and gallop while moving through space.

D5117530DFE70131392068A86D17958E.description: Identify the five simple locomotor steps and the three complex locomotor steps; i.e., walk, run, leap, hop, and jump are simple; skip, slide, and gallop are complex.

D51132C0DFE70131391F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate axial movements of bending, twisting, reaching, and turning.

D510EBC0DFE70131391E68A86D17958E.description: Identify and execute axial and locomotor steps.

D510A3E0DFE70131391D68A86D17958E.description: Discuss a variety of possible goals; identify two personal goals to improve oneself as a dancer; e.g., fully extending feet, focus, balance, rhythmic accuracy, concentration.

D5104500DFE70131391C68A86D17958E.description: Show an increase in coordination, agility, alignment, and balance.

D50FF800DFE70131391B68A86D17958E.description: Show an increase in strength, endurance, and flexibility.

D50FAE50DFE70131391A68A86D17958E.description: Discuss and understand personal and group space.

D50F6C60DFE70131391968A86D17958E.description: Recognize and implement safe dance practices.

D50F2910DFE70131391868A86D17958E.description: Recognize and avoid hazards in the environment; e.g., cold or hot rooms, slippery floors, dancing on concrete or tile.

D50EE350DFE70131391768A86D17958E.description: Participate safely and regularly in warm-up activities followed by strengthening, endurance, and flexibility exercises.

D50E9110DFE70131391668A86D17958E.description: Moving: The student will identify and safely demonstrate knowledge of the body and movement skills in performing dance.

document.title: Utah Social Studies Core Curriculum Secondary 7-12

E11F14D0DFE701314D3568A86D17958E.description: Analyze the impact of international terrorism on the United States.

E11EBBC0DFE701314D3468A86D17958E.description: Determine the impact of environmentalism on the United States.

E11E58D0DFE701314D3368A86D17958E.description: Examine the "Reagan Revolution," its goals, success, and failures.

E11E09A0DFE701314D3268A86D17958E.description: Determine how politics was changed by the end of the Cold War.

E11DBA50DFE701314D3168A86D17958E.description: Trace the development of computers and the Internet and their impact on American business and globalization.

E11D5D40DFE701314D3068A86D17958E.description: Examine the effects of economics on modern society.

E11CFBA0DFE701314D2F68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the economy of the contemporary United States.

E11C8C90DFE701314D2E68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand economic and political changes in contemporary America.

E17E8300DFE701314D9168A86D17958E.description: Examine the impact of drugs on the counter-culture and the United States.

E17E2450DFE701314D9068A86D17958E.description: Assess the development of mass media as the voice of the counter-culture.

E17DB2D0DFE701314D8F68A86D17958E.description: Explain the continuation and contributions of the eastern Roman Empire, referred to as the Byzantine Empire, after the fall of Rome, including its influence on the spread of Christianity in Russia and Eastern Europe.

E17D4F80DFE701314D8E68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the impact of the counter-culture since the 1960s.

E17CF0F0DFE701314D8D68A86D17958E.description: Investigate the gains in civil rights made by the American Indian nations, Mexican Americans, and other ethnic groups in the last half of the twentieth century.

E17C70B0DFE701314D8C68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how the black civil rights movement utilized both social and political actions to achieve its goals.

E17C04B0DFE701314D8B68A86D17958E.description: Investigate the fight for the political, economic, and social equality of women.

E17BA950DFE701314D8A68A86D17958E.description: Identify the causes and consequences of civil rights legislation and court decisions.

E17B5170DFE701314D8968A86D17958E.description: Analyze how the civil rights movement affected United States society.

E17AFF00DFE701314D8868A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the emergence and development of the human rights and culture in the modern era.

E17AAB50DFE701314D8768A86D17958E.description: Examine the superpower status of the United States in the world.

E17A5240DFE701314D8668A86D17958E.description: Trace the events that resulted in the breakup of the USSR.

E179EE70DFE701314D8568A86D17958E.description: Compare differing American reactions to overseas military involvement.

E1799510DFE701314D8468A86D17958E.description: Investigate the end of the Cold War and examine America's role in the changing world.

E17939D0DFE701314D8368A86D17958E.description: Trace the development of space exploration.

E178D500DFE701314D8268A86D17958E.description: Examine the impact of McCarthyism and Watergate on citizens' attitudes toward government.

E17866F0DFE701314D8168A86D17958E.description: Analyze the Great Society programs aimed at ending poverty.

E177EFB0DFE701314D8068A86D17958E.description: Examine the successes and failures of the various political administrations; e.g., Kennedy, Johnson, Nixon.

E1779280DFE701314D7F68A86D17958E.description: Summarize the political, social, and economic reactions to the Cold War in the United States.

E1773460DFE701314D7E68A86D17958E.description: Investigate how the Vietnam War changed the nature of warfare.

E176C000DFE701314D7D68A86D17958E.description: Examine the various factors that drew the United States into conflict with North Vietnam and Ho Chi Minh.

E1765840DFE701314D7C68A86D17958E.description: Trace American and United Nations involvement in the Korean police action.

E1760450DFE701314D7B68A86D17958E.description: Explain America's reaction to the fall of China to Communism under Mao Zedong.

E175A7C0DFE701314D7A68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the Cold War ideology of the United States' involvement in Asia.

E1754E20DFE701314D7968A86D17958E.description: Examine the world's reaction to nuclear weapons.

E174F4B0DFE701314D7868A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the effectiveness of American post-war foreign policy in Europe and the Soviet Union's reaction.

E17492B0DFE701314D7768A86D17958E.description: Analyze the organization and operation of the United Nations.

E1743BB0DFE701314D7668A86D17958E.description: Investigate how the postwar goals and action of the United States and the Soviet Union were manifested throughout the world.

E173E730DFE701314D7568A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the United States' domestic and international position in the Cold War era.

E1738D00DFE701314D7468A86D17958E.description: Evaluate how technology changed the weapons used in World War II and introduced the atomic age.

E1731C50DFE701314D7368A86D17958E.description: Assess how the war expanded beyond military targets to civilian centers.

E172A460DFE701314D7268A86D17958E.description: Evaluate how the rules and weapons of war changed during World War II.

E171EC30DFE701314D7068A86D17958E.description: Examine the role women played in the wartime workforce.

E1718CE0DFE701314D6F68A86D17958E.description: Identify the impact of World War II on minority groups in America.

E1712760DFE701314D6E68A86D17958E.description: Examine the impact World War II had on the American home front.

E1338EB0DFE701314D6D68A86D17958E.description: Investigate the major campaigns of the United States in the European and Pacific theaters; e.g., Midway, D-Day, Battle of the Bulge, island hopping, and the bombing of Japan.

E13331A0DFE701314D6C68A86D17958E.description: Examine how the alliance systems led the United States into World War II.

E132DA30DFE701314D6B68A86D17958E.description: Determine how the attack on Pearl Harbor forced the United States out of isolationism.

E1325EF0DFE701314D6A68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the factors that led to militarism and fascist aggression in the world.

E131E9E0DFE701314D6968A86D17958E.description: Determine how America shifted from isolationism to intervention.

E1319A10DFE701314D6868A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the causes, course, and consequences of the United States' role in World War II.

E1314990DFE701314D6768A86D17958E.description: Investigate the shift of power from state to federal government.

E130F910DFE701314D6668A86D17958E.description: Explore the purposes and effectiveness of the New Deal; e.g., presidency, economics, politics.

E130A820DFE701314D6568A86D17958E.description: Analyze the long-term effects of the New Deal on the United States.

E1305570DFE701314D6468A86D17958E.description: Examine the social effects of the Great Depression.

E12FEFA0DFE701314D6368A86D17958E.description: Analyze the major causes of the Great Depression.

E12F8780DFE701314D6268A86D17958E.description: Investigate the impact of the Great Depression on the United States.

E12F2900DFE701314D6168A86D17958E.description: Students will understand how the Great Depression and the New Deal affected the United States.

E12EC710DFE701314D6068A86D17958E.description: Describe the changes in women's attitudes and roles in society.

E12E4AD0DFE701314D5F68A86D17958E.description: Account for the sudden growth of black consciousness.

E12DD340DFE701314D5E68A86D17958E.description: Examine the experiences of black Americans and women in the early 20th century.

E12D7F60DFE701314D5D68A86D17958E.description: Explain how the automobile affected the business and landscape of America.

E12D2320DFE701314D5C68A86D17958E.description: Assess how new inventions and consumerism influenced daily life.

E12CA7B0DFE701314D5B68A86D17958E.description: Investigate how mass media affected American society.

E12C3CB0DFE701314D5A68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how the United States coped with rapid economic and technological advances.

E12BE560DFE701314D5968A86D17958E.description: Students will understand how Americans reacted to rapid social change during the 1920s.

E12B9010DFE701314D5868A86D17958E.description: Examine the impact World War I had on the United States; e.g., government policy, industrial might, civil liberties.

E12B38B0DFE701314D5768A86D17958E.description: Determine the reasons the United States Senate refused to join the League of Nations.

E12ADBD0DFE701314D5668A86D17958E.description: Identify major causes of World War I and the United States' involvement and influence in the war; e.g., Wilson's Fourteen Points, the Versailles Treaty.

E12A6F70DFE701314D5568A86D17958E.description: Examine how World War I affected the military and the home front of the United States.

E12A0510DFE701314D5468A86D17958E.description: Assess how America's imperialism altered relationships with the Far East and Latin America.

E129A880DFE701314D5368A86D17958E.description: Examine the cause, course, and consequences of the Spanish-American War.

E12937C0DFE701314D5268A86D17958E.description: Determine the economic, social, and military affects of United States imperialism.

E128D7B0DFE701314D5168A86D17958E.description: Investigate how the United States became involved in imperialism and the Spanish-American War.

E12887E0DFE701314D5068A86D17958E.description: Students will understand how war affected the early 20th century.

E1283620DFE701314D4F68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the development of socialism in the United States.

E127E070DFE701314D4E68A86D17958E.description: Determine the impact of collective bargaining.

E1277FB0DFE701314D4D68A86D17958E.description: Trace the development of national labor unions.

E1271040DFE701314D4C68A86D17958E.description: Assess the growth and development of labor unions and their key leaders.

E126BC10DFE701314D4B68A86D17958E.description: Investigate the emerging civil rights movements for women and African Americans.

78719CF7F4E24DBFBE3BD3940316269E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

3609C2866C954998A1117FFF84F3C5A3.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
FFF7A9A3ED12448B98871CC09FC3E541.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
