40197D4FA81941B596BEF3C557E6D502.description: Research and report on the behavior of a species of Utah fish (e.g., feeding on the bottom or surface, time of year and movement of fish to spawn, types of food and how it is obtained).

1C92E45B9546432891976C1176574673.description: Describe how the behavior and adaptations of Utah mammals help them survive winter (e.g., obtaining food, building homes, hibernation, migration).

7EBBCE6D0CCB4656971BDBEE3835FD0B.description: Observe and record the behavior of birds (e.g., caring for young, obtaining food, surviving winter).

C16EDE4858FB44289CB9E20B4206FAD1.description: Observe and record the behavior of Utah animals.

164D16F2459E49D79C418463DC618B9E.description: Use a simple classification system to classify unfamiliar Utah plants or animals (e.g., fish/amphibians/reptile/bird/mammal, invertebrate/vertebrate, tree/shrub/grass, deciduous/conifers).

952C5F973429478B9DA62A5B66E038D4.description: Explain how scientists use classification schemes.

394479BB62F24EE891AFCE21C97093F6.description: Use a simple scheme to classify Utah plants and animals.

0D38F93E2EED41F794AFCBEE0A5AA1A0.description: Find examples of endangered Utah plants and animals and describe steps being taken to protect them.

CA0C49BB73134AD1919E5B7075E94AB8.description: Identify the effect elevation has on types of plants and animals that live in a specific wetland, forest, or desert.

2C2DA7C824B0416C9739BE44E7F97F19.description: Describe some of the interactions between animals and plants of a given environment (e.g., woodpecker eats insects that live on trees of a forest, brine shrimp of the Great Salt Lake eat algae and birds feed on brine shrimp).

1655DB137741486F915EB92B989D19EF.description: Cite examples of physical features that allow particular plants and animals to live in specific environments (e.g., duck has webbed feet, cactus has waxy coating).

069CDC9B2E6E4476AD7452E5CBBF21F2.description: Identify common plants and animals that inhabit Utah's forests, wetlands, and deserts.

2D21F4FF5F9A478C8E7DE535E2736D3B.description: Describe the common plants and animals found in Utah environments and how these organisms have adapted to the environment in which they live.

E82D35EF49B34AA88E982DE9CA7DBDAE.description: Create models of wetlands, forests, and deserts.

B222312B1DD64835B483F18175DD3668.description: Based upon information gathered, classify areas of Utah that are generally identified as wetlands, forests, or deserts.

61FB5770FE634E0EB461BFCD6A9EA932.description: Locate examples of areas that have characteristics of wetlands, forests, or deserts in Utah.

E07927A99F1142A2A4DDE136BFB65FEE.description: Describe Utah's wetlands (e.g., river, lake, stream, and marsh areas where water is a major feature of the environment) forests (e.g., oak, pine, aspen, juniper areas where trees are a major feature of the environment), and deserts (e.g., areas where the lack of water provided an environment where plants needing little water are a major feature of the environment).

DF09E834EDD345F4BAE0CCE444202B67.description: Compare the physical characteristics (e.g., precipitation, temperature, and surface terrain) of Utah's wetlands, forests, and deserts.

C82B6FC8C8C74AB3B0FDA09FBD31B5AA.description: Describe the physical characteristics of Utah's wetlands, forests, and deserts.

98E49FB9B5B440628F6FF321582FBE8C.description: Students will understand the physical characteristics of Utah's wetlands, forests, and deserts and identify common organisms for each environment.

D4D6533D7EDD46039A7D6260301BC124.description: Formulate questions that can be answered using information gathered on the extinction of dinosaurs.

488130F01A30492F8338DD3E0AE12777.description: Research information on two scientific explanations for the extinction of dinosaurs and other prehistoric organisms.

D01A4EE072744040849407AC71F4E9EB.description: Based on the fossils found in various locations, infer how Utah environments have changed over time (e.g., trilobite fossils indicate that Millard County was once covered by a large shallow ocean; dinosaur fossils and coal indicate that Emery and Uintah County were once tropical and swampy).

343B590A258E4468B321E906EDA0DF2F.description: Explain why fossils are usually found in sedimentary rock.

A3CE9EE8FB934ED9B205BA677FC0EBEA.description: Explain how fossils can be used to make inferences about past life, climate, geology, and environments.

2D453537D4CC4A02AD1500B611A6B933.description: Research locations where fossils are found in Utah and construct a simple fossil map.

D0B7DA2C4F11444BA1578424D5C17A70.description: Describe three ways fossils are formed in sedimentary rock (i.e., preserved organisms, mineral replacement of organisms, impressions or tracks).

87F40868BACD47228F30B2D15D90CF81.description: Identify features of fossils that can be used to compare them to living organisms that are familiar (e.g., shape, size and structure of skeleton, patterns of leaves).

5A5CB6B3A45A4935A050AEEC51202A7B.description: Describe Utah fossils and explain how they were formed.

BE6925657ABC4DED97A2E23F0BBB6F9A.description: Students will understand how fossils are formed, where they may be found in Utah, and how they can be used to make inferences.

6B17724AA8804D5987C71B1B31818945.description: Research and investigate ways to provide mineral nutrients for plants to grow without soil (e.g., grow plants in wet towels, grow plants in wet gravel, grow plants in water).

A1ED48A812C541CA969767000F6EF8C5.description: Explain how plants may help control the erosion of soil.

FC0B142907904A8D9D13189890ACEE25.description: Relate the components of soils to the growth of plants in soil (e.g., mineral nutrients, water).

513548455DF14E7FA876349CF53AE2AC.description: Diagram or model a soil profile showing topsoil, subsoil, and bedrock, and how the layers differ in composition.

8D70AA1B2D4842C8A9C502E1BCCDD610.description: Observe and list the components of soil (i.e., minerals, rocks, air, water, living and dead organisms) and distinguish between the living, nonliving, and once living components of soil.

E7D3B39E72D84A0EAE18005FE1728334.description: Observe the basic components of soil and relate the components to plant growth.

42C1A856CB994D79BCF58CFD08DBD876.description: Investigate layers of soil in the local area and predict the sources of the sand and rocks in the soil.

724196D4AEA5406EA3601EC06B0966E4.description: Model erosion of Earth materials and collection of these materials as part of the process that leads to soil (e.g., water moving sand in a playground area and depositing this sand in another area).

7958120461044A1BA000BDC7BA7C3D0F.description: Distinguish between weathering (i.e., wearing down and breaking of rock surfaces) and erosion (i.e., the movement of materials).

46E8357AA1D44B5FB95E290E3BA18F14.description: Identify the processes of physical weathering that break down rocks at Earth's surface (i.e., water movement, freezing, plant growth, wind).

69D6276319514095BA4B3324A9F910FD.description: Explain how the processes of weathering and erosion change and move materials that become soil.

26254BAE348A4476ADDA56F80B32B252.description: Classify common rocks found in Utah as sedimentary (i.e., sandstone, conglomerate, shale), igneous (i.e., basalt, granite, obsidian, pumice) and metamorphic (i.e., marble, gneiss, schist).

6B5C1B8A410E4526BBB7A5C355C8A407.description: Sort rocks by appearance according to the three basic types: sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic (e.g., sedimentary-rounded-appearing mineral and rock particles that are cemented together, often in layers; igneous-with or without observable crystals that are not in layers or with or without air holes or glass like; metamorphic -crystals/minerals, often in layers).

9DBFA53BF7254C9A8E714F2B1C407FAA.description: Observe rocks using a magnifying glass and draw shapes and colors of the minerals.

C1447F3D33E84763A80540741139D5CA.description: Describe the differences between minerals and rocks.

F8C8C5FFB90C480F86B60DD6A0AE50D0.description: Identify basic properties of minerals and rocks.

6FBB14F218F147BDA13BCDD12D602BE3.description: Students will understand the basic properties of rocks, the processes involved in the formation of soils, and the needs of plants provided by soil.

614BFEF3B4744BF9A7BA4C4FDCE39F5D.description: Relate weather forecast accuracy to evidence or tools used to make the forecast (e.g., feels like rain vs. barometer is dropping).

E29C8166018943579B44258A2C188119.description: Evaluate the accuracy of student and professional weather forecasts.

6C25A09F4A504876828F254CE99519FC.description: Predict weather and justify prediction with observable evidence.

A3041DFCBC234FE18011EF46F2AF04C7.description: Describe how weather and forecasts affect people's lives.

B28E2DB824A44EB3BA25C8C3E2A16FCF.description: Identify and use the tools of a meteorologist (e.g., measure rainfall using rain gauge, measure air pressure using barometer, measure temperature using a thermometer).

7545B42AEF974E619AADA18046F98512.description: Evaluate weather predictions based upon observational data.

19AE75C78375444886BE8E20AB0CCDA3.description: Infer relationships between wind and weather change (e.g., windy days often precede changes in the weather; south winds in Utah often precede a cold front coming from the north).

D4C24D503EDA4BFB8D419F179AEA261E.description: Graph recorded data to show daily and seasonal patterns in weather.

A21DFF468CC6481F996AABD4ACEDC5DF.description: Observe and record effects of air temperature on precipitation (e.g., below freezing results in snow, above freezing results in rain).

E69ACA8F439449CD9990A74DE31B426C.description: Interpret recorded weather data for simple patterns.

A35578ADE5F14388B6A9296C69ED1FEB.description: Compare the components of severe weather phenomena to normal weather conditions (e.g., thunderstorm with lightning and high winds compared to rainstorm with rain showers and breezes).

3E1CDF8025E14A8E92ECB18205057FAC.description: Investigate evidence that air is a substance (e.g., takes up space, moves as wind, temperature can be measured).

CAFCF577946542389608EE3C3088B777.description: Observe, measure, and record data on the basic elements of weather over a period of time (i.e., precipitation, air temperature, wind speed and direction, and air pressure).

992E9F778351424E994D9826CED228E7.description: Identify basic cloud types (i.e., cumulus, cirrus, stratus clouds).

4C303C8D3C5641F9B5159915CA2B9F67.description: Observe, measure, and record the basic elements of weather.

AB9EB7F6B3284D55AD43139DBF9F6BCE.description: Students will understand that the elements of weather can be observed, measured, and recorded to make predictions and determine simple weather patterns.

4221F218FEB34681B5AF8035669C5939.description: Describe how the water cycle relates to the water supply in your community.

534291B748C94CE4931CFD96E8E2C66B.description: Construct a model or diagram to show how water continuously moves through the water cycle over time.

F1ABE3568E824A88848127EECE8FAEF7.description: Identify locations that hold water as it passes through the water cycle (e.g., oceans, atmosphere, fresh surface water, snow, ice, and ground water).

D6E7C6C4C76F423A8CC0850C20AE8276.description: Describe the processes of evaporation, condensation, and precipitation as they relate to the water cycle.

A2F3D6BECC3B4AC4B7FC3C66F43090C8.description: Locate examples of evaporation and condensation in the water cycle (e.g., water evaporates when heated and clouds or dew forms when vapor is cooled).

46D41AF40BB94E6EA4B1DCD11236EC97.description: Investigate and record temperature data to show the effects of heat energy on changing the states of water.

77191EB8F4544EEC866B1E23CD30EC26.description: Compare the processes of evaporation and condensation of water.

DF7C1329E794459ABD161C0817D20E8B.description: Identify the sun as the source of energy that evaporates water from the surface of Earth.

6B8A6F038E464F1DABD72234CA7F0CB8.description: Identify the relative amount and kind of water found in various locations on Earth (e.g., oceans have most of the water, glaciers and snowfields contain most fresh water).

477DBC55DA7D4D3999B21E08EE1671A2.description: Describe the relationship between heat energy, evaporation and condensation of water on Earth

C7DB92AB65DD4A77A13166477DAEE11F.description: Students will understand that water changes state as it moves through the water cycle.

2A7C772280834183811FFE4CEBABBC6A.description: Collaborate with peers, experts, and others to contribute to a content-related knowledge base by using technology to compile, synthesize, produce, and disseminate information, models, and other creative works.

DCC27027141C494AA532E6813AFE6915.description: Investigate and apply expert systems, intelligent agents, and simulations in real-world situations.

28D13F74D8F8427EBF149270721C66C3.description: Select and apply technology tools for research, information analysis, problem-solving, and decision-making in content learning.

665E9BBCAB1C4B8E8B1220118474D570.description: Routinely and efficiently use on-line information resources to meet needs for collaboration, research, publications, communications, and productivity.

20CF6CCECB0C482CAE077EF3A652B677.description: Evaluate technology-based options, including distance and distributed education, for lifelong learning.

3719DA930DBD40199B498694F217759D.description: Use technology tools and resources for managing and communicating personal/professional information (e.g., finances, schedules, addresses, purchases, correspondence).

5B9BE9C7AC7C42589FD610993B516DA8.description: Demonstrate and advocate legal and ethical behaviors among peers, family, and community regarding the use of technology and information.

03AE09CC7E9D47529A876048EFB81D74.description: Analyze advantages and disadvantages of widespread use and reliance on technology in the workplace and in society as a whole.

FA2AEF95FF2E4E52B349DF204DC41D26.description: Make informed choices among technology systems, resources, and services.

BACFF96726B147A28635122AF91F3B5B.description: Identify capabilities and limitations of contemporary and emerging technology resources and assess the potential of these systems and services to address personal, lifelong learning, and workplace needs.

comments: All students should have opportunities to demonstrate the following performances as a consequence of learning about other core content. Students will be assessed during the spring of their 12th grade year. The assessment will include a keyboarding skill test, a technology literacy self-assessment, and the inclusion of at least two pieces of student work in an electronic portfolio.

27785DE920924658B12A37F4FF0D5788.description: Students employ technology in the development of strategies for solving problems in the real world.

40C741AEA93641B7BB9B89DC7747A400.description: Students use technology resources for solving problems and making informed decisions.

BE53DC41C6784435B3E7C5CAFFEF26EB.description: Students evaluate and select new information resources and technological innovations based on the appropriateness to specific tasks.

F9F8DA7F84664635974AF768FCF140B0.description: Students use technology tools to process data and report results.

D86643AA09E34ED9928048B519F5CA62.description: Students use technology to locate, evaluate, and collect information from a variety of sources.

26466685AFAB44D3B23CD9E73799C93A.description: Students use telecommunications to collaborate, publish, and interact with peers, experts, and other audiences.

0887705E31C9468C8F2961C491EE6CAF.description: Students use a variety of media and formats to communicate information and ideas effectively to multiple audiences.

7B986BEE3D8641E8A9A07F4A3D398A3B.description: Students use productivity tools to collaborate in constructing technology-enhanced models, preparing publications, and producing other creative works.

6B577989F12046CBA28613023F195C76.description: Students use technology tools to enhance learning, increase productivity, and promote creativity.

1F5A21EBD2A2412290E6F04DB75CF404.description: Students develop positive attitudes toward technology uses that support lifelong learning, collaboration, personal pursuits, and productivity.

AE7C922051C54623B17EEFF56F907CBA.description: Students practice responsible use of technology systems, information, and software.

914B09B8ED6548FBAF4A5AA86E0F7399.description: Students understand the ethical, cultural, and societal issues related to technology.

96D3F0DD784749FA9A6598C927402C94.description: Students are proficient in the use of technology.

E6E7A098A76E470491071357F2B60BD3.description: Students demonstrate a sound understanding of the nature and operation of technology systems.

0A55D52A8E514090B590BE75EE77868C.description: Technology Foundation Standards for Students K-12

D4ED65F0DFE70131391468A86D17958E.description: Create a movement project from an idea from the sciences.

D4ED0BF0DFE70131391368A86D17958E.description: Create a movement project from an idea from literature or poetry.

D4ECBAD0DFE70131391268A86D17958E.description: Create a movement project from an idea from one of the arts.

D4EC73B0DFE70131391168A86D17958E.description: Make connections between dance and other disciplines.

D4EC31B0DFE70131391068A86D17958E.description: Identify the various cultures represented in the community. Discuss the dances, crafts, music, and art that makes each culture unique.

D4EBF1F0DFE70131390F68A86D17958E.description: Study the dance and art of another culture and discuss why these dances were created and why they are still important today.

D4EBB090DFE70131390E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and use the language of dance in world culture.

D4EB6840DFE70131390D68A86D17958E.description: Create an original ritual or ceremonial dance based on planting, harvesting, or the cycles of seasons.

D4EB0A60DFE70131390C68A86D17958E.description: Create an original folk dance based on ideas or events within the community; e.g., ideas from local celebrations, current issues, or traffic patterns.

D4EAC1D0DFE70131390B68A86D17958E.description: Describe the differences in these dance forms, why they are created, and the role they play today.

D4EA73A0DFE70131390A68A86D17958E.description: Observe a live performance or video of ritual and/or folk dance; e.g., Hispanic, Pacific Islanders, Native American, Asian, and African American.

D4EA2ED0DFE70131390968A86D17958E.description: Learn and perform simple traditional folk dances or singing games.

D4E9EDA0DFE70131390868A86D17958E.description: Perform and understand dances and singing games from different time periods and cultures.

D4E9A840DFE70131390768A86D17958E.description: Contextualizing: The student will understand and demonstrate dance in relation to its historical and cultural origins.

D4E95C30DFE70131390668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate by moving, drawing, or writing an awareness of how dance can communicate an idea, feeling, or purpose.

D4E91A50DFE70131390568A86D17958E.description: Explain how to progress from exploring to making choices to creating choreography.

D4E8D710DFE70131390468A86D17958E.description: Evaluate success in using personal space, landing quietly on feet, following directions, remembering sequences, and using unique and/or creative movements.

D4E895F0DFE70131390368A86D17958E.description: Observe and discuss movement solutions of other classmates/dancers.

D4E85170DFE70131390268A86D17958E.description: Create and practice a pattern of movement with a clear beginning and a clear ending.

D4E80B50DFE70131390168A86D17958E.description: Create and discuss movement solutions derived from movement exploration.

D4E7C440DFE70131390068A86D17958E.description: Make symmetrical or asymmetrical shapes that sustain themselves for the length of whole and half notes. Make these shapes on different levels and/or facing different directions.

D4E77B70DFE7013138FF68A86D17958E.description: Experiment with a movement sequence or phrase by combining directional changes of locomotor steps that use quarter notes and eighth notes; e.g., walk, hop, run, and jump.

D4E73D40DFE7013138FE68A86D17958E.description: Experiment with a movement sequence based on a nonmetric image; e.g., sneeze or a tickle.

D4E6FEB0DFE7013138FD68A86D17958E.description: Explore the process of making a dance.

D4E6BEF0DFE7013138FC68A86D17958E.description: Creating: The student will improvise, create, perform, and respond to movement solutions in the art form of dance.

D4E67F20DFE7013138FB68A86D17958E.description: After seeing a dance, describe the element of energy.

D4E63CA0DFE7013138FA68A86D17958E.description: Order a sequence of improvised movements that demonstrate changes in quality of motion; e.g., choose descriptive words such as perch, jab, melt, slither.

D4E5F6F0DFE7013138F968A86D17958E.description: Expand dance vocabulary with movement experiences using the basic qualities of energy and motion.

D4E598E0DFE7013138F868A86D17958E.description: After seeing a dance, discuss the element of space; e.g., recognize the locomotor steps the dancers used.

D4E54DC0DFE7013138F768A86D17958E.description: Create with a partner a repeatable locomotor pattern moving through space with meeting, parting, passing, and circling.

D4E4F1C0DFE7013138F668A86D17958E.description: Create simple locomotor combinations of moving forward, backward, sideways, and circling.

D4E49A50DFE7013138F568A86D17958E.description: Create a series of shapes on different levels and design moving transitions between them.

D4E445A0DFE7013138F468A86D17958E.description: Expand dance vocabulary with movement experiences in space.

D4E3F800DFE7013138F368A86D17958E.description: After seeing a dance, recognize and describe the use of time.

D4E3B450DFE7013138F268A86D17958E.description: Move in metric time to the value of whole, half, quarter, and eighth notes.

D4E36E00DFE7013138F168A86D17958E.description: Explore the timing and dynamics of nonmetric rhythms through movement.

D4E32690DFE7013138F068A86D17958E.description: Clap and then move in 6/8 time, accenting the first beat of every measure. Change the body part, direction, level, or energy with each new accent/measure.

D4E2E0B0DFE7013138EF68A86D17958E.description: Expand dance vocabulary with movement experiences in time.

D4E28180DFE7013138EE68A86D17958E.description: Investigating: The student will identify and demonstrate movement elements in performing dance.

D4E241E0DFE7013138ED68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate increased control in the locomotor steps; e.g., start and stop, vary the tempo, lead with the left as well as the right foot.

D4E20510DFE7013138EC68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate basic locomotor steps with unusual variations of walk, run, hop, jump, leap, skip, slide, and gallop.

D4E1C7E0DFE7013138EB68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate axial movements of bending, twisting, reaching, and turning.

D4E18A20DFE7013138EA68A86D17958E.description: Identify and execute axial and locomotor steps.

D4E149B0DFE7013138E968A86D17958E.description: Show an increase in balance and strength.

D4E0F2E0DFE7013138E868A86D17958E.description: Show an increase in coordination, agility, alignment, and balance.

D4E0B1B0DFE7013138E768A86D17958E.description: Show an increase in strength, endurance, and flexibility.

D4E071D0DFE7013138E668A86D17958E.description: Understand, define, and demonstrate personal space in stationary warm-up activities. Understand group space by filling the space evenly in locomotor activities.

D4E03220DFE7013138E568A86D17958E.description: Participate in dance with an awareness of appropriate safety concerns; e.g., warming up before stretching, never bouncing on a stretched muscle, drinking water, knees over toes.

D4DFF1D0DFE7013138E468A86D17958E.description: Recognize and avoid possible room or outdoor hazards.

D4DFAF30DFE7013138E368A86D17958E.description: Participate safely and regularly in warm-up activities followed by strengthening, endurance, and flexibility exercises.

D4DF62A0DFE7013138E268A86D17958E.description: Moving: The student will identify and safely demonstrate knowledge of the body and movement skills in performing dance.

CEB66F10DFE70131309068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate familiarity with suggested listening selections.

CEB62A40DFE70131308F68A86D17958E.description: Describe and identify the following in familiar songs and listening selections: solo/chorus (call/response), AB, ABA, rondo, theme and variations, introduction, and ending (coda).

CEB5E4F0DFE70131308E68A86D17958E.description: Identify by sight and sound and categorize into instrument families the trombone, tuba, and viola.

CEB58B20DFE70131308D68A86D17958E.description: Illustrate how forms and structures affect an environment and relate to science, art, theatre, dance, mathematics, health, and literature.

CEB50AA0DFE70131308C68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate how the repetition and contrast of phrases create musical forms.

CEB4BEE0DFE70131308B68A86D17958E.description: Explain how the music can communicate a certain meaning or serve a specific purpose.

CEB47FB0DFE70131308A68A86D17958E.description: Explain, demonstrate, and judge ability to exhibit appropriate audience etiquette according to type of musical performance.

CEB43EE0DFE70131308968A86D17958E.description: Perceive and respond to the messages in music and the use of music elements.

CEB3FC50DFE70131308868A86D17958E.description: Plan, practice, self-assess, refine, present, and reflect on a simple performance that demonstrates all of the skills learned in each of the standards.

CEB3B540DFE70131308768A86D17958E.description: Formulate suggestions for improvement in music performances referring to the skills listed above.

CEB36820DFE70131308668A86D17958E.description: Examine personal success and the achievement of others in the following: stage presence; watching the conductor; keeping a steady beat; singing in a voice free from strain; using proper playing and handling techniques of instruments; performing correct volume, pitches, and rhythm; starting and stopping together.

CEB323D0DFE70131308568A86D17958E.description: Recognize quality while creating a music performance.

CEB2DFF0DFE70131308468A86D17958E.description: Listening: The student will listen to, analyze, and describe music.

CEB29CB0DFE70131308368A86D17958E.description: Draw and explain the use of sharps, flats, and key signatures.

CEB24D00DFE70131308268A86D17958E.description: Identify and explain the various intervals in pitch patterns notated on staff and the use of ledger lines.

CEB1FBA0DFE70131308168A86D17958E.description: Explain fermata, tempo markings, sixteenths, half notes, dotted half notes, 2/4, 3/4, and 4/4 meter, and the subsequent bar lines and measures in rhythm patterns.

CEB1AFE0DFE70131308068A86D17958E.description: Notate as a class short rhythm and pitch patterns created by the teacher, individuals, and the class.

CEB16E40DFE70131307F68A86D17958E.description: Use the staff system to document arrangements and compositions limited rhythmically to quarter notes/rests and eighth note pairs, and limited melodically to do, re, mi, so, la.

CEB04CA0DFE70131307B68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast creating style in music with creating style in dance movements, paintings, stories, plays, statues, buildings, commercials, movies, etc.

CEB003A0DFE70131307A68A86D17958E.description: Build and demonstrate a simple instrument to provide sound effects for any of the above projects.

CEAFC070DFE70131307968A86D17958E.description: Create together a new song and/or a new chant ("rap").

CEAF7E20DFE70131307868A86D17958E.description: Create, plan, practice, and perform a familiar song in various styles.

CEAF3CE0DFE70131307768A86D17958E.description: Improvise a soundtrack for a story and/or a poem.

CEAEF7A0DFE70131307668A86D17958E.description: Improvise simple rhythm and/or melody patterns to echo back and forth and manipulate in a variety of ways to create various styles, first with the voice and then with found sounds or instruments.

CEAEAF90DFE70131307568A86D17958E.description: Create original music and add expression and new form to existing music.

CEB12C80DFE70131307E68A86D17958E.description: Balance reason and emotion in creating, practicing, and performing.

CEB0E960DFE70131307D68A86D17958E.description: Exhibit through music an appreciation for the subtle beauties inherent in everyday life.

CEB0A220DFE70131307C68A86D17958E.description: Express ideas, thoughts, and emotions aesthetically through singing, playing, and/or creating.

CEAE6270DFE70131307468A86D17958E.description: Creating: The student will create music through improvising, arranging, and composing.

CEAE1840DFE70131307368A86D17958E.description: Assess ability to make good musical sense by "breathing" where the phrases are.

CEADC430DFE70131307268A86D17958E.description: Determine success in accompanying without covering up the melody.

CEAD7120DFE70131307168A86D17958E.description: Rate success in playing even, dotted, and syncopated and rhythm/melody patterns in echo to the teacher.

CEAD2730DFE70131307068A86D17958E.description: Judge success in playing simple melodies on the recorder or keyboard by rote and/or note reading.

CEACE000DFE70131306F68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate success in playing with a beautiful tone, steady beat, starting/stopping together, and at indicated volume and tempo on a variety of classroom instruments.

CEAC8570DFE70131306E68A86D17958E.description: Perform independently or with others simple melodies and accompaniments on classroom instruments.

CEAC41B0DFE70131306D68A86D17958E.description: Add instrumental sounds to known songs of various cultures.

CEAC0410DFE70131306C68A86D17958E.description: Judge success in using proper playing and handling techniques on a variety of classroom instruments.

CEABC680DFE70131306B68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate various timbres and effects of simple instruments.

CEAB8820DFE70131306A68A86D17958E.description: Discover and demonstrate sounds on simple instruments of the classroom and various cultures.

CEAB4740DFE70131306968A86D17958E.description: Playing: The student will play instruments as a means of musical expression.

CEAB0190DFE70131306868A86D17958E.description: Play singing games, enjoy traditional folk dances and patriotic songs related to the cultures of Utah's history. Explain what they mean personally.

CEAAB850DFE70131306768A86D17958E.description: Describe how music is used by cultures in Utah's history.

CEAA7A90DFE70131306668A86D17958E.description: Share songs, instruments, and music enjoyed by various cultures in the history of Utah.

CEAA3CC0DFE70131306568A86D17958E.description: Discover how songs, singing games, and dances relate to various cultures in the history of Utah.

CEA93860DFE70131306168A86D17958E.description: Determine success in singing simple rhythm and pitch patterns accurately.

CEA8E720DFE70131306068A86D17958E.description: Judge success in performing memorized songs together with expressive precision.

CEA89460DFE70131305F68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate success in singing an assigned part.

CEA853B0DFE70131305E68A86D17958E.description: Use the speaking and singing voice in a creative way to characterize a chosen text through manipulation of pitch, volume, tempo, and timbre.

CEA81290DFE70131305D68A86D17958E.description: Sing a variety of many simple songs and singing games in tune, in a natural voice, free from strain.

CEA7CE00DFE70131305C68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate ability to sing in tune on an assigned part, with expression, accuracy, and free from strain.

CEA9FF10DFE70131306468A86D17958E.description: Show changes in meter, melodic direction, dynamics, timbre, tempo, rhythm, and form through body movement.

CEA9BFE0DFE70131306368A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the beat and the pattern of accents through clapping, tapping, marching, hand jives, and circle games.

CEA97F20DFE70131306268A86D17958E.description: Use body movement to internalize sounds.

CEA77A40DFE70131305B68A86D17958E.description: Singing: The student will develop the voice and body as instruments of musical expression.

document.title: Utah Science with Engineering Education (SEEd) Standards

31BEF82AACBA49249E1AF320D3BCE7DD.description: Analyze data to compare patterns in the embryological development across multiple species to identify similarities and differences not evident in the fully formed anatomy.

A2E33E791BFA4B2E94DCDAFFD07C02F6.description: Construct explanations that describe the patterns of body structure similarities and differences between modern organisms, and between ancient and modern organisms, to infer possible evolutionary relationships.

E0266B4F19314F3FA50A160A052B2C81.description: Analyze and interpret data for patterns in the fossil record that document the existence, diversity, extinction, and change of life forms throughout the history of life on Earth, under the assumption that natural laws operate today as in the past.

209DF4889A804BF1B5697CAD00E49937.description: Construct an explanation that describes how the genetic variation of traits in a population can affect some individuals' probability of surviving and reproducing in a specific environment. Over time, specific traits may increase or decrease in populations. Emphasize the use of proportional reasoning to support explanations of trends in changes to populations over time.
comments: Examples could include camouflage, variation of body shape, speed and agility, or drought tolerance.

F02BA705965A4741AE7BC2ACBA128194.description: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about the technologies that have changed the way humans affect the inheritance of desired traits in organisms. Analyze data from tests or simulations to determine the best solution to achieve success in cultivating selected desired traits in organisms.
comments: Examples could include artificial selection, genetic modification, animal husbandry, and gene therapy.

DF74684032274262AFDEBDBBBA69B79C.description: Develop and use a model to describe why genetic mutations may result in harmful, beneficial, or neutral effects to the structure and function of the organism. Emphasize the conceptual idea that changes to traits can happen because of genetic mutations. Specific changes of genes at the molecular level, mechanisms for protein synthesis, and specific types of mutations will be introduced at the high school level.

D6779DC9C0784BA28D6A7F37B2F4B3AC.description: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about specific animal and plant adaptations and structures that affect the probability of successful reproduction.
comments: Examples of adaptations could include nest building to protect young from the cold, herding of animals to protect young from predators, vocalization of animals and colorful plumage to attract mates for breeding, bright flowers attracting butterflies that transfer pollen, flower nectar and odors that attract insects that transfer pollen, and hard shells on nuts that squirrels bury.

FC3BC60D73264BB1BA01F730983F8D2C.description: Develop and use a model to explain the effects that different types of reproduction have on genetic variation, including asexual and sexual reproduction.

79F62B189EEA43939BA3A0DFB6617544.description: Construct an explanation using evidence to explain how body systems have various levels of organization. Emphasize understanding that cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form systems specialized for particular body functions.
comments: Examples could include relationships between the circulatory, excretory, digestive, respiratory, muscular, skeletal, and nervous systems. Specific organ functions will be taught at the high school level.

4E5886CCEBB54D8CB56B853AF5143779.description: Develop and use a model to describe the function of a cell in living systems and the way parts of cells contribute to cell function. Emphasize the cell as a system, including the interrelating roles of the nucleus, chloroplasts, mitochondria, cell membrane, and cell wall.

D0A4D4F5A2E24167BDC1D1B075868034.description: Plan and carry out an investigation that provides evidence that the basic structures of living things are cells. Emphasize that cells can form single-celled or multicellular organisms, and that multicellular organisms are made of different types of cells.

1BFAFF3FDFFE49FAAC75965A964D6984.description: Make an argument from evidence for how the geologic time scale shows the age and history of Earth. Emphasize scientific evidence from rock strata, the fossil record, and the principles of relative dating, such as superposition, uniformitarianism and recognizing unconformities.

9AF9521FA9994F639F0AF7EA3318B6AF.description:
Ask questions and analyze and interpret data about the patterns between plate tectonics and:
  1. the occurrence of earthquakes and volcanoes.
  2. Continental and ocean floor features.
  3. the distribution of rocks and fossils.
comments: Examples could include identifying patterns on maps of earthquakes and volcanoes relative to plate boundaries, the shapes of the continents, the locations of ocean structures (including mountains, volcanoes, faults, and trenches), and similarities of rock and fossil types on different continents.

2E4362190B7E467284E970E2B3563C17.description: Develop and use a scale model of the matter in the Earth's interior to demonstrate how differences in density and chemical composition (silicon, oxygen, iron, and magnesium) cause the formation of the crust, mantle, and core.

71DA3A6CF02043F0B591FFF52E461198.description: Ask questions to identify constraints of specific geologic hazards and evaluate competing design solutions for maintaining the stability of human-engineered structures, such as homes, roads, and bridges.
comments: Examples of geologic hazards could include earthquakes, landslides, or floods.

CC369A78CCD44846BCBDC3D72315CE23.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how processes have changed Earth's surface at varying time and spatial scales. Examples of processes that occur at varying time scales could include slow plate motions or rapid landslides.
comments: Examples of processes that occur at varying spatial scales could include uplift of a mountain range or deposition of fine sediments.

4E2FA9F851C64F03B87CFDA3B46B736E.description: Develop a model of the rock cycle to describe the relationship between energy flow and matter cycling that create igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks. Emphasize the processes of melting, crystallization, weathering, deposition, sedimentation, and deformation, which act together to form minerals and rocks.

08654A7FCF024B3F81CF2880CBD954F1.description: Engage in argument from evidence to support the claim that gravitational interactions within a system are attractive and dependent upon the masses of interacting objects.
comments: Examples of evidence for arguments could include mathematical data generated from various simulations.

1D24BE742775405F9DFF2C2AC5FF4771.description: Collect and analyze data to determine the factors that affect the strength of electric and magnetic forces.
comments: Examples could include electromagnets, electric motors, or generators. Examples of data could include the effect of the number of turns of wire on the strength of an electromagnet, or of increasing the number or strength of magnets on the speed of an electric motor.

A4C9C3314D2140DA88922954CD585B8A.description: Construct a model using observational evidence to describe the nature of fields existing between objects that exert forces on each other even though the objects are not in contact. Emphasize the cause and effect relationship between properties of objects (such as magnets or electrically charged objects) and the forces they exert.

0BC00F3F33E645DBBB4744801FD9DEFF.description: Apply Newton's Third Law to design a solution to a problem involving the motion of two colliding objects in a system.
comments: Examples could include collisions between two moving objects or between a moving object and a stationary object.

BC4CC5BF99B34040970768CDA498A495.description: Carry out an investigation which provides evidence that a change in an object's motion is dependent on the mass of the object and the sum of the forces acting on it. Various experimental designs should be evaluated to determine how well the investigation measures an object's motion. Emphasize conceptual understanding of Newton's First and Second Laws. Calculations will only focus on one-dimensional movement; the use of vectors will be introduced in high school.

3815149A096B47E4A90285DFB26300A8.description: Participate in an activity that simulates the demands and responsibilities of parenting.

CD38960FC3C446DB85843DC70B658D86.description: Neglect: Failing to adequately provide for the child's safety, as well as physical and emotional needs. Children who are unsupervised also fall under the neglect category.

DC45728AADA249DD9D301466E9818691.description: Viral: have no cure, but are controllable with medications (HIV/AIDS, genital herpes, hepatitis, HPV/genital warts)

5B70FE90AD6A4CCF96502B6E738FB251.description: STI: Sexually Transmitted Infection capable of being spread from person to person through sexual intercourse, oral, anal, genital or digital contact. Can also be spread through IV drug use/blood to blood contact. There are three categories of STI's:

D0A2461C20F84854B720978C470139CA.description: Dealing with Sexual Harassment: let the person know that you are uncomfortable with their behavior. Tell them to stop and be assertive. Tell someone you trust: parent, relative, coach, teacher, counselor, etc. Keep a record of the harassment to show what's been happening. If you see or suspect something, say something.

279840FC0DD84301A9431089B1153D45.description: Examples of Sexual Harassment: name calling, threats, inappropriate jokes, spreading rumors, gestures, leers, writing on bathroom walls, grabbing, pushing, cornering, unwanted kissing/touching, inappropriately touching body

9C1B4C65C04D439293F388E4E6A8D48A.description: Sexual Harassment: any unwanted conduct or communication of a sexual nature that negatively affect a person's relationships, employment opportunities or environment. Harassment may be verbal or physical.

F80257790430442091F3BA664E77EB08.description: Define sexual harassment and develop assertive behavior skills as a means of protection from sexual harassment and abusive situations.

B25DCCE5C4D743A8BEF4E24424876B93.description: Love: slowly built, security and trust, strong friendship, long-lasting, love the entire person, want the other person to grow, willing to compromise, ability and desire to wait for physical intimacy, giving/ focused on "you", dual commitment, self-less

F7780B8C39DE4A569D79F3AAC0AE34FE.description: Explain the difference between infatuation and love.

ACBD50B4370B4D738EF4719891344F86.description: Discuss reasons and motives for dating.

A872E09ABDA34808B2B98C69DF716FA4.description: Teens who are in or suspect someone they know is in an abusive relationships should tell someone (parents, friends, trusted adult, teacher, counselor, police, professional mental health worker, etc.)

3E198F18CDB54CEC92EF098C2FAFEDE2.description: Why Teen Stay In Abusive Relationships: embarrassed or ashamed, afraid violence will escalate if they try to end the relationship, convinced it's their fault, no experience with healthy dating relationships, confuse jealousy with love, ignore reality (don't know their being abused), afraid friends and family won't believe them, feel like there is no one they can turn to for support, mix of "good times" and hope that partner will change, believe that being involved with someone is the MOST important thing in their life (better to be with someone than alone)

8C0821FC9DB54891B7D22DC9018F52E7.description: Relationship Red Flags: wants to get serious quickly, will not take NO for an answer, is overly jealous and possessive, wants to choose their partners friends and activities, is controlling and bossy (makes all the decisions), puts partner down when alone and in front of others, makes partner feel guilty ("If you really loved me you would..."), blames the victim for behavior ("It's your fault I get so angry"), apologies for violent behavior ("I'll never do it again, I promise."), has strong ideas about gender roles

564D177B13474D48AB02F377FB557110.description: Dating Violence: a pattern of behavior to establish power and control over another person through fear and intimidation. Often including the threat or use of violence. It occurs when one person believes they are entitled to control another person and those involved are in an intimate or close relationship.

69EDC2A92B8A41408F61C22998C1050F.description: Emotional/Psychological: mental violence that can include constant verbal threats and abuse, harassment, excessive possessiveness, isolating abused person from others, damage of personal property, intimidation, etc.

701DC81F172546718A37D20F06488957.description: Sexual: any non-consensual, forced sexual behavior. It may escalate to rape or sexual assault.

6A5251F07E9F466FAB79719F9B3C4587.description: Physical: can begin with threats of violence, punching fist through wall, escalates to pushing, slapping, restraining, etc. Finally, it can become life threatening.

E36F8E10271D400B9D248EF557302D5A.description: Define and discuss dating violence and how to report and/or deal with those situations appropriately.

81340C9C4276478EB0BE70B7E5784499.description: How to deal: Realize what happened and why, accept your anger/ pain and move on, keep your distance, think through everything, talk to friends and family, write your feelings down, clean personal space, keep fond memories, don't overreact, find happiness in other areas of your life, stay active, let it go and move forward

04F56EEA1F004EE6AE0602C1B0B75BBA.description: How to end: pick an appropriate place, choose the right time, do it in person, be honest but sensitive, keep your emotions under control, use "I" Messages

944126652A7D4F11B81B068F93F0711D.description: Discuss appropriate ways to end a relationship and how to deal with a relationship that has ended.

CD6DA752DEC74A69BE17495EED275E96.description: Discuss the problems and consequences of early pairing.

1323B0EFB65C4F5FAF7A2339D3DB5D39.description: Advantages of Group Socialization/Dating: safety in numbers, relaxed fun, meet new people, easier to communicate, less opportunity for early physical intimacy

8D9A0A557FD9437285FCAFE6FDC28F18.description: Discuss advantages of group socialization rather than paired dating at an early age.

C63E5AD6D0284FC8B9E04AB2E652DA0E.description: Getting acquainted, friendships, phone calls/texting, socializing with groups, group dating, double dating, and pairing/single dating

C38BDC431923478998C4ED46A401A36D.description: Identify and understand the progression/ avenues of adolescent attractions. Explore the ways relationships begin, develop and grow.

3FD80EFDAE8844969A6956D30423397C.description: Discuss how dating relationships begin and develop.

9C479D96227441B097EA5DAB314F7340.description: Do it Now: It will only get harder the longer you wait.

DAEC01EB1FFD426192C7C31B6B6FB85A.description: Get Help: you are much better off it you don't battle an addiction alone. Some great sources of help are parents, good friends, support groups counselors and teachers

C161F3629DCB4D3C890A4F120DD58988.description: Admit it: recognize that you have a problem

E3F8052A3339438591B2B96B7DD31A04.description: Realities of Addition: Addictions can become stronger than you. Addictions are not just about you. Addictions destroy dream and future opportunities. Addictions can cloud judgment, affect memory, change taste buds, inhibit perception, slow bodily functions/reaction time

D267743359DF4DF891E69DCFF66ADB67.description: You want to escape from your current problems

86705240AEE94E1F97F7B63D001BBF50.description: You feel confined and want to rebel

731B68365C7748F8B8C467D24C3E7ED6.description: Being alone: choosing to be alone, positive time for self, being along doesn't mean someone feels rejected or lonely

2F83A1A85E934B908E9B9EE75F00B9E1.description: Positive: pressure into doing good things, influences you to stick to values/goals, helps you listen to your feelings, help others by setting a good example, etc.

EF633F94DACC4BF289DD6292FF7AB7F4.description: Physical needs must be met before any others can be achieved.

436635BA42E540AD81611A277C29EC18.description: Pyramid (begins at the base): physical needs, safety needs, love and belonging needs, esteem needs, and self-actualization (achieving personal goals).

701CDC6C3C1E44F7A7364AC58D6BF145.description: Strengthen: appreciation, affection, commitment, time together/ build traditions, creative problem solving, constructive communication

EE6B5D19DA3B45898C6960AEEF110C53.description: Positive effects: instant information world-wide, spreads knowledge, educates people on basic rights, skill development, informed advertisements, educational programming, etc.

B8F6DB87CC0145839907C63805493AAD.description: Take a position based on logic (make a decision)

53720FD99ED344998BEC8F1A2292CDAD.description: Identify personal and family values that conflict with the situation

C6C6D4EC6AF742D09A8AA362BB04512D.description: Identify the components of the critical thinking process in order:

B747A5730293480486946112A3830C6D.description: Active Listening Skills: pay attention, look at the speaker and make eye contact, stop other tasks and listen, listen with appropriate body language, give verbal clues that show you are listening, don't interrupt, don't shift your attention to your own problems, don't let your emotions get in the way, don't rush the conversation, put the phone away

04D07F4A3CAF42F7B314DA5E85AAB2A1.description: Positive Conflict Resolution Skills: try to stay positive and calm, be aware of your emotional triggers, use active listening skills to understand, focus on cooperation instead of winning, ask questions, use appropriate body language/nonverbal communication, use "I" Messages, be specific about what is bothering you

3E6A90A20D9C4747838DFB0482F87FD9.description: Problem-Solving: this style shows a willingness to compromise to solve the problem positively. Characterized by: using collaboration to solve the problem, win-win attitude, two-way communication, used "I" Messages

EE353FB03C6344328892152D429DCD2A.description: Confrontation: this style is aggressive and sometimes hostile. Characterized by: "My way or the highway" thinking, very confrontational and competitive, used to gain power and control, uses "You" Messages, can damage relationships

8690B468020D4B7A99C7485DD7DA8CE6.description: Avoidance: this style tries to avoid the problem all together rather than face it. Characterized by: changing the subject, "giving in" to avoid confrontation, avoiding the issue in hopes it will go away, communicating through the "grapevine"

5B48DAD5C52943B49E1ADF335EE26175.description: Identify how positive conflict resolution and active listening skills enhance human relationships.

76FB067BE5C24F88864D8A5227B4F858.description: "I" Messages are a helpful way of communicating how you feel and why you feel that way without losing control of your emotions. They allow you to resolve conflicts without others feeling blaed or attached. They do take time and practice to use effectively.

878324F2522A43E794C5E78ED37BF3D0.description: Utilize I-Messages in developing positive relationships in families, careers and communities.

32C96B5E10AA48FD8E3229D1ADC7435B.description: Nonverbal Communication: the way a person expresses themselves through movement, posture and facial expression. It can often be misread and misunderstood. It is possible to send one type of verbal message and a different type of non-verbal message at the same time.

5A4D5894F3CF44098D26288CE37ADB2B.description: Examples: insults, harassment, teasing, threatening, lying, accusing, using "You" Messages, swearing, sarcasm, gossip, topping / "one upping", not listening

7747B2DC7C414D9BACC44DA1FC5AE187.description: Destructive Communication: negative communication that "tears down" yourself and others.

document.title: Utah Core State Standards for Mathematics (K-5)

082AAF491C024C6DB565A25678C6820D.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares; describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters; and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two or four of the shares. Understand that, for these examples, decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.

6D7095FA180B4424BE8BEED4E7242D1A.description: Compose three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape. First grade students do not need to learn formal names such as "right rectangular prism."

A2A2C2E698DE41D4AFE81FDEA997323F.description: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, halfcircles, and quarter-circles) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.

F74B07B91D3741168D92A92DBAB83BF1.description: Distinguish between defining attributes (for example, triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (for example, color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes that possess defining attributes.

4EE2D0A4C8984B929D81EA339F2BC1E3.description: Identify the values of pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters, and know their comparative values. (For example, a dime is of greater value than a nickel.) Use appropriate notation to designate a coin's value. (For example, 5¢.)

CBBA00F42C9448D2AE283582A202396D.description: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.

8AF3F9C0DF774424A2FA1DCA14AFF3A0.description: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.

94CA123DDBAF4395AAB49B23D77B5E55.description: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps.
comments: Limit to contexts where the object being measured is spanned by a whole number of length units with no gaps or overlaps.

34CF047E28A642C78BF141F8BFC20E5B.description: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.

B692925778FF40FDB5D4EC66A0001784.description: Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

0120585F62F84DF887BB412901026B59.description: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.

40840F9D7DCE463382E3DC0DE24B059E.description: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens to tens and ones to ones, and that it is sometimes necessary to compose a ten.

82FF412A29F94CE8A41E906A83BCFC00.description: Compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, and <.

7E680E2836D6420AB712A2C5FA3094A2.description: The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones).

600DC15694EE406A99BDB98069338205.description: The numbers from 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

92C37604B12446F783C6592CAA9EEDAF.description: 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones, called a "ten."

1153609C2EA447ED885AA5B20FED42F3.description: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases:

BCE048EB35D3427AA66B58C009255FFF.description: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.

79B4D39804F34C33A44922320C1FFB59.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten

A13FBD70BBB7478E8C0A256A1D4DEC48.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 + ? = 11, 5 = ? – 3, 6 + 6 = ?

1D54F160B4C842D584F1DE1A98655E2A.description: Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine whether equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false.
comments: For example, which of the following equations are true and which are false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 – 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.

35EA936277ED481381751FF46AD3970D.description: By the end of Grade 1, demonstrate fluency for addition and subtraction within 10.

A7BF5FABE8D04F80BAB5054164162B3B.description: Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (for example, 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (for example, 13 – 4 = 13 – 3 – 1 = 10 – 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (for example, knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 – 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (for example, adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).

F9C928BF1D63402FA4E29A645A50CF87.description: Relate counting to addition and subtraction.
comments: For example, by counting on 2 to add 2.

73891DFFB3AF4171B579BD66CAB84F2B.description: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem.
comments: For example, subtract 10 – 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.

AA92B2B119FB4D549757215860043DFA.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract.
comments: For example: If 8 + 3 = 11 is known, then 3 + 8 = 11 is also known. (Commutative property of addition.) To add 2 + 6 + 4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2 + 6 + 4 = 2 + 10 =12. (Associative property of addition.) First grade students need not use formal terms for these properties.

51072F435F7C483EBE1061CB77977031.description: Solve word problems that call for addition of three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20.
comments: For example, use objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

4F994B3898FE4AEE9A82ABC2DBFB1453.description: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions.
comments: For example, use objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

ADF5726DBC084A76975539C265A62218.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

87C4AB73CC6847948B599230A2CC4145.description: Look for and make use of structure.

696473E3D94E4282ACABF850E9EEECD8.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

5819182929AE43BDBA46E2B6F80E1AC1.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

F3E85470FEFD40699606BB6D2C60D395.description: Identify shapes as two-dimensional ("flat") or three-dimensional ("solid").

185BD8B27B5E4054967F14A4A3AE3F8A.description: Correctly name shapes regardless of their orientations or overall sizes.

80576E2CF61548B39E00168765E55C8D.description: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes, and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.

D69AF13945394909A98E24C897DB4D7A.description: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count. Limit the category counts to less than or equal to 10.

9CA58290D9844D81AE2AEAEB1F643F2A.description: Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which object has "more of"/"less of" the attribute, and describe the difference.
comments: For example, directly compare the length of two pencils and describe one as shorter or longer.

C67F9C0E70944110B9FAD0F2693D5E1B.description: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight. Describe several measurable attributes of a single object.

20D44B03692448C5896D16B4B82DFBA8.description: Compose and decompose numbers from 11–19 into ten ones and some further ones. Use objects or drawings and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or equation.
comments: For example, 18 = 10 + 8. Understand that these numbers are composed of ten ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

9DAC5E07FEE84AB1BDF578A03EDE907B.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten

1187284BA6E645DA9706063315C6454D.description: Fluently add and subtract using numbers within 5.

37723B20161247F6A949A5AA3455491F.description: Make sums of 10 using any number from 1 to 9.
comments: For example, 2 + 8 = 10. Use objects or drawings to represent and record the answer.

F8D0B591653A4F178238D8DF5646BE5E.description: Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way by using objects or drawings. Record each decomposition by a drawing or equation.
comments: For example, 5 = 2 + 3 and 5 = 4 + 1.

8FA028BB8AF24CB49C91EABCCD354AB0.description: Solve addition and subtraction word problems within 10. Use objects or drawings to represent the problem.

C52B6AC22B7F4146A3CDB8BFD29F4525.description: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, simple drawings, or sounds.
comments: For example, use clapping, act out situations, and use verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.

CA9E6D3279194945AF0CA9ADE6C4FE82.description: Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals using "greater than," "less than," or "equal to."

2F5818E932854618ADC11732C136D313.description: Use matching or counting strategies to identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group. Include groups with up to ten objects.

07E9C7B3FA1642CBA95F355C514CEEDF.description: Use counting to answer questions about "how many."
comments: For example, 20 or fewer objects arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or circle; 10 or fewer objects in a scattered configuration. Using a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.

DF303727108446989CE1BBE1A5F4EAFC.description: Understand that each successive number refers to a quantity that is one greater than the previous number.

88621B6D57AF471CA4BFED85102DD11F.description: Understand that the last number said represents the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.

C6EA0966DEC6499983E27821B85B3F53.description: When counting objects, say the numbers in the standard order. Pair each quantity of objects with one and only one number, and each number with the correct quantity of objects.

2195ABECAD0B444DB9CC5CB8ABFAB9D8.description: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities; connect counting to cardinality.

167F31AED8BA4410BC26EF7DAC1F9D37.description: Read and write numbers using base ten numerals from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral, in or out of sequence (0 represents a count of no objects).

F7EBE47DC4CE4D68A69DD14AC0382F79.description: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).

5888920215AA45ADA9B3833DEBE3B756.description: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.

F09CDE746F314F8084F6E75F61A26ADF.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

EB9D502C7FE14FFBBD643355BD4BC2CE.description: Look for and make use of structure.

79B95EC0C2CB458B906B396049E06C5A.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

F80D8231DD61437D948F472041C518E0.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: Utah Core State Standards for Mathematics (6-8)

548B78DBF44A4EC48607F8A5F577549F.description: Relating the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered.

4A5FD37F5DC84C22B12C4A18E0C55F12.description: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations (for example, outliers) from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.

0AC1E3EC4F674648BD383C3495EA4679.description: Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement.

F61E9E9CD9894C4D8E4750E21236BE28.description: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by:

D5260FDC672547ACAF971986B7D4EBAF.description: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms and box plots. Choose the most appropriate graph/plot for the data collected.

FFB1CCBC1E6C442AB6A2D1AEFC0BE668.description: Recognize that a measure of center for a numerical data set summarizes all of its values with a single number, while a measure of variation describes how its values vary with a single number.

E59EE5B57F344C4A94CB5F574EFDC84B.description: Understand that a set of data collected to answer a statistical question has a distribution that can be described by its center, spread/range and overall shape.

B2B36CE2613A4F52B538A65521B447A4.description: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers.
comments: For example, "How old am I?" is not a statistical question, but "How old are the students in my school?" is a statistical question because one anticipates variability in students' ages.

8C2F3D86112049A09822093032C27CB0.description: Represent three-dimensional figures using nets made up of rectangles and triangles, and use the nets to find the surface area of these figures. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

42998F40F2B2451B9840C0E53B972B04.description: Draw polygons in the coordinate plane given coordinates for the vertices; use coordinates to find the length of a side joining points with the same x coordinate or the same y coordinate. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

3240440EF6C84F58B83D86ECE56FBCE5.description: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with appropriate unit fraction edge lengths by packing it with cubes of the appropriate unit fraction edge lengths (for example, 3½ × 2 × 6), and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths of the prism. Apply the formulas V = lwh and V = bh to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.
comments: Note: Model the packing using drawings and diagrams.

B2C41C5FA01343ACA310C9374AD0B644.description: Find the area of right triangles, other triangles, special quadrilaterals, and polygons by composing and decomposing into rectangles, triangles and/or other shapes; apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

2C20A4465F1E48A0AD751813BAAF37B8.description: Use variables to represent two quantities in a real-world problem that change in relationship to one another; write an equation to express one quantity, thought of as the dependent variable, in terms of the other quantity, thought of as the independent variable. Analyze the relationship between the dependent and independent variables using graphs and tables, and relate these to the equation.
comments: For example, in a problem involving motion at constant speed, list and graph ordered pairs of distances and times, and write the equation d = 65t to represent the relationship between distance and time.

19F53B9D52F14A3A8E9F7C92BB629FFD.description: Write an inequality of the form x > c or x < c to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or mathematical problem. Recognize that inequalities of the form x > c or x < c have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions of such inequalities on number line diagrams.

08296BA8104945588EB890A8825687DB.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by writing and solving equations of the form x + a = b and ax = b for cases in which a, b and x are all non-negative rational numbers.

A1E7CC76598D40FABBE45ABBF736B609.description: Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem; understand that a variable can represent an unknown number, or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set.

A191A42C547F4D30B9E1A233571043C1.description: Understand solving an equation or inequality as a process of answering the question: Which values from a specified set, if any, make the equation or inequality true? Use substitution to determine whether a given number in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true.

50818780B78844CEB8A2CBC87E42F588.description: Identify when two expressions are equivalent.
comments: For example, the expressions y + y + y and 3y are equivalent because they name the same number, regardless of which number y represents.

2E8DEAB640C8423490B8D660CEE766AE.description: Apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.
comments: For example, apply the distributive property to the expression 3(2 + x) to produce the equivalent expression 6 + 3x; apply the distributive property to the expression 24x + 18y to produce the equivalent expression 6(4x + 3y); apply properties of operations to y + y + y to produce the equivalent expression 3y.

9B08763DE5BD41A891A59364853917FE.description: Evaluate expressions at specific values of their variables. Include expressions that arise from formulas used in real-world problems. Perform arithmetic operations, including those involving whole-number exponents, applying the Order of Operations when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order.
comments: For example, use the formulas V = s³ and A = 6s² to find the volume and surface area of a cube with sides of length s = ½.

62B66EEA18504AC5A59D275F103F9B8A.description: Identify parts of an expression using mathematical terms (for example, sum, term, product, factor, quotient, coefficient); view one or more parts of an expression as a single entity and a sum of two terms.
comments: For example, describe the expression 2(8 + 7) as a product of two factors; view (8 + 7) as both a single entity and a sum of two terms.

AEE8D4BBEB3A4AB1A9DDF8F4FA9035A6.description: Write expressions that record operations with numbers and with letters representing numbers.
comments: For example, express the calculation "Subtract y from 5" as 5 – y and express "Jane had $105.00 in her bank account. One year later, she had x dollars more. Write an expression that shows her new balance" as $105.00 + x.

EE5D9293DF6F425F9CFDF5E7C9DFA5F9.description: Write, read, and evaluate expressions in which letters represent numbers.

974C24977E8846D09EBF4AC7A82CE63A.description: Write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents.

5F8DD32E6CA44B1C989515683E6D7392.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane. Include use of coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points with the same x-coordinate or the same y-coordinate.

679E1CE7189D4EB180B10E45ACF0BBE1.description: Distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order.
comments: For example: Recognize that an account balance less than –30 dollars represents a debt greater than 30 dollars.

817E53617BB043A7BD992E3E4AF7E94C.description: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from zero on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world context.
comments: For example, for an account balance of –30 dollars, write |–30|= 30 to describe the size of the debt in dollars.

B51FD1D548CD4AF38273D3B0C7FE1652.description: Write, interpret, and explain statements of order for rational numbers in real-world contexts.
comments: For example, write –3° C > –7° C to express the fact that –3° C is warmer than –7° C.

585F118E14A7428999ECBB8D656CAB79.description: Interpret statements of inequality as statements about the relative position of two numbers on a number line diagram.
comments: For example, interpret –3 > –7 as a statement that –3 is located to the right of –7 on a number line oriented from left to right.

4C9A3B5A96804EDF91A98F01DDB49E37.description: Understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers.

6D29855553CC4579A862C916464154F8.description: Find and position integers and other rational numbers on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram; find and position pairs of integers and other rational numbers on a coordinate plane.

D6013DCAB3C14360B2BB21A8E3814783.description: Understand that the signs of numbers in ordered pairs indicate their location in quadrants of the coordinate plane; recognize that when two ordered pairs differ only by signs, the locations of the points are related by reflections across one or both axes.

1371794AF9AB461F8FAD0640C5A74037.description: Recognize opposite signs of numbers as indicating locations on opposite sides of zero on the number line; recognize that the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself.
comments: For example, -(-3) = 3, and zero is its own opposite.

621757935A42430B917ED48B94128821.description: Understand a rational number as a point on the number line. Extend number line diagrams and coordinate axes familiar from previous grades to represent points on the line and in the plane with negative number coordinates.

F46882D081694F729BAEA457ED1A6306.description: Understand that positive and negative numbers are used together to describe quantities having opposite directions or values (for example, temperature above/below zero, elevation above/below sea level, credits/debits, positive/negative electric charge); use positive and negative numbers to represent quantities in real-world contexts, explaining the meaning of zero in each situation.

DB2078621CDA4F12BD9C7A5C473C0DFF.description: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to 100 and the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to 12. Use the distributive property to express a sum of two whole numbers 1–100 with a common factor as a multiple of a sum of two whole numbers with no common factor.
comments: For example, express 36 + 8 as 4(9 + 2).

6266B4DD5E714F88A789548BF3E868D6.description: Solve division problems in which both the dividend and the divisor are multi-digit decimals; develop the standard algorithm by using models, the meaning of division, and place value understanding.

E7D093536BD143EE99C6D41366ACA293.description: Fluently divide multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm, limited to a whole number dividend with a decimal divisor or a decimal dividend with a whole number divisor.

9EFE92FA5AB94808AC6DD65870925382.description: Fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm for each operation.

0C879E90413D4B0FBE91A691E8FBDC5E.description: Fluently divide multi-digit numbers using the standard algorithm.

8E89245816A3430CABD39D70CF3E7916.description: Explain the meaning of quotients in fraction division problems.
comments: For example, create a story context for (2/3) ÷ (¾) and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (2/3) ÷ (¾) = 8/9 because ¾ of 8/9 is 2/3. (In general, (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = ad/bc.)

03BAE9C1295B4C0D9EDD30F6D8FB3D6E.description: Solve real-world problems involving division of fractions by fractions.
comments: For example, how much chocolate will each person get if three people share ½ pound of chocolate equally? How many ¾-cup servings are in 2/3 of a cup of yogurt? How wide is a rectangular strip of land with length ¾ mile and area ½ square mile?

7043D1F85E2A4C96AA329AC6214FDCDA.description: Compute quotients of fractions by fractions, for example, by applying strategies such as visual fraction models, equations, and the relationship between multiplication and division, to represent problems.

5580E4724D23408F9E26E5580EBEA23E.description: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions.

9017A65BCEA44671A48F63C7AE1992A4.description: Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units; manipulate and transform units appropriately when multiplying or dividing quantities.

D8748133ED9545A8B82D77C4D317B9D9.description: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100. Solve problems involving finding the whole, given a part and the percent.
comments: For example, 30% of a quantity means 30/100 times the quantity.

094BE55632F54D79B49826432CAC12E5.description: Solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed.
comments: For example, if it took four hours to mow eight lawns, how many lawns could be mowed in 32 hours? What is the hourly rate at which lawns were being mowed?

E127147706D540CDAD89E24E3F3FF038.description: Make tables of equivalent ratios relating quantities with whole-number measurements, find missing values in the tables, and plot the pairs of values on the coordinate plane. Use tables to compare ratios.

9C1D5CEC75834CF0BFA360D1E0E76DE0.description: Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world (with a context) and mathematical (void of context) problems, using strategies such as reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number line diagrams, or equations involving unit rate problems.

D8CF28AEDC2E48489692EF4139F627C6.description: Understand the concept of a unit rate a/b associated with a ratio a:b with b ≠ 0, and use rate language in the context of a ratio relationship. The following are examples of rate language: "This recipe has a ratio of four cups of flour to two cups of sugar, so the rate is two cups of flour for each cup of sugar." "We paid $75 for 15 hamburgers, which is a rate of $5 per hamburger."
comments: (In sixth grade, unit rates are limited to non-complex fractions.)

31DDC65230684FBBA7B801B09F42745B.description: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities.
