The following are examples of ratio language: "The ratio of wings to beaks in the bird house at the zoo was 2:1, because for every two wings there was one beak." "For every vote candidate A received, candidate C received nearly three votes."

23B73615A5634D2BA2359D569FC3DFBE.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

8F5518B58D7B4CA4A071F30E7E3D5D2F.description: Look for and make use of structure.

DE6B9886F01A45E4BFE53504C40CB24E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

582CDEAEE06C46278909BC466FE09F99.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: Utah Core State Standards for Mathematics (6-8)

19AC8C61141B4600B1D67980D5538693.description: Design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events.
comments: For example, use random digits as a simulation tool to approximate the answer to the question: If 40% of donors have type A blood, what is the probability that it will take at least 4 donors to find one with type A blood?

EA60E76EC4FF478FA7EC89451B1560C1.description: Represent sample spaces for compound events using methods such as organized lists, tables and tree diagrams. For an event described in everyday language (e.g., "rolling double sixes"), identify the outcomes in the sample space which compose the event.

6916E47BA5B14565B0475E4EEFB45846.description: Understand that, just as with simple events, the probability of a compound event is the fraction of outcomes in the sample space for which the compound event occurs.

07F9244FB24743F281FA58D943AF5538.description: Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and simulation.

DD70EF1C9CC446C1A462FEDE62661D5A.description: Develop a probability model (which may not be uniform) by observing frequencies in data generated from a chance process.
comments: For example, find the approximate probability that a spinning penny will land heads up or that a tossed paper cup will land open-end down. Do the outcomes for the spinning penny appear to be equally likely based on the observed frequencies?

18A48AA41E3047BFAAEE07F439A8EABA.description: Develop a uniform probability model by assigning equal probability to all outcomes, and use the model to determine probabilities of events.
comments: For example, if a student is selected at random from a class, find the probability that Jane will be selected and the probability that a girl will be selected.

9DDEF5C83B994271ABBCD0DE4C0B598F.description: Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events. Compare probabilities from a model to observed frequencies; if the agreement is not good, explain possible sources of the discrepancy.

0CD547F8C87C4630908A521B6C9F0F04.description: Approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data on the chance process that produces it and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability.
comments: For example, when rolling a number cube 600 times, predict that a 3 or 6 would be rolled roughly 200 times, but probably not exactly 200 times.

6372B5839CBD4802B81DA625B42FD56B.description: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Larger numbers indicate greater likelihood. A probability near 0 indicates an unlikely event, a probability around ½ indicates an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near 1 indicates a likely event.

21F200B4D7914564A5FB7F01D0D502CE.description: Use measures of center and measures of variability for numerical data from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.
comments: For example, decide whether the words in a chapter of a seventh grade science book are generally longer than the words in a chapter of a fourth grade science book.

52585D7F1FA5458C901C20B66A8D059C.description: Informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities, estimating the difference between the centers by expressing it as a multiple of a measure of variability.
comments: For example, the mean height of players on the basketball team is 10 cm greater than the mean height of players on the soccer team, approximately twice the variability (mean absolute deviation) on either team; on a dot plot, the separation between the two distributions of heights is noticeable.

B8DA8404C6F64C64B327FB6F21F0A379.description: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest. Generate multiple samples (or simulated samples) of the same size to gauge the variation in estimates or predictions.
comments: For example, estimate the mean word length in a book by randomly sampling words from the book; predict the winner of a school election based on randomly sampled survey data. Gauge how far off the estimate or prediction might be.

BDCDB9C28D0B48F0801BA8D23D150FB1.description: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population, and that generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population. Understand that random sampling is more likely to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.

A198DB15CCF04F11BE076DE201F3BB28.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, volume and surface area of two- and three-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms.

EF2598623914413B9DD3FA69E940BF0A.description: Use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles in a multi-step problem to write, and use them to solve simple equations for an unknown angle in a figure.

DFF69C6A0FE74B489B45DF45D5050A9B.description: Know the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle, and solve problems; give an informal derivation of the relationship between the circumference and area of a circle.

F9D35A62FA1B4FF8BC7959F01899A655.description: Describe the two-dimensional figures that result from slicing three-dimensional figures, as in plane sections of right rectangular prisms and right rectangular pyramids.

46F40E4C34814DD895662C939BA43D6F.description: Draw (freehand, with ruler and protractor, and with technology) geometric shapes with given conditions. Focus on constructing triangles from three measures of angles or sides, noticing when the conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.

6B27AE38538A4C12B253D1967FD17D06.description: Solve problems involving scale drawings of geometric figures, such as computing actual lengths and areas from a scale drawing and reproducing a scale drawing at a different scale.

DFAC3FDA74AD463A8DBD9D4F0A88D2CF.description: Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem.
comments: For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions.

B759AAE3999A4B7BB8E74EE0F10B54AB.description: Solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach.
comments: For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width?

D110A7C447F04B8CBC5F685335E2745E.description: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities.

89D702963E2B490390850B7F5CF94047.description: Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form, convert between forms as appropriate, and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies.
comments: For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9¾ inches long in the center of a door that is 27½ inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation.

ACC3CC86AC43452AB9C7F75398FE2EF1.description: Understand that rewriting an expression in different forms in a problem context can shed light on the problem, and how the quantities in it are related.
comments: For example, a + 0.05a = 1.05a means that "increase by 5%" is the same as "multiply by 1.05."

DC3F9A5E4D4240EB890F33AD1178A1CC.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients.

634A9FAD7AEF4E57A5FA5C49EB3600E5.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers. Computations with rational numbers extend the rules for manipulating fractions to complex fractions.

30A3462F6AF64A2FA7F2B27EBEB5F766.description: Convert a rational number to a decimal using long division; know that the decimal form of a rational number terminates in 0s or eventually repeats.

3A6D5705DAB745019EAD586EDFABC5A4.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide rational numbers.

23256936B5274AFD88329CBCD3187EE6.description: Understand that integers can be divided, provided the divisor is not zero, and that every quotient of integers (with non-zero divisor) is a rational number. If p and q are integers, then –(p/q) = (–p)/q = p/(–q). Interpret quotients of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

A7C21A99CE824A8686988FC352DB3FCE.description: Understand that multiplication is extended from fractions to rational numbers by requiring that operations continue to satisfy the properties of operations, particularly the distributive property, leading to products such as (–1)(–1) = 1 and the rules for multiplying signed numbers. Interpret products of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

ABE66AE1846F4B1CA3F296AE7CD705FE.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division and of fractions to multiply and divide rational numbers.

9479779E71FA4AB590F6DFBE2468F51E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers.

5D20FC967C134604B1134BECA2585834.description: Understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p – q = p + (–q). Show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, and apply this principle in real-world contexts.

28C6831DECA94DCBA4DA5EB6558E1D87.description: Understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p in the positive or negative direction, depending on whether q is positive or negative. Show that a number and its opposite have a sum of 0 (are additive inverses). Interpret sums of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

173DCA6FEBF84515AFE51F7184C08828.description: Describe situations in which opposite quantities combine to make 0.
comments: For example, a hydrogen atom has 0 charge because its two constituents are oppositely charged.

23AFE64BF17F4C26AF841DD456530A94.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of addition and subtraction to add and subtract rational numbers; represent addition and subtraction on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram.

5969568DF8C24F6BACF1754735F66FA0.description: Use proportional relationships to solve multi-step ratio and percent problems.
comments: Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error.

09FA807B09AF4DA2BB05DBA6EC473684.description: Explain what a point (x, y) on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate.

comments: For example, if total cost t is proportional to the number n of items purchased at a constant price p, the relationship between the total cost and the number of items can be expressed as t = pn.

5334984A3CBC4C559A2700F8FE07957A.description: Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships.

E7150C315C054E34BE5F0DA95E489CB5.description: Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin.

58D985009D2A4F46A93212571453C661.description: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.

59D3AC9FF86D4E0C8A846BDD62FCEEA1.description: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios oflengths, areas and other quantities measured in like or different units.
comments: For example, if a person walks ½ mile in each ¼ hour, compute the unit rate as the complex fraction ½/¼ miles per hour, equivalently 2 miles per hour.

F83BD1D6C0714775BC745EEA4E4E6819.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

DC39F41A89794A32B5D5726DF88ED1B3.description: Look for and make use of structure.

4A98EF1080664647B8DB3F65D247DD61.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

0AACA963C4164E68848978A694242F3F.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: Utah Core State Standards for Mathematics (K-5)

56F20B1A1233495FBDE7572E6BBC1634.description: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas. Express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.
comments: For example, partition a shape into four parts with equal area, and describe the area of each part as ¼ of the area of the shape.

933190073F38462088FF2690406D3FCC.description: Understand that shapes in different categories (for example, rhombuses, rectangles, and others) may share attributes (for example, having four sides), and that the shared attributes can define a larger category (for example, quadrilaterals). Recognize rhombuses, rectangles, and squares as examples of quadrilaterals, and draw examples of quadrilaterals that do not belong to any of these subcategories.

705192EDD1EA444CAEF7BE558B059190.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters.

13A1E8C341144B349ACA97D5EBDB70F9.description: Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real-world problems.

04600C6CA92D43659414507D03721983.description: Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning.

D9F84031CD2142F3A3CDFACBCCB41F08.description: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole-number side lengths in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems, and represent wholenumber products as rectangular areas in mathematical reasoning.

AF0745448E884B66A066E569CB1B1CB5.description: Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths.

90D4C784812046B489DEA93E16D8B5D8.description: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition (refer to 3.OA.5).

1EB3023B5F63429CB3A884C205E434A7.description: Measure area by counting unit squares (square centimeters, square meters, square inches, square feet, and improvised units).

0609FECA1D1E4F739AA1C52088E291A9.description: A plane figure which can be covered without gaps or overlaps by n unit squares is said to have an area of n square units.

2305698108F34434AA3C72D0DDD98DCA.description: A square with side length one unit, called "a unit square," is said to have "one square unit" of area, and can be used to measure area.

5CA271F15E694BC4AFC91756876184F1.description: Recognize area as an attribute of plane figures and understand concepts of area measurement.

825914DFB742419CA80E28EFA6584AA0.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch. Show the data by making a line plot where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units-whole numbers, halves, or quarters.

80AB39B3DF5E4DE68026CCA82E70B2CE.description: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step "how many more" and "how many less" problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs.
comments: For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent five pets.

9A66BB01061A4147924EF9B8BFF33C72.description: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units of grams (g), kilograms (kg), milliliters (ml), and liters (l). (Excludes compound units such as cubic centimeters [cc or cm3] and finding the geometric volume of a container.)
comments: Add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step word problems involving masses of objects or volumes of liquids that are given in the same units, for example, by using drawings (such as a beaker with a measurement scale) to represent the problem. (Excludes multiplicative comparison problems.)

C3B212533479430D98C9174F5ACA8CFC.description: Tell and write time to the nearest minute and measure time intervals in minutes. Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of time intervals in minutes, for example, by representing the problem on a number line diagram.

B88CE41954CB4173911F41C38D033DFF.description: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole.
comments: Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, for example, by using a visual fraction model.

246530137DE94142BBFA037200BA56C2.description: Express whole numbers as fractions, and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers.
comments: For example, express 3 in the form 3 = 3/1; recognize that 6/1 = 6; locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point of a number line diagram.

D53CEA7885804AE28789EA85D320BCD7.description: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, such as ½ = 2/4, 4/6 = 2/3.
comments: Explain why the fractions are equivalent by using a visual fraction model, for example.

1FA632C8385B4EB4AF0C918A04726696.description: Understand two fractions as equivalent if they are the same size, or the same point on a number line.

83411DA214EC4C35B3B95C76C9B94F48.description: Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size.

4F6DE5FB5DE64CADABC75E20AF8B09D2.description: Represent a fraction a/b on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths 1/b from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval has size a/b and that its endpoint locates the number a/b on the number line.

8EB6C2BFA47B4B5AA4A324DF9F8AC346.description: Represent a fraction 1/b on a number line diagram by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into b equal parts. Recognize that each part has size 1/b and that the endpoint of the part based at 0 locates the number 1/b on the number line.

7570824D8CFC454C96CBC6D32A5AF947.description: Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram.

E067119711FF46B49C94C80EC7AD7864.description: Understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b.
comments: For example: ¼ + ¼ + ¼ = ¾.

19F6AC96033F4148BE10FC96262BF994.description: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by one part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts.

8D1ACD812C604D1C828DA2B12B71E7A2.description: Understand that a unit fraction has a numerator of one and a non-zero denominator.

1E10868DA90F450DBE2779199C36C2DC.description: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 (for example, 9 × 80 and 5 × 60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.

283D7BD686C24C6F87B5187F39501E69.description: Fluently add and subtract within 1,000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.

8A81CEC5E0CD4716A89D42E5AD5330B5.description: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100.

8465648D185A4D128EA8779FF8D841C2.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten

47FA593990384FA9B63F217DFEA53D20.description: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations.
comments: For example, observe that four times a number is always even, and explain why four times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.

2986EA36C774474EA1EE02F2BC6CFFED.description: Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies, including rounding.

1D05DF08736E438598B0030274557183.description: Represent two-step problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Create accurate equations to match word problems.

97963F570CBB48A88EAC3697802B3F8B.description: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Know how to perform operations in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations). (Limit to problems posed with whole numbers and having whole number answers.)

E30D27E05CCB4FBC878D059B2ADD11D9.description: By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.

51D5159B909241A19A78DADF3E6825F1.description: Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division or properties of operations.
comments: For example, knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8.

D4CAB0AD176C4135A0AA5AC948A2C069.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem. Understand the relationship between multiplication and division (multiplication and division are inverse operations).
comments: For example, find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.

096187B4FA89458FA392930FD2F9D96C.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.
comments: For example: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known (commutative property of multiplication). 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30 (associative property of multiplication). Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56 (distributive property). (Third grade students may, but need not, use formal terms for these properties.)

7B3B2423421043D095BACD657F571C4B.description: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number— product, factor, quotient, dividend, or divisor—that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 × ? = 48, 5 = ? ÷ 3, and 6 × 6 = ?

968DEA8D16FC4362B2B3C112D877D195.description: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities.
comments: For example, use drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

D77B6EC2CB3B48A18232189AE181FBAD.description: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers.
comments: For example, interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into eight shares (partitive), or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of eight objects each (quotative).

777EF1023F1744C0B8A357DA4682C732.description: Interpret the products of whole numbers, such as interpreting 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects each.
comments: For example, describe a context in which a total number of objects can be expressed as 5 × 7.

6185681888914C52AA27C6321D3FDB17.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

DFFC23AA7968497A8584F40C60033D3C.description: Look for and make use of structure.

F15FE45CF0864E98B9C6DB87221126C5.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

352BB9C2B1C142DCB688BF453687E98A.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: Utah Core State Standards for Mathematics (6-8)

2F1EAF9DE23C4253AA9032F7E39A7D3D.description: Understand that patterns of association can also be seen in bivariate categorical data by displaying frequencies and relative frequencies in a two-way table. Construct and interpret a two-way table summarizing data on two categorical variables collected from the same subjects. Use relative frequencies calculated for rows or columns to describe possible association between the two variables.
comments: For example, collect data from students in your class on whether or not they have a curfew on school nights and whether or not they have assigned chores at home. Is there evidence that those who have a curfew also tend to have chores?

272780257B20495EBF45AED1B2585A48.description: Use the equation of a linear model to solve problems in the context of bivariate measurement data, interpreting the slope and intercept.
comments: For example, in a linear model for a biology experiment, interpret a slope of 1.5 cm/hr as meaning that an additional hour of sunlight each day is associated with an additional 1.5 cm in mature plant height. (Calculating equations for a linear model is not expected in grade 8.)

EBFD7FEFC3774D2CAFEBFEED4D425351.description: Know that straight lines are widely used to model relationships between two quantitative variables. For scatter plots that suggest a linear association, informally fit a straight line, and informally assess the model fit by judging the closeness of the data points to the line.

9E0D6658F9F5482D922A79604B7D2E90.description: Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data to investigate patterns of association between two quantities. Describe patterns such as clustering, outliers, positive or negative association, linear association, and nonlinear association.

CC5AD6D2DADF49368EB993FCCC916DFD.description: Know the formulas for the volumes of cones, cylinders, and spheres, and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

E7BBC1D67E34464DA17FEEF56111BED3.description: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find the distance between two points in a coordinate system.

AF7434AE80134CEDBEAAFF2BDC4A1AA7.description: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to determine unknown side lengths in right triangles in real-world and mathematical problems in two and three dimensions.

F804B61DD555497C8284A90FBB85B65D.description: Explore and explain proofs of the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse.

8BE35262178541AD9A97B619387F8306.description: Use informal arguments to establish facts about the angle sum and exterior angle of triangles, about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal, and the angle-angle criterion for similarity of triangles.
comments: For example, arrange three copies of the same triangle so that the sum of the three angles appears to form a line, and give an argument in terms of transversals why this is so.

058DF8FDA9154BEBB0F8EE6C87FD96CD.description: Understand that a two-dimensional figure is similar to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rotations, reflections, translations, and dilations; given two similar two-dimensional figures, describe a sequence that exhibits the similarity between them.

3920D7A69FAD47C1A0F1390EB39274FD.description: Observe that orientation of the plane is preserved in rotations and translations, but not with reflections. Describe the effect of dilations, translations, rotations, and reflections on two-dimensional figures using coordinates.

06BD6294E5044DDCB13D46D16849BFC3.description: Understand that a two-dimensional figure is congruent to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rotations, reflections, and translations; given two congruent figures, describe a sequence that exhibits the congruence between them.

8311908A4DEF4206BE0C42DA378750BA.description: Parallel lines are taken to parallel lines.

CC5FEC671EB646B4B9BC95C92543BCB8.description: Angles are taken to angles of the same measure.

AC26C7005C1346C68B2752097856CC51.description: Lines are taken to lines, and line segments to line segments of the same length.

8780D939107F41F28F99A386752C4B83.description: Verify experimentally the properties of rotations, reflections, and translations:

3BC38C948311495E938F6928EEA66CDB.description: Describe qualitatively the functional relationship between two quantities by analyzing a graph (e.g., where the function is increasing or decreasing, linear or nonlinear). Sketch a graph that exhibits the qualitative features of a function that has been described verbally.

54179C5493274522BB63309E21484EED.description: Construct a function to model a linear relationship between two quantities. Determine the rate of change and initial value of the function from a description of a relationship or from two (x, y) values, including reading these from a table or from a graph. Interpret the rate of change and initial value of a linear function in terms of the situation it models, and in terms of its graph or a table of values.

02C25684B8E949AA80E23EA91138D0C6.description: Interpret the equation y = mx + b as defining a linear function whose graph is a straight line; give examples of functions that are not linear.
comments: For example, the function A = s², giving the area of a square as a function of its side length, is not linear because its graph contains the points (1,1), (2,4) and (3,9), which are not on a straight line.

3BC1FC1FFC64494A90B4F56139FD422A.description: Compare properties of two functions, each represented in a different way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions).
comments: For example, given a linear function represented by a table of values and a linear function represented by an algebraic expression, determine which function has the greater rate of change.

A6B7B4FC93C04FABAF94FA696C75E3E2.description: Understand that a function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output. The graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs consisting of an input and the corresponding output. (Function notation is not required in grade 8.)

45320A0E0F3C40D18F8E7FE1B867F9F2.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems leading to two linear equations in two variables graphically.
comments: For example, given coordinates for two pairs of points, determine whether the line through the first pair of points intersects the line through the second pair.

9E4D88F681A14E9E88FA72FFC225FA46.description: Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables graphically, approximating when solutions are not integers and estimate solutions by graphing the equations. Solve simple cases by inspection.
comments: For example, 3x + 2y = 5 and 3x + 2y = 6 have no solution because 3x + 2y cannot simultaneously be 5 and 6.

1106C779C95646B3AFC8785375BBC5AC.description: Understand that solutions to a system of two linear equations in two variables correspond to points of intersection of their graphs, because points of intersection satisfy both equations simultaneously.

50362E50A98D448DB8209FB092B74583.description: Analyze and solve pairs of simultaneous linear equations.

6D8D9062393E4D67AE1C2C036B638617.description: Solve single-variable linear equations and inequalities with rational number coefficients, including equations and inequalities whose solutions require expanding expressions using the distributive property and collecting like terms.

4049630B6AF04C83836E6BB33403D825.description: Give examples of linear equations in one variable with one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solutions. Show which of these possibilities is the case by successively transforming the given equation into simpler forms, until an equivalent equation of the form x = a, a = a, or a = b results (where a and b are different numbers).

BF19EA9EA1144CC080D53EC525FD7EC3.description: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable.

6EAF1849119A415498A45B54280A1F1B.description: Use similar triangles to explain why the slope m is the same between any two distinct points on a non-vertical line in the coordinate plane; derive the equation y = mx for a line through the origin and the equation y = mx + b for a line intercepting the vertical axis at b.

3876B54D08674B2E84B54EDDD71C230A.description: Graph proportional relationships, interpreting the unit rate as the slope of the graph. Compare two different proportional relationships represented in different ways.
comments: For example, compare a distance-time graph to a distance-time equation to determine which of two moving objects has greater speed.

DA2665E01D7B45EDB3839DEDA9714186.description: Perform operations with numbers expressed in scientific notation, including problems where both decimal and scientific notation are used. Use scientific notation and choose units of appropriate size for measurements of very large or very small quantities (e.g., use millimeters per year for seafloor spreading). Interpret scientific notation that has been generated by technology.

F8AE193BC5EB46E4B1854F55750FF694.description: Use numbers expressed in the form of a single digit times an integer power of 10 to estimate very large or very small quantities, and to express how many times as much one is than the other.
comments: For example, estimate the population of the United States as 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> and the population of the world as 7 × 10<sup>9</sup>, and determine that the world population is more than 20 times larger.

4D4FAD7411984A5193C484B62C5495AA.description: Use square root and cube root symbols to represent solutions to equations of the form x² = p and x³ = p, where p is a positive rational number. Evaluate square roots of small perfect squares and cube roots of small perfect cubes. Know that √2 is irrational.

6A4E84F215F84CDBBA09666B06EC3673.description: Know and apply the properties of integer exponents to generate equivalent numerical expressions.
comments: For example, 3² × 3<sup>–5</sup> = 3<sup>–3</sup> = 1/3³ = 1/27.

B5A0C955E0864A4A81A43EEE4845331D.description: Understand how to perform operations and simplify radicals with emphasis on square roots.

11048C2E7CAC472A9FC8E56647A298CF.description: Use rational approximations of irrational numbers to compare the size of irrational numbers, locate them approximately on a number line diagram, and estimate the value of expressions (e.g., Π²).
comments: For example, by truncating the decimal expansion of √2, show that √2 is between 1 and 2, then between 1.4 and 1.5, and explain how to continue on to get better approximations.

09EFEC2A76ED42E38160689C414DC4C9.description: Know that numbers that are not rational are called irrational. Understand informally that every number has a decimal expansion; for rational numbers, show that the decimal expansion repeats eventually, and convert a decimal expansion which repeats eventually into a rational number.

E3D29CE43FCC4EE0BAC0FB719917DAEC.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

5813567A712E463F8A1DC5A10B7663EA.description: Look for and make use of structure.

852D640A120D4DD5AF6A6334709B5C61.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

B131D2DA8BFB440AA627218F4335A7C5.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: Utah Core State Standards for Mathematics (K-5)

66C17CEFE3BD497985E842CC850C797E.description: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.

4376272B965D40FABF0F07A5EE55CCA1.description: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size. Recognize right triangles as a category, and identify right triangles.

9B26D23672154740B0D5C061DBF7862A.description: Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, and obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.

44753972AA8E49D895476C76C27B7C7C.description: Solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram in real-world and mathematical problems, for example by using an equation with a symbol for the unknown angle measure.

8C1FDC39F4D0480396F644FFBCB065F0.description: Understand that when an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the angle measure of the whole is the sum of the angle measures of the parts.

04A02D25FD8745739DF78660FE65EBD7.description: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor. Sketch angles of specified measure.

38F569D9A1EC49EBBC89F68A7C341506.description: Understand that an angle that turns through n one-degree angles is said to have an angle measure of n degrees.

A550586E276247A6A81085576CC0829D.description: Understand that an angle is measured with reference to a circle with its center at the common endpoint of the rays, by considering the fraction of the circular arc between the points where the two rays intersect the circle. An angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is called a "one-degree angle," and can be used to measure other angles.

59066CD570504786AFA18A9653E443B6.description: Recognize angles as geometric figures that are formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint, and understand concepts of angle measurement.

15B4DA5334DF4B57AA437FAEAADE0E30.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (halves, quarters, and eighths). Solve problems involving addition and subtraction with like denominators of fractions by using information presented in line plots.
comments: For example, use a line plot to find and interpret the difference in length between the longest and shortest pencils in a classroom.

2936289B6EE34FEEA8448EC56C9840C5.description: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real-world and mathematical problems.
comments: For example, find the width of a rectangular room given the area of the flooring and the length, by viewing the area formula as a multiplication equation with an unknown factor.

21CFE12F47B646AB9DB17AFE68B4F78B.description: Represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale.

46E7BA4F2C594BD2A0D2078245B0422A.description: Include problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit.

54E62A9FEDEC4CF784F0735592CCAD73.description: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money.

8F4DD58497D643389CBBD62BA8433D0B.description: Know relative sizes of measurement units within each system of units (standard and metric), including kilometers, meters, and centimeters; liters and milliliters; kilograms and grams; pounds and ounces; hours, minutes, and seconds. Within a single system of measurement, express measurements in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Record measurement equivalents in a two-column table.
comments: For example, know that one foot is 12 times as long as one inch. Express the length of a four-foot snake as 48 inches. Know that one meter is 100 times as long as one centimeter. Generate a conversion table for feet and inches listing the number pairs (1, 12), (2, 24), (3, 36)

A977B389077F4ED09AB13212864AF0D0.description: Compare two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two decimals refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, for example, by using a visual model.

0DA7D06166CE450BA6DC7F67CAD01823.description: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100.
comments: For example, rewrite 0.62 as 62/100, describe a length as 0.62 meters; locate 0.62 on a number line diagram.

A208545B5B57441A976D855C4D5DCFE5.description: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, and use this technique to add two fractions with respective denominators 10 and 100.
comments: For example, express 3/10 as 30/100, and add 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100.

0122532F686C4230834C2D334F9E0E67.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number
comments: For example, by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem). For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be five people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?

F64EE24C5D5E4518948C4B8374A7C6AF.description: Understand a multiple of a/b as a multiple of 1/b, and use this understanding to multiply a fraction by a whole number.
comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to express 3 × (2/5) as 6 × (1/5), recognizing this product as 6/5. (In general, n × (a/b) = (n × a)/b).

587D7EFD85FF4BE6A7E63D4CE937588A.description: Understand a fraction a/b as a multiple of 1/b.
comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to represent 5/4 as the product 5 × (¼), recording the conclusion by the equation 5/4 = 5 × (¼).

26F9B32D97E54D9199349C8D63F39A3E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction by a whole number.

CB161666255B44B1AED9C3BB9DF516A5.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators
comments: For example, by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

5B91738A559F4D65B2C097E9EB1252B7.description: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators
comments: For example, by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction. For example, 3¼ + 2¼ = 13/4 + 9/4 = 22/4; 3¼ + 2¼ = (3 + 2) + (¼ + ¼) = 5 + 2/4 = 5 2/4, which is equivalent to 22/4.

23C2DBA1003040A69512ED05CA8B0189.description: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way, recording each decomposition by an equation. Justify decompositions, for example, by using a visual fraction model.

C06744B5316344A0B77A08C67AD3EB29.description: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole.

E39881A14C2A4203BB3F0A39104DD600.description: Understand a fraction a/b with a >1 as a sum of fractions 1/b. In other words, any fraction is a sum of unit fractions.

EBDA4A69C4B04E5CB95A85F87026E844.description: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators, for example, by creating common denominators or numerators, or by comparing to a benchmark fraction such as ½. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, for example, by using a visual fraction model.

BBC4B984216E471CAC2B76F679BB8EA1.description: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to a fraction (n × a)/(n × b) by using visual fraction models, with attention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.

C37357587F5F4025B0EE1056F394D46E.description: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

8BBC8F60B8C346678711208A15BF26E0.description: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

A9C242EF1F4C42C89C73AF6933E28D72.description: Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

D9B1039DE57843A7ACB1F2352A324424.description: Use place value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.

1313C8E0B6C24A2CA4BC5CD86DEF5C50.description: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form. Compare two multi-digit numbers based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

ED8AC91002CA45DE9BB9E063A22C8C9A.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right.
comments: For example, recognize that 700 ÷ 70 = 10 by applying concepts of place value and division.

F14462167E4443EE99EBB95384C82899.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten

1F22874E029148A7835ACAF48F64BCB8.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself.
comments: For example, given the rule "add 3" and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.

74C3E5C2666F4582A9A2775EBB4F1537.description: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1-100. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1-100 is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1-100 is prime or composite.

621B7C0903F84422A2CE0465099BF924.description: Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies, including rounding.

9DF3F089C4284E39B04319E927AEE5DE.description: Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity.

E9D8956F676B4D7C8D86B38CED6FFDA9.description: Solve multi-step word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted.

A1169893F3F940E190F016D3FC007943.description: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison
comments: For example, by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.

97743AAD0D4948C7817E7ABD2A65163E.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison (for example, interpret 35 = 5 × 7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5). Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.

78C2993E119D4329B020562782164628.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

6B0F241B66974249A1B7EC5510FA8F77.description: Look for and make use of structure.

78E53B5CDE4B4AD881718237EF1C5F1C.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

5A1BB4A34F5748DE8A9E5B5E4EE13188.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: Utah Core State Standards for Mathematics (K-5)

AB39B9E2C35D45508A911E6D80BAEB41.description: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties.

16292F8D699D4ABA9F481B48E16C556C.description: Understand that attributes belonging to a category of two-dimensional figures also belong to all subcategories of that category.
comments: For example, all rectangles have four right angles and all squares are rectangles, so all squares have four right angles.

7FF6C603EC1F4E13B8BD5B6B08AA7FD7.description: Represent real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane, and interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation.

178AE67DC7604DEB80246F30AB293684.description: Using quadrant one on the coordinate plane, understand that the first number in a coordinate pair indicates how far to travel from the origin in the direction of the horizontal axis, and the second number indicates how far to travel in the direction of the vertical axis, with the convention that the names of the two axes and the coordinates correspond (x-axis and x-coordinate, y-axis and y-coordinate).

A01C0F8A9B30457994DA83C4814198C1.description: Use a pair of perpendicular number lines, called axes, to define a coordinate system, with the intersection of the lines (the origin) arranged to coincide with the zero on each line and a given point in the plane located by using an ordered pair of numbers, called its coordinates.

17A69059BEBD4570AA8913B7B771AFD8.description: Compose and understand the coordinate plane.

8800163CD1DE410395C0625CC2730F42.description: Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two nonoverlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real-world problems.

DCDD37BFD1B741D49A15BCDAEA5CF0FB.description: Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with whole-number edge lengths in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

B0853FB86F334138B7338FB131F949A0.description: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base. Represent threefold whole-number products as volumes
comments: For example, to represent the associative property of multiplication.

F47F0C0E53FB4A519A100A642D058FA8.description: Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real-world and mathematical problems involving volume.

F22642F9DE1F4D44B884CB5B580F70FD.description: Measure volumes by counting unit cubes, using cubic cm, cubic in., cubic ft., and improvised units.

72454818D44D429DA501D4DE8B0EC9FD.description: A solid figure which can be packed without gaps or overlaps using n unit cubes is said to have a volume of n cubic units.

5E61CCC8D590497C8DF445F389DA4BD7.description: A cube with side length one unit, called a "unit cube," is said to have "one cubic unit" of volume, and can be used to measure volume.

5A1A3523760E4B6DAC2FA26C7B2723C9.description: Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures and understand concepts of volume measurement.

63E6CB94E37A4BDEB54FF6E5134B6BBB.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (halves, quarters, eighths). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots.
comments: For example, given graduated cylinders with different measures of liquid in each, find the amount of liquid each cylinder would contain if the total amount in all the cylinders were redistributed equally.

CC013360818645B993CE8ECCF3B90FF6.description: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given measurement system (for example, convert 5 cm to 0.05 m); use these conversions in solving multi-step, real-world problems.

A675DDFF76264BD3988E458FA33CB86F.description: Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers and division of whole numbers by unit fractions, for example, by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
comments: For example, how much chocolate will each person get if three people share ½ lb. of chocolate equally? How many 1/3-cup servings are in two cups of raisins?

69CAE4DA885341E998695F3D2785D912.description: Interpret division of a whole number by a unit fraction, and compute such quotients.
comments: For example, create a story context for 4 ÷ (1/5), and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 because 20 × (1/5) = 4.

FCB42FAD8F1D4B7CB85183F667929672.description: Interpret division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number, and compute such quotients.
comments: For example, create a story context for (1/3) ÷ 4, and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (1/3) ÷ 4 = 1/12 because (1/12) × 4 = 1/3.

2111573EF9C94D398CA68DD280961805.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions. Use strategies to divide fractions by reasoning about the relationship between multiplication and division. Division of a fraction by a fraction is not a requirement at this grade.

029C59A9274A48999190EA73678798A7.description: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, for example, by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.

7270FA785BBF4735BBCC4112171B423F.description: Explain why multiplying a given number by a fraction greater than one results in a product greater than the given number (recognizing multiplication by whole numbers greater than one as a familiar case); explain why multiplying a given number by a fraction less than one results in a product smaller than the given number; and relate the principle of fraction equivalence.
comments: For example, 6/10 = (2 × 3)/(2 × 5). In general, a/b = (n × a)/(n × b) has the effect of multiplying a/b by one.

6DAC03446AB94A90A8642A45F8A8DF5F.description: Compare the size of a product to the size of one factor on the basis of the size of the other factor, without performing the indicated multiplication.
comments: For example, the products of expressions such as 5 × 3 or ½ × 3 can be interpreted in terms of a quantity, three, and a scaling factor, five or ½. Thus in addition to knowing that 5 × 3 = 15, they can also say that 5 × 3 is five times as big as three, without evaluating the product. Likewise they see ½ × 3 as half the size of three.

CF38089208EC49BEB492FACC047CBF9F.description: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. Multiply fractional side lengths to find areas of rectangles, and represent fraction products as rectangular areas.

7AAA2E7BD05546AABC860FE5CE75AFAE.description: Interpret the product (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b equal parts; equivalently, as the result of a sequence of operations a × q ÷ b using a visual fraction model.
comments: For example, use a fraction model to show (2/3) × 4 = 8/3, and create a story context for this equation. Do the same with (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15. (In general, (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd.)

DFAFE65E24224EBB9606837C6E757C9D.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction.

664DC48A77A8423F956ABF9DA55C4428.description: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). Solve real-world problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers, through the use of visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.
comments: For example, interpret ¾ as the result of dividing three by four, noting that ¾ multiplied by four equals three, and that when three wholes are shared equally among four people each person has a share of size ¾. If nine people want to share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds of rice should each person get? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?

85816BA72E8E4704A1D8A76BBDEB375B.description: Solve real-world problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole, including cases of unlike denominators by, for example, using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem. Use benchmark fractions and number sense of fractions to estimate mentally and assess the reasonableness of answers.
comments: For example, recognize 2/5 + ½ = 3/7 as an incorrect result, by observing that 3/7 < ½.

6D49F6A32669429FA31B079B089C9DA5.description: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators.
comments: For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12. (In general, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd.)

C9CD3F2939B24F73AB2D4150B5480A77.description: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. In this standard, dividing decimals is limited to a whole number dividend with a decimal divisor or a decimal dividend with a whole number divisor. Compare the value of the quotient on the basis of the values of the dividend and divisor.

BE71A2B32B154982837812EF7BB703EF.description: Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

2BEE64DF8217475F9B758E83FD0860B7.description: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

C054BAF3674C4B0AAE2675E7FE8BD04A.description: Use place value understanding to round decimals to any place.

8F9D4798E06645E2BD8468FB56137DE6.description: Compare two decimals to thousandths based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

5374CED63A254579B355C9DB13E103E1.description: Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.

B6B90077531949CA800492E37E32E4EC.description: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths.

26B7CE3DEBA24358ABBC7CB40D9638B3.description: Explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10, and explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10. Use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.

3825291E98104C28AE37B40040F9CD08.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.

9EE8C9C3B4094161A1C0E78A42695B99.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten

DD6F50873D1B41ED905D5C8DE34243DE.description: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules. Identify apparent relationships between corresponding terms. Form ordered pairs consisting of corresponding terms from the two patterns, and graph the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane.
comments: For example, given the rule "add 3" and the starting number 0, and given the rule "add 6" and the starting number 0, generate terms in the resulting sequences, and observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other sequence. Explain informally why this is so.

461DA5137F8140E4866C3843FD9C7ACB.description: Interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them.
comments: For example, use conceptual understanding of multiplication to interpret 3 × (18939 + 921) as being three times as large as 18932 + 921 without calculating the indicated sum or product.

1D872DD2A3F24E79862E7688C8A0D86F.description: Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers.
comments: For example, use 2 × (8 + 7) to express the calculation "add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2."

A3654D43F59F472E84F002E7B098C371.description: Write and interpret simple numerical expressions.

762C95149BF94A36854F6CF8D4F4C235.description: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions, and evaluate expressions with these symbols.

29A80A9D123F450BAA57EAFC6FD4CC41.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning. Notice

26056EBD99304D7AA90505CC4AF4D517.description: Look for and make use of structure.

DACEE7FD890F4DD6BD70B2DE981CDCCB.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

F0F1A9B22F6B483DB82DCDC271E777F8.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: Utah Core State Standards for Mathematics (K-5)

EB7F26D95419445F8B3B1704F120BB32.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares; describe the shares using the words halves, thirds, half of, a third of, etc.; and describe the whole as two halves, three thirds, or four fourths. Recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.

8D3586B57D384F0F871CF08C671A9C8E.description: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of squares.

2E6AADD4B2CE447D9B23EFCC5039C67D.description: Recognize and draw shapes having specified attributes, such as a given number of angles or a given number of equal faces. Sizes are compared directly or visually, not compared by measuring. Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.

123CD47FC14B421F807E7EA33442CBE3.description: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put-together, take-apart, and comparison problems using information presented in a bar graph.

3E30627F7C274515B5BD17F019E4A744.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths of several objects to the nearest whole unit, or by making repeated measurements of the same object. Show the measurements by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in whole-number units.

1BEF4E807D5847DEB5621F85148F8267.description: Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately.
comments: For example, if you have 2 dimes and 3 pennies, how many cents do you have?

1A6CB65D67964F3CB13E0C491F00B210.description: Tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m.

39C8147855E946AB8F7A410C3E4A0EF9.description: Represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line diagram with equally spaced points corresponding to the numbers 0, 1, 2… Represent wholenumber sums and differences within 100 on a number line diagram.

321DB799252143139B5A639E2C2A3798.description: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve word problems involving lengths that are given in the same units.
comments: For example, use drawings (such as drawings of rulers) and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

43D56396849047FB89831C1A7E50AA05.description: Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressing the length difference in terms of a standard length unit.
comments: For example, after measuring a pencil and a crayon, a student uses the measurements to determine that the pencil is two inches longer than the crayon.

1FDD6FA29F1A4FE8883ABD06ACA97007.description: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimeters, and meters.

E990EABF4E3B4EE2AB4CF0D1AE66BF4A.description: Measure the length of an object twice, using length units of different lengths for the two measurements; describe how the two measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen.

C39F7B7C7CD54DF3812AC0D23311BE78.description: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, meter sticks, and measuring tapes.

7373804752194DF89036DFBFF3139979.description: Explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations. Explanations may be supported by drawings or objects.

23721E221E674DEE9F46D921EA41855B.description: Mentally add 10 or 100 to a given number 100-900, and mentally subtract 10 or 100 from a given number 100-900.

B7B8CBB1E8EB40CFBE8C21BDB858174C.description: Add and subtract within 1,000 using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method. Understand that in adding or subtracting three-digit numbers, one adds or subtracts hundreds and hundreds, tens and tens, and ones and ones, and that it is sometimes necessary to compose or decompose tens or hundreds.

C5601F40999A41D6949A41C787F00E2C.description: Add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.

45E46C27F34A4E51A1970575E3B8E262.description: Fluently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.

A3FFD69ABDF4494CB0C7D042D9E07F83.description: Compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens, and ones digits, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

35659A817E6D49D1B3937490A31775F8.description: Read and write numbers to 1,000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.

E9159C5B57964D18A692E9DB2E13DCDB.description: Count within 1,000; skip-count by fives, tens, and hundreds.

394E7C63122D4120ADB157C590EAFC17.description: The numbers 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones).

D6D6C75A33D648EAA0943EF0B16A1EE5.description: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens called a "hundred."

2DE40EBFC9564988B573EAC2B1B8EF01.description: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones; for example, 706 equals 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones. Understand the following as special cases:

C733D0ED3815469AA42406781F6D5E52.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten

F4F8D90AE66F4F0CB9A727D913DB1B04.description: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends.

A3F080281BD947BFA0E978F26BF5439B.description: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, (for example, by pairing objects or counting them by twos). Write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.

2C0B55549AB748099CA000A708CB0B14.description: By the end of Grade 2, know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers.

C906839009B04AAE8F81653B53BD07E8.description: Add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies such as counting on; making ten (for example, 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (for example, 13 – 4 = 13 – 3 – 1 = 10 – 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (for example, knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 – 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (for example, adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).

92F962DEF9104E4CBB692E588078CA02.description: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing with unknowns in all positions, for example, by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

52E6CF1CDDBE4EDE968AE6F3DA86CB32.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

DBCA5F0281874217A10C75FA1D83CD2D.description: Look for and make use of structure.

4D93387E51E946F5B96D25186B39E203.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

37003640354D49EE9DBD2088BD1B1487.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: Utah Core State Standards for Mathematics (9-12)

7D649DEE9FA14EC1B4ED5210E939CF25.description: Use permutations and combinations to compute probabilities of compound events and solve problems.

C2C0CFA0079B4EF788BE9F6FAFB31A61.description: Apply the general Multiplication Rule in a uniform probability model, P(A and B) = P(A)P(B|A) = P(B)P(A|B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

A81B0656623B402981AA71C2DEB32058.description: Apply the Addition Rule, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) – P(A and B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

27AD0412F05549EC884FFB2AFC0DB016.description: Understand the conditional probability of A given B as P(A and B)/P(B), and interpret independence of A and B as saying that the conditional probability of B given A is the same as the probability of B.

93020393D0394876AC444B6B4B42EF21.description: Understand that two events A and B are independent if the probability of A and B occurring together is the product of their probabilities, and use this characterization to determine if they are independent.

C8F24C5D77C24FE38C7495F1E9D6133B.description: Statistics — Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability

99EDC2B84D0E47399E5E587AD1EF533B.description: Derive the equations of ellipses and hyperbolas given the foci, using the fact that the sum or difference of distances from the foci is constant.

38F399B335D546B9BF1ED3FBC6D409E5.description: Derive the equation of a parabola given a focus and a directrix.

C0950D0D1E3443E9A22F9369B4438B0F.description: Geometry — Expressing Geometric Properties With Equations

0943A1CB86D74E46AF40241280A51385.description: Give an informal argument using Cavalieri's principle for the formulas for the volume of a sphere and other solid figures.

5209A726A7F049C4B124550BAE730265.description: Prove the addition and subtraction formulas for sine, cosine, and tangent, and use them to solve problems.

B454141ADB0441799F8CA45054916F5B.description: Use inverse functions to solve trigonometric equations that arise in modeling contexts; evaluate the solutions using technology, and interpret them in terms of the context

C0CA5B20CBCA471096B6F9940B02130D.description: Understand that the zero and identity matrices play a role in matrix addition and multiplication similar to the role of 0 and 1 in the real numbers. The determinant of a square matrix is nonzero if and only if the matrix has a multiplicative inverse.

7CECDF050C6F4E13B5AE7C44C3F1FF87.description: Understand that, unlike multiplication of numbers, matrix multiplication for square matrices is not a commutative operation, but still satisfies the associative and distributive properties.

042AE486E2F64B4EBB6097D3C895339C.description: Use matrices to represent and manipulate data, e.g., to represent payoffs or incidence relationships in a network.

977B5917CEF94E87B38AD477C8078A01.description: Compute the magnitude of a scalar multiple cv using ||cv|| = |c|v. Compute the direction of cv knowing that when |c|v ≠ 0, the direction of cv is either along v (for c > 0) or against vs (for c < 0).

1B39B1680B36440D94F4D854D21E2B1D.description: Represent scalar multiplication graphically by scaling vectors and possibly reversing their direction; perform scalar multiplication component-wise, e.g., as c(vx , vy) = (cvx, cvy).

40722317A2DA4E778B03D5ADCDD468E3.description: Multiply a vector by a scalar.

A9D8D927C9C3439EA72284B679B81202.description: Understand vector subtraction v – w as v + (–w), where –w is the additive inverse of w, with the same magnitude as w and pointing in the opposite direction. Represent vector subtraction graphically by connecting the tips in the appropriate order, and perform vector subtraction component-wise.

6963114B293D4CA193F7AC4955417F94.description: Given two vectors in magnitude and direction form, determine the magnitude and direction of their sum.

58CF6DA50B724D3AB263067E4A65C538.description: Add vectors end to end, component-wise, and by the parallelogram rule. Understand that the magnitude of a sum of two vectors is typically not the sum of the magnitudes.

9B650A0FBFEA4F5590B2AC505F7DDE73.description: Solve problems involving velocity and other quantities that can be represented by vectors.

EE8A2C7373CE4F0C9EC0B2F7F9314858.description: Find the components of a vector by subtracting the coordinates of an initial point from the coordinates of a terminal point.

61F1DC320CEB4A72BBE2D57A8B874E10.description: Recognize vector quantities as having both magnitude and direction. Represent vector quantities by directed line segments, and use appropriate symbols for vectors and their magnitudes (e.g., v, |v|, ||v||, v).

39301492B98544E894CCF9743E388809.description: Number and Quantity — Vector and Matrix Quantities

D29A7BF38D074C2EAA18F93332F1D67F.description: Statistics and Probability — Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability

925049484AB44EF582102B75C3965FE4.description: Give an informal argument using Cavalieri's principle for the formulas for the volume of a sphere and other solid figures.

78F4B54BDD574CEABE65E55527230298.description: Prove the addition and subtraction formulas for sine, cosine, and tangent, and use them to solve problems.

3B6E5710493F4F7E99F1BC2125D3D476.description: Use the inverse functions to solve trigonometric equations that arise in the modeling contexts; evaluate the solutions using technology, and interpret them in terms of the context.

E9B8ADD404404A3784A940632D88E717.description: Understand that restricting a trigonometric function to a domain on which it is always increasing or always decreasing allows its inverse to be constructed.

61F55F22A4224E3D8B2A8C8157859C9C.description: Use the unit circle to explain symmetry (odd and even) and periodicity of trigonometric functions.

BD3FFFD02273463FBFC678FFDD3833C0.description: Statistics — Interpreting Categorical and Quantitative Data

9E0C1F932929470BAEC1A684B3F6BC49.description: Apply geometric methods to solve design problems (e.g., designing an object or structure to satisfy physical constraints or minimize cost; working with typographic grid systems based on ratios).

F108B09C29A34EDA85C62A2F64A5C0EC.description: Apply concepts of density based on area and volume in modeling situations (e.g., persons per square mile, BTUs per cubic foot).

B039CB8CED2C4CB6B180AD277EAFFF4C.description: Use geometric shapes, their measures, and their properties to describe objects (e.g., modeling a tree trunk or a human torso as a cylinder).

26E5773888644A15ABDD15DA96DC2B46.description: Understand and apply the Law of Sines and the Law of Cosines to find unknown measurements in right and non-right triangles (e.g., surveying problems, resultant forces).

69BE27E045064F62ACF34495E90E85E9.description: Prove the Laws of Sines and Cosines and use them to solve problems.

03AF31E7D18D4175A1B0D7B48A628607.description: Derive the formula A = ½ ab sin(C) for the area of a triangle by drawing an auxiliary line from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side.

04E16CF83499421CBBE8CD993C14223C.description: Use inverse functions to solve trignometric equations that arise in modeling context; evaluate the solutions using technology and interpret them in terms of context. Limit solutions to a given interval.

B1D3871B49F54638B874F383311EEB26.description: Choose trigonometric functions to model periodic phenomena with specified amplitude, frequency, and midline.

17CFAF7F348042868FB97624AA80D308.description: Use special triangles to determine geometrically the values of sine, cosine, tangent for π/3, π/4 and π6, and use the unit circle to express the values of sine, cosine, and tangent for π – x, π + x, and 2π – x in terms of their values for x, where x is any real number.

314C321B8068440F8C28ABEC62DC1A6A.description: Explain how the unit circle in the coordinate plane enables the extension of trigonometric functions to all real numbers, interpreted as radian measures of angles traversed counterclockwise around the unit circle.

D123A6833DEA433F8601397E61B7B035.description: Understand radian measure of an angle as the length of the arc on the unit circle subtended by the angle.

5483534FBC224138A43BEE23441986B4.description: Interpret the parameters in a linear, quadratic, and exponential functions in terms of a context.

D9991CAE88964C1E9AC10059C35D4A2E.description: For exponential models, express as a logarithm the solution to ab<sup>ct</sup> = d where a, c, and d are numbers and the base b is 2, 10, or e; evaluate the logarithm using technology. 50F253BB5CBE4A1F89AA823D0491EE3E.description: Observe using graphs and tables that a quantity increasing exponentially eventually exceeds a quanitity increasing linearly, quadratically, or (more generally) as a polynomial function.

962892FCB18A428AB48BE4C743F405D2.description: Solve an equation of the form f(x) = c for a simple function f that has an inverse and write an expression for the inverse. Include linear, quadratic, exponential, logarithmic, rational, square root, and cube root functions.
