FCE5CA2C0D3041E1969BE8AB03476798.description: Analyze how two or more texts address similar themes or topics in order to build knowledge or to compare the approaches the authors take.

F470FDE0669C445392D909AD39D4CD76.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.

950459667F084EA2A1B23B1D4D5C165E.description: Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse media and formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words.

7576B8DF8C2740EB85C5E1CBB7D3A88A.description: Assess how point of view or purpose shapes the content and style of a text.

80A31B57638F4788BCE7517FFFA475E3.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

1A21932D9C964B509AC6DEFB334291D0.description: Interpret words and phrases as they are used in a text, including determining technical, connotative, and figurative meanings, and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning or tone.

B899B04F14BD4F3B892EA7DA72618C96.description: Analyze how and why individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over the course of a text.

471CA8FC989C48D3B295923E7D7CED9A.description: Determine central ideas or themes of a text and analyze their development; summarize the key supporting details and ideas.

BC378C08672348D6BAC5F2C1F0CFC09C.description: Read closely to determine what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences from it; cite specific textual evidence when writing or speaking to support conclusions drawn from the text.

6976198C2A97432FB96F59B898A66045.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Reading

B7CC6694C54B4445A56929B173F7EE70.description: Analyze data to determine how a design solution causes a change in the speed or direction of an object with a push or a pull. Define the problem by asking questions and gathering information, convey designs through sketches, drawings, or physical models, and compare and test designs. Examples of problems requiring a solution could include having a marble or other object move a certain distance, follow a particular path, or knock down other objects. (PS2.A, PS2.B, PS2.C, PS3.C, ETS1.A, ETS1.B, ETS1.C)

0B3810D166BD4D18B5AAE9A1DECD83DD.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to compare the effects of different strengths or different directions of forces on the motion of an object. Emphasize forces as a push and pull on an object. The idea of strength should be kept separate from the idea of direction. Non-contact forces, such as magnets and static electricity, will be taught in Grades 3 through 5.(PS2.A, PS2.B, PS2.C, PS3.C)

3481298BE1B241178ECDB3E72B617C85.description:
FORCES, MOTION, AND INTERACTIONS
The motion of objects can be observed and described. Pushing or pulling on an object can change the speed or direction of an object’s motion and can start or stop it. Pushes and pulls can have different strengths and different directions. A bigger push or pull makes things go faster and when objects touch or collide, they push on one another and can change motion.

5E8AE6FFFC6C4ED6AA7D82C197645905.description: Design and communicate a solution to address the effects that living things (plants and animals, including humans) experience while trying to survive in their surroundings. Define the problem by asking questions and gathering information, convey designs through sketches, drawings, or physical models, and compare designs. Emphasize students working from a plant, animal, or human perspective. Examples could include a plant growing to get more sunlight, a beaver building a dam, or humans caring for the Earth by reusing and recycling natural resources. (ESS3.C, ETS1.A, ETS1.B, ETS1.C)

8285A4C923AD44D381F23B13A7301A01.description: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about how living things (plants and animals, including humans) affect their surroundings to survive. Examples could include squirrels digging in the ground to hide their food, plant roots breaking concrete, or humans building shelters. (ESS2.E)

BB5968141FBF43AE92D537792EA49A56.description: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about patterns in the relationships between the needs of different living things (plants and animals, including humans) and the places they live. Emphasize that living things need water, air, and resources and that they live in places that have the things they need. Examples could include investigating plants grown in various locations and comparing the results or comparing animals with the places they live. (LS2.B, ESS3.A)

1EE4871E0C3E4F39A11405608A5D2803.description: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information to describe patterns of what living things (plants and animals, including humans) need to survive. Emphasize the similarities and differences between the survival needs of all living things. Examples could include that plants depend on air, water, minerals, and light to survive, or animals depend on plants or other animals to survive. (LS1.C)

41F881EBFB0B40C0A956F54B5927B325.description: LIVING THINGS AND THEIR SURROUNDINGS: Living things (plants and animals, including humans) depend on their surroundings to get what they need, including food, water, shelter, and a favorable temperature. The characteristics of surroundings influence where living things are naturally found. Plants and animals affect and respond to their surroundings.

5669F29097ED457D801A4E822188EBE5.description: Design a solution that will reduce the warming effect of sunlight on an area. Define the problem by asking questions and gathering information, convey designs through sketches, drawings, or physical models, and compare and test designs. (PS3.B, ETS1.A, ETS1.B, ETS1.C)

74E49C8112AE4E899494188636F734A6.description: Carry out an investigation using the five senses, to determine the effect of sunlight on different surfaces and materials. Examples could include measuring temperature, through touch or other methods, on natural and man-made materials in various locations throughout the day. (PS3.B)

E5C2F319476C445683677B6176AB9B6E.description: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information on the effect of forecasted weather patterns on human behavior. Examples could include how humans respond to local forecasts of typical and severe weather such as extreme heat, high winds, flash floods, thunderstorms, or snowstorms. (ESS3.B)

80586A9E2F314818B84BAC061A32484E.description: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about local, observable weather conditions to describe patterns over time. Emphasize the students’ collection and sharing of data. Examples of data could include sunny, cloudy, windy, rainy, cold, or warm. (ESS2.D)

D66B83C6ACFB406E84E0088BBABDD448.description:
WEATHER PATTERNS
Weather is the combination of sunlight, wind, snow or rain, and temperature in a particular region at a particular time. People measure these conditions to describe and record the weather to identify patterns over time. Weather scientists forecast severe weather so that communities can prepare for and respond to these events. Sunlight warms Earth’s surface.

69535FAAD6E74FD6825ABF88F6CAE9F2.description: Recognize the importance of both "hard" and "soft" skills in the workplace.

84F8373EDE0A42AF967FE4327E45EA4C.description: Investigate different types of occupational training. (For example: Trade school, Community College, University, Graduate Training)

5BF76172DC614E42AA1F09306ED8FE58.description: List and differentiate among different engineering disciplines. (For example: Aerospace, Biomedical, Civil, Chemical, Computer (both Hardware & Software), Electrical, Energy, Manufacturing, Mechanical)

4F8C45C7E1DD4BB59AE5188B060107AD.description: Investigate the USBE's CTE engineering pathway.

71F671380E0C4D7AAE6EC772EE0B3B13.description: Students will investigate future training opportunities and careers in engineering.

EDDF6FC742914BDA9A1E1B9B6FE8F715.description: Mass and energy balances, and chemical reactions.

4DEC41B43A87430F837CF397501902B6.description: Learn and exhibit traits of good citizenship.

CB8E1768D2AE4981BD6FC98396DAA242.description: Recognize and describe geographical features in their community that make it unique (for example, mountains, rivers, lakes, roads).

177B0D6F86684387A97BFDED17F121E6.description: Explain how a globe is a model of the Earth.

216169AB61CC4BDA9DC56D3D6CF4A769.description: Construct a simple map, and explain how the map represents a place.

910737232631480EA8C1A8B022333EE1.description: Demonstrate knowledge of basic physical and human geographical concepts.

9675773C06E54B6892B37684A0784CC1.description: Explain how families provide physical, social, and emotional support and how each family has its own unique history.

94890A3B3B8A475ABF5BD16D412B84A7.description: Use a variety of texts to analyze and retell the stories of a diverse range of key historical figures, including some from United States history, and make inferences about why they are remembered and honored as people who exemplify the traits of honesty, integrity, morality, civility, duty, honor, service, respect, and obedience to law.

2D0C91CFADB040CD9024BC6EDC33109E.description: Understand that history is the study of events, people, and places of other times.

document.title: Utah Core Standards Elementary Social Studies

8C9F1B434C4B4C8797B8E5AA492156F3.description: Identify and explain the roles and contributions of consumers, producers, and distributors in the community.

56679681A50B43A59865ED77C23A1951.description: Identify ways people make a living in the community.

75AEA537E9B2442F9DAF31DBD6AFFAEA.description: Explain the costs and benefits of spending and saving in order to meet needs and wants.

1CBA19797B8D40F0876E9D36284E7D0C.description: Explain how to prioritize their economic wants and make basic financial decisions.

B46E4423C82D4928B55BE2E329F8A7F3.description: Demonstrate characteristics of responsible citizenship (for example, respect others' property, treat people with dignity, find solutions to conflicts, take responsibility for one's actions, take care of school grounds).

765F023FBBAE4A88AB3B788C199CC8F2.description: Identify the symbols, landmarks, and essential documents of the school, community, state, and nation (including the national motto and state emblem). Demonstrate how to show respect for those items, including care and disposal of the United States flag.

5AC739A819EB45A4ADC564C349E513A7.description: Explain how diverse community groups work together to accomplish common tasks, solve problems, and fulfill responsibilities.

E7D0D4389A3F4098BB5D2094DEA8D756.description: Identify the ways that people can function as members of a school and/or community by sharing principles, goals, and traditions.

5F4655D0737A41ECAFD927CF4BD5FA0C.description: Compare how classroom rules are similar to laws in the community.

2D709A1B3AC64B74948876442D2F1721.description: Analyze their role as citizens in a school and a community.

83D162270C2847C88BC2BCB7522DCDDD.description: Explain the reasons that people, animals, and goods move.

BA39CA2E3F5F4B7EA27D0343AE01E578.description: Use maps and globes to locate their local community, Utah, the United States, the seven continents, and the five oceans (that is, Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, South America; Antarctic [Southern] Ocean, Arctic Ocean, Atlantic Ocean, Indian Ocean, Pacific Ocean).

43AB01F389864F9DAE64846E6A1F2E1B.description: Differentiate between natural and engineered geographical features in an area (for example, engineered geographic features include highways, bridges, airports, railroads, buildings, dams, reservoirs).

3AAAA49705204CF49C48CF49B0F07AA0.description: Construct a simple map of a neighborhood, classroom, school, or the setting of a story.

D072F097F8574A9283C42F8C26713508.description: Use geographic tools and map skills to explore the ways geography, climate, and natural resources affect the way people live and work.

C5CE903B605949D4BB9C6F0D8123EE2E.description: Create a primary source to show how their personal histories are shaped by family, school, and community (for example, timeline, interview, artifact collection, recipe book).

99E78D91CD5B4BE581DF984A32B5A63F.description: Use primary sources (for example, artifacts and documents such as photographs, newspapers, speakers, stories, songs) to make inferences about why certain events in history are remembered.

9DBF09B8783A49F0BAFBAB5EBA8A50F9.description: Summarize the contributions of a diverse range of historical figures and groups in their community, state, and nation, and evaluate their significance (for example, figures might be chosen based on their examples of honesty, integrity, morality, civility, duty, honor, service, respect, obedience to law).

26B774BE022A49668F2B5823541004FB.description: Explain why people may see historical events from different points of view.

88B3AAB07C51439CB4C6C252E3519DCF.description: Examine important events and historical figures in the community, state, and nation.

document.title: Utah Core Standards Elementary Social Studies

4776C9F687DD48D48C3EEE6DC33B46EA.description: Identify the specialized work necessary to manufacture, transport, and market goods and services.

161D1EF589E24BDAA2A87E60D5EFB91F.description: Describe how people can be both producers and consumers of local goods and services.

E8BA2020B0024AD5B701EBB647301C82.description: Describe and compare a variety of services provided by local economic institutions, including businesses and non-profit organizations.

9B09542187384606B8F3572D1B2F11C6.description: Explain how scarcity of resources and opportunity cost require people to make choices to satisfy wants and needs.

134A7A5E8D5E4221B2938F802564FA94.description: Explain the benefits of personal savings.

AC757E22C4384971AC691E39A33DCA7D.description: Develop an understanding of basic economic concepts necessary to make informed individual and family decisions. Students use basic economic principles to explain how businesses supply goods and services to consumers.

E8C86E0EE6314E50A19ECE13C032AFE3.description: Identify celebrations and state and national holidays that remember and honor people and events in the history of Utah and the United States.

EF659FDEE28049C8893126E30C0B9C63.description: Identify current leaders (for example, family, school, community, governor, national leaders) and their responsibilities. Discuss the traits of effective leaders.

5F19CBCB10F2475F9914232CB7A8A633.description: Consider why it is necessary for cities and towns to have governments, and describe ways local representative government promotes the general welfare of their community (for example, water, sewer, garbage pick-up, road and trail maintenance, public schools).

2E58C4E4782845B6B13577B5AFEA653F.description: Provide examples of ways in which responsible community members have worked together to resolve conflicts, solve problems, and create unity within their community.

B2967E4105894EE3920A5C07FF094720.description: Describe the rights and responsibilities of citizens in the United States and Utah.

32F9745F990E4ED998F836B9BC08EE86.description: Define the essential qualities of good community members (for example, honesty, integrity, morality, civility, duty, honor, service, respect, and obedience to law).

DAD871AC95214E18B6A5D1B86B61754F.description: Learn about the rights and responsibilities of citizenship, explain how people must work together to resolve conflict, and understand the importance of respecting differences.

EC9709E5127F4001A54ED55A855AAD34.description: On a map of the world, locate where their families or other families in the community historically came from. 0055971F835C4654B4C3313649129970.description: Identify natural resources, and cite ways people show stewardship through responsible use, conservation, protection, and replenishment.

BA1A7BAE4D5B45C79C3C0FE9D1A61E9A.description: Describe and give examples of interdependent relationships between vegetation, animal life, geographic features, and people specific to a local region (for example, irrigation, water conservation, farming, helping neighbors, ranching, providing vegetation that supports pollinators, protection of endangered animals).

A53CDBF7EDB0458CAA29D8CBDE5F791A.description: Describe how location, climate, and physical features affect where people live and work, and how communities modify the environment to meet their needs over time (for example, irrigation, dams, reservoirs, roads, buildings, bridges).

3C8152D9DEFE498193066D461507DD58.description: Identify examples of major geographical features in their local region, state, and country and their significance for the people who live there.

974E2A35FABA4E599108E3940ADC8A8B.description: Interpret and construct physical maps using the title, key, symbols, 8-point compass rose, cardinal directions, and alphanumeric grids.

B598CBDA631449148B731A2BC3358704.description: Locate and identify the poles, equator, continents, oceans, the United States, Utah, and their town or city. Identify and name the states that border Utah and the countries that border the United States.

0BC85DABDFC34A699B1A84C85A2BFA7D.description: Develop an understanding of the relationship between people and their physical environment using geographic tools, technology, and map skills.

D49060753B524327ACD72AB42CDDB112.description: Identify the achievements of significant Americans, including those from local and other diverse perspectives, and explain their importance.

E7B690FFF887493B84F4C6E013D8498E.description: Retell the histories of key people and events connected to state and national symbols, landmarks, and essential documents (for example, Thomas Jefferson and the Declaration of Independence, Francis Scott Key and The Star Spangled Banner, Abraham Lincoln and the Lincoln Memorial, Theodore Roosevelt and Woodrow Wilson and national parks, Utah pioneers and Utah's nickname and motto).

3EA8173605924FCDA8410C89DD5AACF7.description: Summarize key ideas included in the Declaration of Independence (for example, purpose of government, equality, representative government, limited government, rule of law, natural rights, common good).

FA24BAF6719C4E5E99F274C47C20F9F7.description: Use primary sources to identify how their community has changed or remained the same over time, and make inferences about the reasons why.

E7960511E2EF469691D68960D2048531.description: Use primary sources (for example, artifacts and documents such as interviews, photographs, newspapers, speakers, stories, songs) to document the chronology of important events in their personal, family, school, local, or broader community history (including three significant events).

DFBCD21C34F74D0EA7BA5C501E30E16E.description: Use historical thinking skills to explore continuity and change in their community, Utah, and the United States.

document.title: Utah Core Standards Elementary Social Studies

B3A64403C52E434B8D6A595EA8703974.description: Examine how and why the community they chose in 3.4.1 has adapted to and/or modified its environment over time, and identify the consequences of these environmental changes.

B63FF23FB0DF4F5C95952596B67ECC81.description: Examine the types of government found in the community they chose in 3.4.1, and compare them with the government of their community (for example, how community leaders are selected, how the government maintains order, keeps people safe, and makes and enforces rules and laws; the role of a community member; the inclusion of immigrants).

468B00F1C15B4407A5CFF3ACA04181BD.description: Define the cultures of the community they chose in 3.4.1 (for example, art, music, food, dance, system of writing, architecture, government, religion).

8ABB5B78A7D74FBB9BA6F4F02213B4B0.description: Research the geography (that is, physical features and natural resources) of the community they chose in 3.4.1, and make inferences regarding how the geography influenced the cultures that have developed there.

70E4BA28CCC44BE2ADDCBDB70BE32B45.description: Choose a community outside of the United States. Locate that community on both print and digital maps of the Earth, their continent, country, and city or town, and contrast their sizes and the relationships in scale.

9FED0366C64342A0B6EEBB50458B6C41.description: Learn about one or more communities in other regions of the world. Students use what they have learned in the first three Strands about their own community as a basis for comparison. These communities could reflect the diverse heritage of class members and community members.

E75C92B1B289452FA3EC4E41458CD5EC.description: Connecting Your Community To The World

FB4340A5747444CBA7CF4B23DF6E7A21.description: Collaborate with peers to address a need in their local community through service.

9B429F639C7147AE9B0D1B81DEC5014A.description: Discuss how the choices of individuals and leaders affect their community and its future (for example, supporting local businesses, volunteering, voting).

3F9D51E980EA41A5A2B23BC051B225DC.description: Describe why governments collect taxes and how they decide how to use them.

1C5B99301631480180F8D4EA7CE885E0.description: Explain how their community's leaders are elected or appointed and effective ways to work together with them to improve the community.

0B49E731A6874211BB176E664D51FD22.description: Describe some of the civic roles that people fulfill within their community, and explain the reasons why people choose to serve in those roles and how they benefit the community.

C339073E79E04587975DD6A1D662879D.description: Research improvements that have been made in their community over time (for example, schools, roads, emergency services, utilities, jobs, recreation, libraries, clean environment, protection of civil rights).

9106D93C3C3141CCA5230134DF96DEDA.description: Reflect upon the processes used to address needs and reach solutions within their family, their classroom, or other groups of which they are a part. Compare those to the democratic processes used to address needs and reach solutions within their communities.

9BEB5E8B6E79406D8A219B03AD615BA3.description: Analyze how their community has been shaped by the diverse people who have resided within it. Compare primary and secondary sources (when available) from or about these people.

964ECC3FAFE9441DA5B89B7663B3B506.description: Students delineate their civic rights and responsibilities as members of their community and the limits to their rights when they conflict with the rights of others. 364050753B2045DFAF471C1DBEE4066E.description: Evaluate how their community has changed over time (for example, economic interdependence, changes to the environment).

77064A48F82C41EC88DA7A9C9B45F73D.description: Define their own cultures or the cultures of their communities (for example, art, music, food, dance, system of writing, architecture, government to which they are regularly exposed or of which they are part).

4AFC891E726D4126B86B4FE46F07FD5A.description: Describe how geography (that is, physical features and natural resources) has shaped where and how their community developed, how it sustains itself, and how it will sustain itself in the future.

E2A0BA73EF314825BD42007FFCA7FBE5.description: Locate their community, city or town, state, country, and continent on print and digital maps of the earth, and contrast their sizes and the relationships in scale.

C56FE6ABC07F454ABCDA26A48E249101.description: Analyze the communities in which they live, including geography, relative size, and interdependent relationships.

3D31E16CEDC54D628F24CCF1B6436E8E.description: Explain how the Constitution balances power between the three branches of government at both the state and federal levels (checks and balances).

EFDA23D651B34A59A00BEF28CB0245F0.description: Identify the rights protected by the First Amendment in the Bill of Rights, and analyze how those rights affect them.

2F9AFCF17471496C8FF8279559F5051E.description: Summarize how the Constitution of the United States is the supreme law of the land, and explain how laws provide order and stability.

C7CB9044AD7C418887188B3F750AD82F.description: Explain why the first three words of the United States Constitution are vital to the workings of representative government.

ED79C8CB6F9143FCB263BBF5E1C8F52C.description: Discuss the basic differences between different forms of government, including a constitutional republic, a pure democracy, an oligarchy, and a monarchy.

1276678F800D486D9C0415BB12C3136A.description: Identify significant ideas in the United States and Utah Constitutions, as well as compare similarities and differences between the documents.

89E18F4655464F42BA58D732C07F0D13.description: Types Of Government And The United States And Utah Constitutions

document.title: Utah Core Standards Elementary Social Studies

9F5F6F17AA9544FD925B416EE26D96B2.description: Choose one of Utah's cultural institutions (for example Utah Symphony, The Tabernacle Choir at Temple Square, Utah Opera Company, Ballet West, Utah's Shakespeare Festival, Utah Festival Opera), and explain its historical significance as well as the cultural benefits to Utah families and our nation.

CC41B6277460466F8E1BFDDBF1621203.description: After studying examples of individuals or groups making positive changes in Utah, propose positive steps individual students or groups of students can implement (for example, raising awareness through digital media, energy and resource conservation, letter writing, fundraising).

2BFC54AFF98D47718F069EAB8F42817A.description: Explain continuity and change over time by comparing experiences of today's immigrants in Utah with those of immigrants in Utah's past.

9C9C5494ADFB416F90955C4645C41DDE.description: Use data and trends to make recommendations for the best sustainable development of Utah's resources (for example, forests, state lands, geology, coal, minerals, oil and gas, state parks, water, wildlife, School Trustlands).

AE7B729E13714876AE091085AA8DC61E.description: Make a case for the lasting historical significance of an event in recent Utah history (2000–present), and create an argument for including it in a historical text.

C87E2D38E4174034BA0817C5D8CD9DAF.description: Describe sovereignty as it relates to Native American sovereign nations (Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray reservation, Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah, San Juan Southern Paiute Tribe, Navajo (Diné) Nation, Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation, Confederated Tribes of Goshute, Skull Valley Band of Goshute) existing within Utah, and explain efforts to preserve and maintain their culture.

622E9B00D8E443C9909D54CBF64D4DF0.description: Understand that, while forced to make even further adaptations as they came into contact with European explorers, Native Americans still thrive as eight sovereign tribal nations in Utah.

D3C2F37D0B8743B5963D03F76E480F53.description: Recognize that most current events (for example, interactions between Native American sovereign nations and state and federal governments, concerns about water, tensions and questions about the proper role and jurisdiction of local, state, and federal governments, ideas about how best to grow Utah's economy) have their roots deeply embedded in Utah's rich history.

5A221016ABF64FCEABEBE0FCE70C50B3.description: Examine, through a 21st century lens, the enduring central themes of diffusion of cultures, global interconnectedness, the importance of creating and sustaining community, and the need for a strong economy.

F3B613704BDF4B58A63C43901ACADC89.description: Use case studies to explain how national or global events between 1896–1999 (for example, World War I, the Spanish Flu Epidemic, the Great Depression, World War II, Japanese American Incarceration, the Cold War, civil rights movements, Americans with Disabilities Act) had an impact in their local communities and state.

584BC5BFEB2C429CAF99B3959E3260BF.description: Analyze the way local, state, tribal, and federal governments interact with one another.

EAD1330426104EB6BBEC72A4696CA744.description: Use primary and secondary sources to explain how Utah's economy has changed over time (for example, recreation, tourism, mining, information technology, manufacturing, agriculture, petroleum production).

82A9F03538FC45DF8A33B82632914AA8.description: Identify Utah symbols, their connection to history and geography, and what these symbols tell us about our shared culture. Explain how they can show respect and appreciation for those symbols.

5DC66985BDB2482A992F7DA9914A0A0C.description: Compare the Utah Constitution with the United States Constitution, noting the similarities (including legislative, executive and judicial branches, rights of citizens) and important/ significant differences (for example, role in education, public lands, local governance).

F92C882D8BAB4DAF9136B8AB5938DB1E.description: Identify the function and location of state government. Analyze Article 1 of the Utah Constitution to explain how the enumerated rights reflect shared values.

113BC8D1D00E44B994558375268CCB84.description: Identify and explain the cultural connections that Utah's diverse communities share.

56E89DE1FFEC4916BE94903C4F6C8E73.description: Evaluate the roles and functions of different levels and types of governments.

D18F30F7D29F455BA167AABA7251D2FE.description: Study Utah's continued development as a state, including learning about its Constitution and the role of geography in Utah's economy and settlement patterns.

2617E2F8B3EF4EEBB36BE138F9D1B122.description: Explain how the creation of the Transcontinental Railroad and other transportation and communication networks changed Utah's economy and led to greater economic interdependence.

2B956F715556493092F8BC3159B559A3.description: Describe how and why humans have changed the physical environment of Utah to meet their needs (for example, reservoirs, irrigation, climate, transcontinental railroad) between 1847-1896.

15A1185803E34E699A02088470882B04.description: Cite multiple perspectives to explain the historical significance and context of at least one conflict of this period (for example, The Utah War, The Mountain Meadows Massacre, The Bear River Massacre, The Black Hawk War).

BD87A45CA9CA4C788E057EE9897CB95E.description: Identify the political challenges that delayed Utah's statehood, and explain how these challenges were overcome. Describe the involvement of Utah women in the state and national Women's Suffrage Movement.

1FEAC95C4FAC47BFB7A776D60AE04E06.description: Describe the establishment of communities and the economic development of the Great Basin area under the direction of Brigham Young as the first Territorial Governor of Utah.

2C084086DC814D4A8FA4BDE3EFC5D9A0.description: Explain how Utah's physical geography provided opportunities and imposed constraints for human activities between 1847- 1896 (for example, agriculture, mining, settlement, communication, transportation networks) and how people changed the physical environment to meet their needs.

3F6A7D6B91D643A1952CF16ADC0A5800.description: Use primary sources to compare experiences of at least three groups' migration to Utah between 1847–1896 (for example, members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, people from Greece, Italy, China).

9BE51F38CB8C415589B725390115F1DD.description: Learn about the process and challenges Utah faced transforming from a territory to the 45th state.

E601D795A82E417BB9EAA22A0159EDEE.description: Evaluate the relationships between the Industrial Revolution, the completion of the transcontinental railroad, other technologies, and the human and physical geography of the region.

B8DBF2C4A717428B9F20FDBC1DE2530C.description: Learn about some of the implications of this settlement on Native American communities.

837F81B40D9A47009A54D30B299979C9.description: Study the migration of diverse populations who settled across the region that would become Utah.

B1FC58CCA595436BA1CBC2707944824A.description: Students will learn about the unprecedented migration, dramatic cultural change and conflicts, and new technologies of this era.

725FB2798930460A97220B140BCC65D2.description: Investigate the reasons why early explorers and frontiersmen came to the land now called Utah, and determine how their contributions are relevant to Utahns today.

F3278A22826B453BBF524679E11D6114.description: Use primary and secondary sources to compare important aspects of the ways of life of at least two Native American tribal groups (for example, Ute, Paiute, Navajo (Diné), Shoshone, Goshute) existing within the land now called Utah and how those ways of life changed as settlers from Europe arrived prior to 1847.

FE275A5F44894FB59399290DB5914F1F.description: Explain the economic concepts of trade, scarcity, and supply and demand. Apply these concepts in analyzing the economic activity of Native American tribal groups that existed during this period in the land now called Utah and their trade with European-American trappers and traders..

24024B35CCDF4CEB9039FBCF5BF2C6D0.description: Use evidence (for example, artifacts, texts, oral traditions, geographic inquiry) to make inferences about, and explain the importance of, the geography of the land that would become Utah in the culture of one or more prehistoric or historic Native American cultures.

C62A24D69B084A6A86A26FCECA557123.description: Identify the factors that encouraged early trade and exploration among varied explorers and frontiersmen.

E5AD3BC2120B48DF99CD0717BA465795.description: Understand that more adaptations occurred due to contact and trade while Utah was part of the Spanish Empire and later Mexico.

1A87DB0BE6D14DB69B86E3E3E7C2AF05.description: Recognize that for centuries the historic tribal groups of Utah—the Goshute, Navajo (Diné), Paiute, Shoshone, and Ute—adapted to their ever-changing environment.

A193913A34134834BA05F25662EA7859.description: Learn that while recorded history spans only a few centuries, humans have lived in the land now called Utah for thousands of years.

9C322F47AFB34D4B98AD6874E65970E6.description: Describe how the physical geography of Utah has both negative and positive consequences on our health and safety (for example, inversions, earthquakes, aridity, fire, recreation).

506588D437734F69BBB62BC46F829325.description: Examine maps of Utah's precipitation, temperature, vegetation, population, and natural resources; make inferences about relationships between the data sets. Describe how and why humans have changed the physical environment of Utah to meet their needs (for example, reservoirs, irrigation, climate, transcontinental railroad).

C7C3DE6E52DE4EF090FB73F6A9BA7C92.description: Use a variety of geographic tools to identify Utah and its surrounding states: latitude, longitude, hemisphere, climate, natural resources, landforms, and regions (for example, Rocky Mountains, Colorado Plateau, Basin and Ridge Region).

948DEFB677A14C43ADD2D1372F3D9286.description: Evaluate the methods and impact of individuals and/or groups making positive changes in the United States today as models for civic engagement.

EAA9A148E86541FAB86C54CAEBEDF903.description: Investigate and report on current pressing issues facing the United States, and propose potential solutions that they can support (for example, raising awareness through digital media, energy and resource conservation, letter writing, fundraising).

4CBE9B367135405C97E2961FEFCAA7A5.description: Understand current national issues and explore their rights and responsibilities as citizens and residents of the United States.

200C6901A9284D22942E9DBEE137013D.description: Make an evidence-based claim about the role the United States should play as a world power and leader in solving current global problems.

E1F9AD3B4D2B4598A1DF11BAA26BB08F.description: Craft an evidence-based argument for why a particular event should be considered the most significant moment in United States history from 1900–now (for example, Stock Market Crash of 1929, Great Depression, Voting Rights Act of 1965, terrorist attack on 9/11, the launch of the Internet).

29ACB19025904FCABA7935735E3B65FE.description: Compare the motivations for and desired outcomes of the entry of the United States into World War I and World War II.

73DB582C3F194A24966F06CF95F5D80B.description: Compare the motivations for and desired outcomes of U.S. entry into two or more of the wars of the 20th and 21st centuries.

911B462C3FF54F8C855F927BD5FC18CA.description: Examine impactful conflicts, moments, movements, communities, and people of the 21st century. They will analyze the role of the United States as a world power and the effects of its territorial and colonial expansion.

4207AD1564264D1A9CAB86ED9BEB1ACB.description: Identify the Civil War's most important outcomes (for example, end of slavery, Reconstruction, expanded role of the federal government, industrial growth in the North), and explain how outcomes of the Civil War continue to resonate today.

ECFD286BAC2B4710A49666322F1E952D.description: Use evidence from primary and secondary sources to craft an argument that explains how the United States of America prevailed over the Confederate States of America in the United States Civil War.

84681578421A436790A57B00D0475D13.description: Explain how the actions of key individuals and groups influenced the outcome of the Civil War (for example, Abraham Lincoln, Jefferson Davis, Clara Barton, Robert E. Lee, Ulysses S. Grant, Stonewall Jackson, William Tecumseh Sherman, Harriet Beecher Stowe, Rose O'Neal Greenhow, Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman).

5E64D90FB7D24CE48BA78EF944D7C66E.description: Use primary and secondary sources to compare how differences in economics, politics, and culture (for example, slavery, political and economic competition in Western territories) between the North and South led to the United States Civil War.

FCAD3F60E5B34666950885A59434FB72.description: Summarize the impacts of forced relocation and assimilation on Native American people and how they have preserved their communities in the face of such adversity.

FD21D8C9E52B4DD6B2CF5C04DD1F9B32.description: Use evidence from multiple perspectives (for example, pioneers, 49ers, Black Americans, Chinese Americans, Native Americans, new immigrants, people experiencing religious persecution) to make a case for the most significant social, economic, and environmental changes brought about by Westward Expansion and the Industrial Revolution.

A02D9B1FA36C47D495A4FAE6FEB137E2.description: Examine how conflicts and division led to the United States Civil War and the lasting impacts of its outcome.

846ED170FF094475B7BB11A7F61F6787.description: Understand the effects of this expansion and movement on Native American people and the preservation of those communities while facing adversity.

64E09DBAF44D4490A7170155C453E6EC.description: Analyze changes brought by Westward Expansion, the Industrial Revolution, and the movement of people.

823890AE095A4235B1A5EC3E1D7C8639.description: Describe the civic duties members of American society have today (for example, voting, holding public office, jury duty).

142A638516A14D1E8D3C30A1BAA45E58.description: Investigate how constitutional amendments are passed, and provide examples of how amendments to the Constitution have extended rights to groups originally denied protection under the Constitution (for example, women, enslaved people, immigrants, Black Americans, Native Americans).

6151C03871F44CF5B316B846AFC656D4.description: Explain the significance of the Bill of Rights, and identify the impact of one of these amendments in history, a current event, and/or your daily life.

C52420972E614C4BA96C92789DCE4C59.description: Explain why the Founders established a compound constitutional republic with three branches, and cite historic and current examples of checks and balances.

930B114AE4BC4C4DBDA55194063CBC4C.description: Apply the ideals found in the Preamble of the United States Constitution to historic and current events and issues.

683377FC7CA54E2E97D0A7810801E7AE.description: Use examples from the Constitution to investigate and explain the development, general purpose, and significant foundational principles of the United States government (a compound constitutional republic), as well as earlier documents and philosophies used to help develop the Constitution (for example, the Magna Carta, Mayflower Compact, Articles of Confederation, Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy).

3EC92D3E79824D629A934E50DD1E6D81.description: Demonstrate understanding of the Constitution and its relevance in their lives, including the Bill of Rights, the branches of government, and how the Constitution has changed and been interpreted over time.

52C6F02C3AE8430EA45B1F45175E0DE0.description: Use evidence from primary and secondary sources to craft an argument that explains how the American colonists prevailed over one of the world's most powerful empires.

2338A8315D2B4050B36D8BB38E7A89A8.description: Explain how the actions of key individuals and groups influenced the outcome of the American Revolution (for example, George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Thomas Paine, Benjamin Franklin, Mercy Warren, Alexander Hamilton, King George III, Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy, Marquis De Lafayette, Phillis Wheatley).

E0EB4DC2A4B44B6EB7BBE2546AA0D86C.description: Summarize the most significant ideas found in the Declaration of Independence.

ECD0EDECBDDA4C8D9B2B264FEFF0C0B9.description: Use primary sources to craft an argument representing different perspectives during the period leading to the American Revolution (for example, men and women who were Loyalists, Patriots, Native Americans, enslaved people).

7143559F25504FED9E11DA3B8449E7F3.description: Explain how the colonists prevailed in gaining their independence and summarize significant ideas in the Declaration of Independence.

1B41E639E2064396AA4BD31103021D56.description: Recognize how the actions of key individuals influenced the outcome of the Revolution.

EC3ECECC432C4DDA95D550ED30D4018D.description: Examine British colonial policies that led colonists to becoming Loyalists, Patriots, or neutral leading up to the American Revolution.

C08203215A154706931CB354325C39EE.description: Describe how conflicts over land, trade, and alliances sometimes arose during colonization in North America (for example, Bacon's Rebellion, King Philip's War, the French and Indian War).

0A8E7B7E46F84FB9B5FDEED12CC6F9BB.description: Use maps and primary/secondary sources to evaluate the push and pull factors that led to exploration and colonization of North America (for example, fleeing persecution, enslavement, economic advancement, indentured servitude, religious freedom/isolationism).

E8FDE17A130C429A8A8B7E05BB296A20.description: Identify ideas, innovations, and contributions of Native Americans that have had a lasting impact on human civilization (for example, agriculture, respect for the earth and environment, inventions, fashion, art, government, language, medicines, ritual and ceremony).

03D7C72B6C374512B386C275954F228A.description: Evaluate how the Age of Exploration and early colonization opened the way for the global movement of ideas, innovations, foods, and values and how the world was affected in ways that we can still see today.

9F1179B3C8C84423AA557D8B1530DE24.description: Understand how geography had a major impact on the more than 500 tribes and over 50 million indigenous people living in North America prior to European exploration, as well as how it affected methods of exploration.

503CDB59A7A94935B03D8941C53FA892.description: The Impacts Of Geography And Human Interaction In North America (Pre-Contact To Early Colonization)

document.title: Utah Core Standards Elementary Social Studies

6A9FC687AA634A1DBD03299B507459E8.description: Cite current national and/or global events that exemplify the concept of global interconnectedness.

8CD27DC111D14F75813300FD9FA434A8.description: Determine how human rights and responsibilities around the world have developed over time, and identify ways individuals and organizations work to protect rights considered essential for all humans.

D1F7FEC9369845E99A11BE00F17790CB.description: Summarize the main differences between economic systems across the world (including communism, free market capitalism, individualism, socialism). Discuss the relationship between these systems and the concepts of freedom, equality, and fairness.

3C4D89305008450AB73B3B7CC28BA30F.description: Review how human and civil rights have developed over time, and use current events to increase awareness and identify possible solutions.

CD0BEF1B7BF64189832A14C444AE5455.description: Our Modern World (World Religions, Cold War Era, Current Global Events/Issues)

BDA546156EF044E18C6F97E0FC3A48C6.description: Cite evidence to identify the causes and effects of World War I, the Great Depression, and World War II.

51D0A3C6D7C74C26A7C766FF7085EEC1.description: Explain the causes and effects of at least three events that created political, social, economic, industrial, and/or scientific revolution during the 18th–20th century (for example, the French Revolution, Vietnam, Latin American revolutions, the Enlightenment, independence movements of India and African nations).

CEBF043E019B48E3982245315BF05EB6.description: Use primary and secondary sources to draw conclusions about the positive and negative economic impacts of expansion and major global conflicts (for example, Colombian Exchange, economic depressions, rise of factories, effects of famine, slave trade).

2C52A6B77F704A05B361F98810D86D97.description: Describe how the conditions and motivations of exploration, colonization, and/or imperialism around the world connect to globalization.

AA812A26557C4167A7F2C8F65867527D.description: Describe how the political and economic impacts of this time period (c. 1500 C.E.–2000 C.E.) created new political ideologies and technology, providing prime conditions and motivations for colonization, imperialism, and independence that continue to be echoed in current conversations.

A1D3E3648B95494481EDC87F5E7BDB20.description: Identify the most historically significant inventions and innovations from Ca. 500 C.E.–1500 C.E. (for example, printing press/ moveable type, astronomy, medicine), and argue their ongoing importance.

1E11C161CC12419E9B9AD058A9BED80A.description: Use primary and secondary sources to explain how the spread of religious ideas during the post-classical era influenced globalization (for example, spread of Islam, Crusades, cultural expression through art and architecture, Reformation).

CAC39F5D44FF462E972CCDFC02072CDD.description: Summarize key tenets of the major world religions (including Buddhism, Christianity, Confucianism, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism, Sikhism, Taoism).

4012C8B777DE49C2AAA02E509D625CA8.description: Understand how this created and encouraged a global interconnectedness among distant societies and civilizations that ripples into modern history.

760AA9F4F05847F0BB0AED6B02CBF576.description: Compare how the transformation and changes of the post-classical era (Ca. 500 C.E.–1500 C.E.) set in motion the expansion of knowledge through science, language, writing, religion, and technological innovations.

0EF1646383C84296BE4466E21D89615D.description: Use primary and secondary sources to compare the cultures of three civilizations found in different regions of the world and identify examples of cultural expression (for example, architecture, writing, philosophy, artwork).

6E97EF11EE7841BDAD1F4036BBDADEB9.description: Identify some of the economic systems and technologies (for example, irrigation, writing systems, farming techniques, trading and bartering, coins and currency) created by three civilizations found in different regions of the world, and categorize how they met specific human needs or wants.

E8E7C8AF607B4B53B065A2A39E773A1A.description: Throughout their study of world history, recognize the origins of major world religions (including Buddhism, Christianity, Confucianism, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism, Sikhism, Taoism). Evaluate the role religion played in the development of civilizations, colonization, imperialism, and independence movements.

BDE646B884434229A9DDDE9445C6351D.description: Compare early governments to the foundations of modern governments.

0C64D34AAA3B494E9D3DEDDD69CC8ACD.description: Compare how the aspects of geography, culture, religion, government, technology, and systems in ancient civilizations met human needs and wants, as well as allowed and encouraged the growth and development of civilizations as humans migrated across the earth.

420E7955BFE343AD964559DEB6C0F230.description: Cite relevant textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as what inferences can be drawn from the text, including identifying where the text implies ambiguity.

F35D763C766C4CFC9E4267C5A67B44F1.description: Read grade-level text with accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.

0E135BCEED354B18970C65EDFE2BEB9D.description: Convey a clear perspective by concisely presenting and citing information, findings, and supporting evidence so that listeners can follow the line of reasoning.

F3444BF593D940189FCDACB1467CF287.description: Use appropriate language, grammar, organization, development, and delivery styles appropriate to purpose and audience for formal or informal contexts.

1EFA20F299334E6AA62EA25B09CE5084.description: Interpret and evaluate the credibility of multiple sources of information presented in various formats and media to solve problems and make informed decisions.

298B1F95FCED415BAA8AE85C893F87E5.description: Identify contradictions when applicable, and determine if additional information or research is required to deepen the investigation or conversation.

2ECCF1D3A91C48909A4350A20DE60D3B.description: Participate in conversations by asking and responding to questions and provide the opportunity to consider a range of perspectives and clarify, verify, or challenge ideas and conclusions with evidence.

5A7C9A7CC2514F689CA8BF80EEA80414.description: Respond thoughtfully to diverse perspectives in democratic discussions that involve decision-making and role-taking; synthesize comments, claims, and evidence.

9205EB57F04240CBBC04D6E2641A7C4D.description: Participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations on topics, texts, and issues.

document.title: P-12 Utah State Standards for English Language Arts

07CB8799E6A24076BC98669766F906FE.description: Interact and collaborate with others throughout the writing process.

7AED8AEDA92D46EF81AA2B130B8E5EBC.description: Avoid plagiarism by quoting, paraphrasing, and citing, using a standard format for citation of evidence.

17FECA8C56224496AF627D600E5A9ADF.description: Evaluate the evidence and generate ideas to demonstrate understanding of the topic and purpose.

31549190AB8340D59C9C6D50299D216F.description: Gather, assess, and synthesize information from credible sources on the topic.

8C614157F3EB41D4A2A7C6C8E165BE6C.description: Conduct research projects to craft an argument, answer a question, or provide an analysis.

D822F16A83C54E199303DD085ADA1EE1.description: Use appropriate conventions and style for the audience, purpose, and task.

FC1A7C74B94D4EB1951DDBA8FF5DEAEC.description: Apply narrative techniques, such as dialogue, pacing, description, reflection, flashback, and multiple plot lines to develop characters and well-structured event sequences.

B674913E82DC46CE9E5FD6B0B3EA8632.description: Establish one or multiple point(s) of view, and develop a setting, narrator and/or characters.

2569EA644A6A4C8F810403C60E038FFA.description: Engage and orient the reader by describing a complex problem, situation, or observation.

0EFFA975250D4358BD7F19DD5E898564.description: Write narrative texts to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, well-structured event sequences, well-chosen details, and provide a resolution with closure.

2C9F58253A8A48A6943094EADBA6E829.description: Use appropriate conventions and style for the audience, purpose, and task.

7741E9FE069F4989B0343A519945F560.description: Use precise language and content-specific vocabulary to clarify the complexity of the ideas.

585DF6FBA49641029ED2D7B95E2CC997.description: Use appropriate and varied transitions and syntax to link the major sections of the text, create cohesion, and clarify the relationships among complex ideas.

AC1474698D5245AA81F18593C9D67E3E.description: Develop the topic thoroughly with relevant and sufficient facts, extended definitions, concrete details, quotations, examples, and figurative language.

10E37B53313E499D9B17D94DC3E7F3AD.description: Introduce a topic; organize complex ideas and information so that each new element builds on that which precedes it to create a unified whole; utilize formatting, graphics, and multimedia to illustrate complexities.

CBAFEAF7F35146A999C938F812CB6E63.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas and information clearly and accurately through the effective selection, organization, and analysis of content, and provide a conclusion that follows from and supports the information or explanation presented.

FB8B70BA681249D8BD76ED1149C6D5F6.description: Use appropriate conventions and style for the audience, purpose, and task.

F8F12FB348C14F968545620A79AD7C2A.description: Use words, phrases, and clauses as well as varied syntax to link the major sections of the text, create cohesion, and clarify the relationships between claims and reasons, between reasons and evidence, and between claims and counterclaims.

18E48F6EDA17435E86339F6FB5FBEE93.description: Develop claims and counterclaims by interpreting the most relevant evidence from accurate, credible sources for each; elaborate on the strengths and limitations that anticipate the audience.

AD295D9CE07C46CA8719CBEF083AB7D7.description: Introduce claims, establish the significance of the claims, distinguish the claims from alternate or opposing claims, and create an organization that logically sequences claims, counterclaims, reasons, and evidence.

75D57AC01B424CE9B47594EF56060A42.description: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of complex topics or texts, using logical reasoning and relevant, sufficient evidence, and provide a conclusion that follows from and supports the argument presented.

6A19E3F5D70142FFBC8F82A4BCB38A85.description: Analyze and evaluate works of cultural significance for the way in which these works treat similar themes, conflicts, issues, or topics, and maintain relevance for current audiences.

62FCDE7B426640D5B36E8AC5840A8D4F.description: Analyze two or more texts of literary significance across and within time periods with similar topics and themes, drawing on their purposes, stylistic choices, and rhetorical features.

08544D8468A8413F9265E5243D0C703E.description: Delineate and evaluate arguments and specific claims across multiple texts on the same subject, assessing the validity or fallacy of key statements by examining whether the supporting evidence is relevant and sufficient. Recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.

BFCAC004533642BA92321939ADDA632D.description: Analyze how a subject and/or content is presented in two or more mediums by determining which details are emphasized, altered, or absent in each account and how these details influence audiences' experiences and interpretations.

3ACBF3D38DD6406285F783C9B9CEDB47.description: Analyze how an author's geographic location, identity or background, culture, and time period affect the perspective, point of view, purpose, and implicit/explicit messages of a collective body of work.

4866382546494D5F9D8F0C657C2F3D8F.description: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of structures across multiple texts about similar topics/themes, including whether the structures make points or events clear, effective, convincing, or engaging.

D716BE3D720B4695940F1ACC479A34FD.description: Determine and consult appropriate reference materials, to find the pronunciation of a word, its precise meaning, its part of speech, its etymology including Greek or Latin affixes and roots, and its usage.

318FC188BD424BDB9E96BBABA7C1DB4E.description: Analyze patterns of word changes that indicate different meanings or parts of speech.

CF4AC3AA7BE7412BAC882223662440D0.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.

BAA7AFC36E244272ACAA9AEBD55FAA1D.description: Determine the meaning and impact of words and phrases on tone and mood, including words with multiple meanings. Analyze figurative language, connotative meanings, and figures of speech. Examine how the author uses and refines the meaning of domain-specific vocabulary and how language differs across historical time periods, cultures, regions, and genres.

73DFF9880D774D5FA9637478CF9025A4.description: Analyze how the author develops a text through an analysis or argument, including the sequence, the introduction and development and connections of ideas.

8558FD87F7434B42AAD0D37064B85A8A.description: Analyze how an author develops a text through complex and/or dynamic characters, interaction with other characters, and advancement of the plot or development of the theme.

3B180CDB265949D7AB7A33F1327EB497.description: When reading texts, including those from diverse cultures, determine main ideas of two or more texts, analyze the main ideas, supporting details, and the relationship between/among the texts; provide an objective synthesis of the texts that includes textual evidence.

1647CDF5B31249C8BAA7F671731DD705.description: When reading texts, including those from diverse cultures, determine two or more themes and analyze their development, including how they interact and build on one another to produce a complex account, and provide an objective summary that includes textual evidence.

1CDBE200354741C28803D671ACA5537E.description: Cite relevant textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including analyzing where the text implies ambiguity.

A1622D53517544CB9F92A68A9CCB242F.description: Read grade-level text with accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.

5ED3B1FA299645B084D9CB7918AD9ADD.description: Strategically use visual displays of data and digital media, to convey information and enhance understanding of presentations.

BB13AC27607343759BB0A4C1B92D2FF3.description: Use appropriate language, grammar, organization, development, and delivery styles appropriate to purpose and audience for formal or informal contexts.

9B798768DA634F3CB81898E6A16CA5EF.description: Interpret, evaluate, and integrate multiple sources of information presented in various formats and media to verify the credibility and accuracy of each source, and note any discrepancies among the data in order to make informed decisions.

8374161218AE467790FF46AEB5B2DAD4.description: Resolve contradictions when applicable, and determine if additional information or research is required to deepen the investigation or conversation.

298B006320284C6EA3A89F4879499F7D.description: Participate in conversations by asking and responding to questions that examine reasoning and evidence, ensuring the opportunity to consider a range of perspectives, and clarify, verify, or challenge ideas and conclusions with evidence.

6FFA3CAA2685445F89136AC50C812FAE.description: Respond thoughtfully to diverse perspectives in democratic discussions that involve decision-making and role-taking; resolve claims and evidence.

37F6A0E59AAA4201A7BC1AE8A6FC4692.description: Participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations on topics, texts, and issues.

6136B2AE7072451E8EB1256A6DD7404B.description: Design a device in which the structure of the device uses light or sound to solve the problem of communicating over a distance. Define the problem by asking questions and gathering information, convey designs through sketches, drawings, or physical models, and compare and test designs. Examples of devices could include a light source to send signals, paper-cup-and-string telephones, or a pattern of drum beats. (PS4.C, ETS1.A, ETS1.B, ETS1.C)

D581379A296A46459416368ED61D9F97.description: Plan and carry out an investigation to determine the effect of materials in the path of a beam of light. Emphasize that light can travel through some materials, can be reflected off some materials, and some materials block light causing shadows. Examples of materials could include clear plastic, wax paper, cardboard, or a mirror. (PS4.B)

07F17F0EAB474606B65B1991BB0245C7.description: Use a model to show the effect of light on objects. Emphasize that objects can be seen when light is available to illuminate them or if they give off their own light. (PS4.B)

1C005D66B88D4CDCADF050768CE59536.description: Plan and carry out an investigation to show the cause and effect relationship between sound and vibrating matter. Emphasize that vibrating matter can make sound and that sound can make matter vibrate. (PS4.A)

54D5A3C6A4C94380BA22B46780A63632.description: Construct an explanation of the patterns in the behaviors of parents and offspring which help offspring to survive. Examples of behavioral patterns could include the signals that offspring make such as crying, chirping, and other vocalizations or the responses of the parents such as feeding, comforting, and protecting the offspring. (LS1.B)

009393063091429A926B626633A46574.description: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about the patterns of plants and nonhuman animals that are alike, but not exactly like, their parents. An example could include that most carrots are orange and shaped like a cone but may be different sizes or have differing tastes. (LS3.A, LS3.B)

996BB1F2B60A4217812FC186B60254E2.description: Construct an explanation by observing patterns of external features of living things that survive in different locations. Emphasize how plants and nonhuman animals, found in specific surroundings, share similar physical characteristics. Examples could include that plants living in dry areas are more likely to have thick outer coatings that hold in water, animals living in cold locations have longer and thicker fur, or most desert animals are awake at night. (LS1.A, LS1.D)

1BE67424DABB4D988AA8C3D016314A7B.description: Plan and carry out an investigation to determine the effect of sunlight and water on plant growth. Emphasize investigations that test one variable at a time. (LS1.C, LS2.A)

67E2DC1DBEC8407084FBF27B2408E6DF.description: The Needs of Living Things and Their Offspring

B1322746053F4E1AAB4CA08593D724EB.description: Design a device that measures the varying patterns of daylight. Define the problem by asking questions and gathering information, convey designs through sketches, drawings, or physical models, and compare and test designs. Examples could include sundials for telling the time or tracking the movement of shadows throughout the day. (ESS1.B, ETS1.A, ETS1.B, ETS1.C)

DCF64130EB7E4403AA31FFB8EBA33AB4.description: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about the patterns observed at different times of the year to relate the amount of daylight to the time of year. Emphasize the variation in daylight patterns at different times of the day and different times of the year. Examples could include varying locations and regions throughout the state, country, and world. (ESS1.B)

9A4B2A3EECBA4DA8AD4138FB562E36F6.description: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about the movement of the Sun, Moon, and stars to describe predictable patterns. Examples of patterns could include how the Sun and Moon appear to rise in one part of the sky, move across the sky, and set; or how stars, other than the Sun, are visible at night but not during the day. (ESS1.A)

F4B6B6192EA6498689DFFF19826FE236.description: Professional and Ethical Conduct - Treating all with respect and maintaining professional and ethical conduct with students, families and colleagues.

B89F7C13298E49509041A98083E7925E.description: Communication - Using effective and responsible communication with students, families and colleagues about student learning.

B571AEF8D9504E08AE855367E03C8AF5.description: Continuous Professional Learning - Engaging in and valuing constructive feedback, reflective practices, professional learning and collaborative activities that support professional, instructional and schoolwide improvement.

FA99AA59ACD549C9A5C1279713C44573.description: Adherence to Laws, Rules and Policies - Maintaining a current educator license and adhering to relevant laws, rules and policies impacting educators.

D456036E2FC542D097A27648A1EA8656.description: Professional Responsibility: Effective teachers demonstrate an awareness of and adherence to professional and ethical standards within their school and with families and communities by:

779B4FAE23FC44E8AFDA7469BBC3733C.description: Growth-Oriented Classroom Climate - Cultivating a classroom culture that encourages rigorous learning, perseverance and promotes critical thinking.

F166D704E93840E1952AA70B9D5227EF.description: Classroom Organization - Strategically organizing and structuring the physical classroom environment for optimal student learning.

6C4C9FD33A40436AAA8CD0349B3E0163.description: Classroom Safety - Involving students in establishing clear guidelines for behavior that support a developmentally appropriate and safe learning environment while consistently following through with clear expectations, procedures, norms and protocols.

9CF6AC0E47C64324BEAD52F280CBC739.description: Respectful Learning Environment - Modeling and fostering respectful communication with students while appreciating differences of opinion and facilitating respectful classroom discussion.

10A69AD0932C4B6586CAEED5B102184C.description: Classroom Climate: Effective teachers create academic, physical, social, and emotional conditions, with emphasis on academic performance by:

34D198EAD5F048C2B46A78B4991E2099.description: Innovation and Technology - Intentionally selecting the use of technological and non-technological tools to enhance and deepen student learning, encourage creativity and innovation in learning and facilitate students’ appropriate use of available tools and resources to achieve desired student outcomes.

6DF206139D8549D18F154DBD01849612.description: Relevance - Providing relevant learning opportunities that value students’ interests and backgrounds and allow learner agency and choice in accessing learning and demonstrating competency.

664DD15C3FD34AA3A9FD6C93F4AC63EF.description: Assessment Practices - Critically analyzing evidence from both formative and summative assessments to inform and adjust instruction and provide feedback to students to support learning and growth.

6E8759799E8341C581A42545EA97CBAA.description: Instructional Strategies - Using appropriate academic language and evidence-based strategies to stimulate higher-level thinking, discourse and problem solving and to scaffold learning experiences to meet the needs of all students.

54AA2679518441EA99EA0AA4E1E7B4C5.description: Instructional Practice: Effective teachers engage in high quality instructional practices that are data-informed, exhibit a collaborative approach to teaching and learning and meet the learning needs of each student by:

1D32EA06A4D442C6BD61FA87A822C765.description: Engagement - Designing lessons and activities that actively engage students in their learning and use a variety of effective tools and strategies.

1D7D1D6C76D344D2A80843F4A242E61B.description: Instructional Planning - Planning high quality, personalized instructional activities that are informed by student progress data, provide multiple opportunities for students to reflect upon and assess their own growth and allow multiple opportunities and means for demonstration of competency.

62B282783DB742C7AA8940DD8593EC6B.description: Learning Progression - Demonstrating a comprehensive understanding of where students have been, where they are now and where they are going using strategically sequenced learning experiences aligned within and across grade levels.

E568528E31D34EF38AFF3F18A4D6957F.description: Content - Demonstrating a comprehensive understanding of Utah Core Standards, communicating relevance of content, communicating clear pathways to student mastery and designing learning experiences aligned to clear learning intentions and success criteria.

34AFDC7EE55C4213BD56F70B28F42A63.description: Instructional Design Clarity: Effective teachers preview classroom content, demonstrate clarity in how they organize and sequence instruction and effectively plan for learning and student engagement by:

9F31ECBE2F384918BAAE4C3C7AD6145A.description: Fostering Student Self-Awareness - Providing formative and timely feedback to guide students in self-assessment of learning and demonstration of competency to support students in understanding themselves as learners.

AAD2F659F90F4585B9311D6F7072EF17.description: Respecting Learner Backgrounds and Perspectives - Demonstrating respect for each learner and exhibiting actions consistent with recognizing learners’ diverse backgrounds and perspectives as assets to the classroom community.

E0A92BBC2D7549F49BE216ACC9C39E84.description: Building Relationships - Building positive and authentic relationships with students as learning partners and supporting students in developing similar relationships with each other.

3DE4DB394C0B4B05A554F273467F4119.description: Personalizing Learning - Designing learning that builds on background knowledge while providing opportunities for each student to access, practice and refine new learning.

2C64CCB28A594435A37F2E3AC0C40EB0.description: Learners and Learning: Effective teachers demonstrate attention to the impact of unique learner characteristics on development and growth by:

American Sign Language, Oralism, Cued Speech, Bilingualism-Biculturalism,
Total Communication and Signed Exact English.

Education history: French Deaf education in the 1700s, American Deaf

Clerc, Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet, Alice Cogswell, Dr. Mason Cogswell, Edward
Miner Gallaudet, Gallaudet University, Alexander Graham Bell, the Milan
Conference, Public Law 94-142, Deaf President Now protest, Section 504 of
Rehabilitation Act of 1973.

 Cheers, ABC stories, handshape stories, poetry, songs and drama.

Western Union TTYs, modern TTYs, alarm clocks, baby cry signal lights, closed
caption devices, televisions with built-in closed captioning, relay services, door
lights, phone lights, Reveille and cochlear implants.

document.title: STRANDS AND STANDARDS FOOD AND NUTRITION

55E01E6D37FB4CB58A4A3C20FC9C3834.description: Oils – Choose vegetable oils and naturally occurring oils in foods like seafood and nuts.

FF95606F9E6D4FDFBEC0B50E02C0BE89.description: Dairy—Choose a variety of dairy products. Check for added sugars in low fat dairy products.

E9157E8B6A8149B5B7CEBEBB7F15BE51.description:
Fruit—Choose whole or cut-up fruits more often than fruit juice. Make half your plate fruits and
vegetables.

AE6680AC9C9A4277B388356F4490024D.description:
Vegetable—Choose a variety including fresh, frozen, canned, or dried. Eat more red, orange, and
dark green vegetables.

AE1EF8EF54C045F58ADDD5BD144257C4.description:
Protein—Choose a variety of foods from complete and incomplete protein sources. Keep portions
small and lean.

75BF2130F57F4A3891275D7B719D6E6E.description: Grains—Choose 100% whole grain. Make at least half of the grains consumed whole grain.

03488387972F46559B0B9B58B7E16918.description: Identify the characteristics of MyPlate. “Make every bite count.”

03C3CE5F29BB43499DAE3C867B3C5BA3.description: Children and teens should be physically active for at least 60 minutes every day.

4241DB8E18214ABBA55BFEA44EF5DDB8.description: Include physical activity as part of a healthy lifestyle.

3506E71B51424444AD444B8F0E4BD043.description:

saturated fats with very little nutrient value.

7E06874EDA3A4E5DACDF7E58998D9EE1.description: No more than 10% should be from saturated fats.

49697FECA6B9448399B5ABF8EA1198B6.description: No more than 30% lipids—9 calories per gram.

within all food groups in recommended amounts.

AE651B91FF8B42D987E1362B37801B5D.description: Nutrient-dense foods provide vitamins, minerals, and other beneficial substances with relativelyfew calories.

8CA7874166E648DB966034348A808436.description:
Focus on variety, nutrient density, and portion sizes as defined by a nutrition facts label. Nutrition
facts labels are based on a 2,000-calorie diet.

0A09FEDB89C24DDEB742EE72394563B1.description:
Choose a healthy eating pattern at an appropriate calorie level to help achieve and maintain a
healthy body weight, support nutrient adequacy, and reduce the risk of disease.

54A965D1A765499594213DE3DC3C0DFE.description: Students will explore healthy nutrition guidelines.

bruises and have good color.

activities lasting longer than 60 minutes.

Athletes or anyone physically active needs to drink higher quantities of water, particularly in hot
environments (heat of the day).

fruit.
